source_text:
This study was conducted on 42 male rats weighing  $180 \pm 20$  g. ... The rats were randomly divided into six groups each including seven animals... The sham-operated animals underwent laparotomy only without undergoing any procedures or receiving any treatments. Other groups, however, underwent a surgery to induce PUO.

After the rats were anesthetized with ketamine/xylazine ... the abdominal cavity was opened by a midline incision to reach the posterior urethra. claim: In male Sprague–Dawley rats, partial bladder outlet obstruction was induced under ketamine/xylazine anesthesia via a low midline abdominal incision to enter the pelvic cavity, with distal retraction of the prostate, removal of perivesical fat at the level of the bladder neck, circumferential dissection of the prostatic urethra, and passage of a 2–0 silk suture between the urethra and rectum at the level of the bladder neck; the urethra was tightened by tying the silk over a pre-placed 1-mm intraurethral catheter to reduce urethral diameter to nearly 2/3 of original size and prevent complete obstruction, then the catheter was removed and the abdominal incision closed in layers. source_text: “General anesthesia was induced with intramuscular injections of ketamine (44 mg/kg) and xylazine (8 mg/kg). Before the operation, the animals received a single intramuscular injection of gentamicin (1 mg/kg) to prevent infection. Through a low midline abdominal incision, the pelvic cavity was entered. After distal retraction of the prostate, removal of the perivesical fat at the level of the bladder neck, and circumferential dissection of the prostatic urethra, a 2–0 Silk suture was passed between the urethra and rectum at the level of bladder neck. By tying the 2–0 silk material, the urethra was tightened over a pre-placed 1-mm intraurethral catheter. The catheter was placed to reduce the urethral diameter to nearly 2/3 of its original size and to prevent complete obstruction of the urethra. After removing the catheter, the abdominal incision was closed in layers. The rats in the sham group only underwent general anesthesia and abdominal exploration without any intervention on their urinary tract.”

source_text:
Four weeks after the operation and/or treatment, all the animals were killed and their bladders were totally removed and weighted. ...

Contractility of the isolated detrusor strips was measured isometrically by force transducers (K30, Hugo Sachs Electronic, Germany). In one chamber, the strip was treated

by cumulative concentrations of carbachol ( $10^{-7}$ – $10^{-4}$  M) and pEC50 (the negative logarithm of the concentration of carbachol which produced half maximal contraction) and maximum tension (mg tension/100 mg wet tissue weight) were calculated. The other strip was stimulated electrically (Stimulator type 215, Hugo Sachs Electronic, Germany) with 120-S periods of 20 S stimulation and 100 S rest. The stimulation specifications were as follows: frequency 1 HZ, pulse width 2 ms, and voltage 20 % above the threshold. The stimulation was run for about 1–1.5 h, and the mean of the maximum induced tensions was calculated and normalized by dividing the tensions by the wet tissue weight.

All the data were expressed as mean  $\pm$  SD. Comparison of muscular contractility indices between the groups was done using one-way ANOVA followed by LSD post hoc test. ...

The mean bladder weight was significantly higher in the animals with BOO ( $P < 0.001$ ). However, no statistically significant difference was found between the animals receiving PTX and the control group regarding bladder weight (Fig. 1).

... The maximum

carbachol-inducing muscle tension was significantly higher in the sham group in comparison with the rats with BOO ( $P < 0.001$ , Fig. 2). In the latter group, PTX treatment caused no significant improvement in the maximum carbachol-induced muscle tension compared to the control group. However, no significant difference was observed among the study groups concerning the pEC50 of carbachol ( $5.77 \pm 0.10$ ,  $5.96 \pm 0.64$ , and  $5.84 \pm 0.17$  in the sham, control, and treatment groups, respectively).

BOO (control group) resulted in a great but statistically non-significant ( $P = 0.074$ ) decrease in electrically induced bladder contraction in comparison with the sham group.

Rats with BOO treated with PTX (Treated group) showed a significant improvement in the tension of their bladder muscle after electrical stimulation in comparison with animals with BOO (control group) ( $P = 0.023$ ). This value was almost the same as that of the sham group (animals with intact bladder neck) (Fig. 3).

**Fig. 1** The bladder weight in normal rats (normal), rats with partial bladder outlet obstruction (control), and rats with partial bladder outlet obstruction that received pentoxifylline (treated). \* $P < 0.001$  in comparison with the normal group

**Fig. 3** The effect of electrical stimulation on the tension of isolated bladder in normal rats (normal\sham), rats with partial bladder outlet obstruction (control), and rats with partial bladder outlet obstruction that received pentoxifylline (Treated). \**P* = 0.023 in comparison with the control group
verdict_explanation: Directionality and statistical inferences are supported: BOO increased bladder weight (P<0.001) and PTX did not significantly change bladder weight vs BOO control; maximal carbachol-induced tension was higher in sham vs BOO (P<0.001) with no significant PTX improvement vs control; pEC50 values and the stated lack of significant differences are explicitly given; EFS context (1 Hz, 2 ms pulse width, 20% above threshold; 20 s stim/100 s rest cycles) and P=0.074 (BOO vs sham) and P=0.023 (PTX vs BOO control) are supported, and the post-hoc is LSD. However, the candidate’s specific numeric bladder-weight values (~60 mg vs ~230 mg; units) and specific numeric maximal carbachol tension values (~12.5 vs ~3.0–3.5 g/100 mg) are not stated as exact numbers in the text and appear only as approximate readings from the embedded figure renderings; additionally, the methods define maximum tension as "mg tension/100 mg wet tissue weight" (not g/100 mg) and the figure axis/embedded table shows "g tension / 100 mg tissue", creating a unit inconsistency that prevents confirming the candidate’s exact numeric units. Therefore only the qualitative/statistical parts are fully supported.

citation.locator: Discussion (paragraphs beginning “In the present study, we assessed the protective effect of PTX…” and “The findings of the present study showed…”)

claim: In the Discussion, the authors propose/explain that (1) PTX’s beneficial effect could relate to phosphodiesterase inhibition and activation of nitric oxide (NO) synthase, increasing tissue NO and intracellular cGMP; (2) PTX may have antifibrotic effects via enhancing VEGF expression and reducing TGFβ1 expression; and (3) because PTX improved detrusor contractions in response to electrical stimulation but did not improve carbachol-stimulated contractions, they assume PTX’s protective effects are not via cholinergic nerves but instead are related to purinergic or other non-cholinergic, non-purinergic pathways.
source_text:
“In the present study, we assessed the protective effect of PTX on bladder dysfunction in rats with partial BOO. PTX is a potent anti-inflammatory and antioxidant agent. As an inhibitor of phosphodiesterase and activator of nitric oxide (NO) synthase, PTX increases the level of tissue NO and intracellular cGMP. These mechanisms can describe the promising effect of PTX on improvement of contractile abilities of cardiac papillary muscles after ischemic injury [6]. The same effect has been seen on improvement of contractility of ischemic skeletal muscles [7]. PTX also has antifibrotic effects which were mediated by enhancing the expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and reducing the expression of TGFβ1. This protective antifibrotic characteristic of PTX has been elucidated on prevention of tubulointerstitial tissue fibrosis in rats with unilateral ureteral ligation [15–17].

The findings of the present study showed that PTX improved detrusor muscle contractions in responses to electric stimulation in obstructed bladder. In contrast, no improvement was detected in contractile responses to the carbachol stimulation. Therefore, it was assumed that the protective effects of PTX were not via cholinergic nerves, but were related to the purinergic or other non-cholinergic, non-purinergic pathways.”
verdict_explanation: Supported in Discussion as proposed/explanatory mechanisms: PDE inhibition + NO synthase activation with increased NO/cGMP; anti-fibrotic effects framed via VEGF up and TGFβ1 down; and the inference from electrical stimulation vs carbachol dissociation leading to an assumption of non-cholinergic (purinergic or other NANC) pathways. However, the candidate claim adds an additional proposed mechanism—“protection of microvascular perfusion against cyclic ischemia–reperfusion injury”—that is not explicitly proposed as a mechanism of PTX’s effect in the Discussion (the Discussion describes ischemia/reperfusion and perfusion issues generally, but does not explicitly attribute PTX’s effect to protecting microvascular perfusion against cyclic ischemia–reperfusion injury).
readiness_reason: The original candidate claim is compound and includes at least one unsupported mechanism element (explicit PTX protection of microvascular perfusion against cyclic ischemia–reperfusion injury). Split into supported children for witness construction.

claim: In sham-operated rats (n=3), intravenous pentoxifylline (50 mg/kg body wt) infused over 30 minutes decreased mean arterial pressure from 114 ± 3 mm Hg to 94 ± 3 mm Hg at the end of infusion; mean arterial pressure was restored to preinfusion levels 20 minutes after pentoxifylline administration was completed. Heart rate increased from 417 ± 18 to 473 ± 32 beats/min at the end of infusion and returned to preinfusion level within 10 minutes after pentoxifylline administration was completed. source_text:
**Fig. 1.** Effects of intravenous administration of pentoxifylline (PTX, 50 mg/kg body wt during 30-minute period) on mean arterial pressure (MAP, A) and heart rate (HR, B) in sham-operated group up to 60 minutes after PTX administration. There were three animals in this portion of experiment. Data are presented as mean  $\pm$  SEM.

**Effects of pentoxifylline on mean arterial pressure and heart rate.** As shown in Fig. 1, A), mean arterial pressure before pentoxifylline infusion in the sham-operated group was  $114 \pm 3$  mm Hg, and it decreased to  $94 \pm 3$  mm Hg at the end of pentoxifylline infusion (30 minutes after infusion). This moderate reduction in mean arterial pressure, however, was transient, and it was restored to preinfusion levels at 20 minutes after pentoxifylline administration was completed (Fig. 1, A). Between July 2007 and January 2009 we analysed retrospectively 21 men diagnosed as having nonbacterial CP with DV. ...

claim: He et al. report that, after urodynamic testing, pelvic floor biofeedback (PFB) for these 21 men with dysfunctional voiding used an anal electrode to record EMG and measured abdominal pressure via a 6 F balloon catheter in the rectum; sessions lasted ≈30 minutes, were administered twice or three times per week, and after nearly 10 weeks the NIH-CPSI and uroflowmetry with EMG were repeated; throughout the biofeedback sessions, antibiotics, α-blockers, and anticholinergic agents were suspended.
source_text:
Urodynamics was conducted according to the recommendations of the ICS after discontinuation of all drugs for 3–5 days.

PFB was used by patients with DV after the urodynamic tests. An anal electrode was used to record the EMG. The abdominal pressure was measured through a 6 F balloon catheter in the rectum. Patients were maintained in the optimum position for pelvic floor relaxation and were taught to void while sitting, with the thighs spread to relax the perineum, the back straight and tilted slightly forward. They were taught to perceive differences in relaxation and contraction of the anal sphincter, and instructed to constrain it while simultaneously keeping the abdominal pressure curve stable. Each session lasted ≈30 min, was administered twice or three times a week, and could be done intermittently for several weeks. After nearly 10 weeks, the NIH-CPSI and uroflowmetry with EMG were repeated to evaluate the results. Throughout the sessions, all the antibiotics, α -blockers and anticholinergic agents were suspended.
verdict_explanation: Supported: 21 patients; PFB after urodynamic tests; anal electrode for EMG; abdominal pressure via 6 F balloon catheter in the rectum; sessions ≈30 min; frequency twice or three times/week; reassessment after nearly 10 weeks; antibiotics, α-blockers, and anticholinergics suspended during sessions. ## CONCLUSIONS

There might be DV in patients with chronic prostatitis and lower urinary tract symptoms. Urodynamics showed a low  $Q_{max}$  and increasing intravesical pressure and, in some patients, increasing urethral pressure. claim: In a retrospective chart review of patients seen by benign urologists at one ambulatory clinic from April 2022 to September 2022, 120 patients were referred to PFPT; the flowchart reports 73 (60.8%) scheduled an appointment, 46 (~38.3%) did not schedule, and 1 (0.83%) was scheduled outside a 6-month window. In the RESULTS text, 74 (8.1% of total, 62% of referred) were scheduled. Among those who scheduled, 52 attended, 14 cancelled, and 8 were no-shows. The CONCLUSIONS state that approximately 1/12 patients are referred to pelvic floor PT.
source_text:
**METHODS:** This was a retrospective chart review of patients seen by benign urologists at one of our ambulatory clinics from April 2022 to September 2022 using ICD codes for BPH, OAB, LUTS, CP/CPPS, Pelvic Pain/PFD, Chronic Bladder Pain and Urinary Urgency.

**RESULTS:** 74 (8.1% of total, 62% of referred) were subsequently scheduled for a PT appointment. Of the patients who scheduled an appointment, 52(5.7% of total, 70.3% of scheduled) attended their

appointment, 14 patients cancelled their appointment (1.5% of total, 18.9% of scheduled), and 8 patients were a ‘no show’ (0.9% of total, 10.8% of scheduled). Only 1 patient (0.11% of total, 0.83% of scheduled) was scheduled outside of a 6-month window. The mean wait time between referral and appointment was 54.7 days (SD=37.3, Range=1-215).

CONCLUSIONS: At our institution, approximately 1/12 patients are referred to pelvic floor PT and over half of referred patients follow through with at least one therapy visit. Barriers to therapy include low referral rates, long wait times for therapy appointments, and difficulties for patients to complete scheduled appointments due to cancellations and no-shows.

claim: Kaplan et al. report a retrospective analysis of video urodynamic studies in 43 men aged 23–50 years (mean age 36.7) with chronic voiding dysfunction secondary to pseudodyssynergia. In the ABSTRACT Results, symptom duration is reported as 17–146 months (mean 43.6), while in the RESULTS section symptom duration is reported as 17–146 months (mean 33.6). In RESULTS, 39/43 (91%) were firstborn men; 38/43 (88%) had symptoms longer than 1 year; all 43 had previously been treated with antibiotics, with 40/43 (93%) receiving more than 1 course; average previous antibiotic days ranged 53–186 (mean 67.6). Both ABSTRACT Results and RESULTS state that empirical trials of α-blockers were unsuccessful.
source_text:
ABSTRACT

"Materials and Methods: The video urodynamic studies of 43 men 23 to 50 years old with chronic voiding dysfunction secondary to pseudodyssynergia performed between January 1990 and June 1996 were retrospectively analyzed." ...

"Results: Of the patients 39 (91%) were firstborn men. Duration of symptoms ranged from 17 to 146 months (mean 43.6). Average number of previous antibiotic days ranged from 53 to 186 (mean 67.6). In addition, empirical trials of  $\alpha$ -blockers were unsuccessful."

RESULTS

"Mean age of the 43 men was 36.7 years (range 23 to 50) and 39 (91%) were firstborn men. The duration of symptoms ranged from 17 to 146 months (mean 33.6) and 38 men (88%) had symptoms for longer than 1 year. All 43 men were previously treated with antibiotics, with 40 (93%) receiving more than 1 course. Average number of previous antibiotic days ranged from 53 to 186 (mean 67.6). In addition, empirical trials of  $\alpha$ -blockers were unsuccessful."
verdict_explanation: Supported: retrospective analysis of 43 men age range 23–50 and mean age 36.7; firstborn 39/43 (91%); symptom-duration discrepancy (Abstract mean 43.6 vs Results mean 33.6) with same range 17–146 months; symptoms >1 year 38/43 (88%); all previously treated with antibiotics; >1 antibiotic course 40/43 (93%); antibiotic days mean 67.6 range 53–186; α-blocker trials reported as unsuccessful. verdict_explanation: All mean±SD baseline measures (AUA symptom score 17.5±3.7; maximum flow rate 13.3±4.2 ml/s; detrusor pressure at maximum flow 46.3±13.7 cm water; detrusor contraction duration 132.8±27.7 s) and all categorical counts/percents (detrusor instability 17/43 [40%]; bladder outlet obstruction 30/43 [70%]; impaired detrusor contractility 13/43 [30%]; acontractile 0/43 [0%]) are explicitly reported in ABSTRACT and/or RESULTS. The operational definitions in MATERIALS AND METHODS also match the candidate with one material repair: the source states BOO requires "radiographic evidence of prostatic obstruction" (not generic urethral narrowing), and the BOO sustained detrusor contraction threshold is "more than 45 cm. water" (not ≥45). The detrusor instability definition (phasic increase at least 15 cm water or associated with increased urgency), impaired detrusor contractility definition (Pdet <30 with catheterized flow <12; and 30–45 with flow <12 considered impaired for classification), and pathologic detrusor contraction duration association statement (>120 seconds associated with increasing AUA symptom scores and urodynamic evidence of BOO) are supported.
readiness_reason: Statement and association are explicitly described; can be compressed without losing meaning.
original_claim: Kaplan et al. (1997) report baseline measures in the 43 men including AUA symptom score 17.5±3.7, Qmax 13.3±4.2 mL/s, Pdet at Qmax 46.3±13.7 cm H2O, and detrusor contraction duration 132.8±27.7 s; they also classify urodynamics as detrusor instability in 17/43 (40%), bladder outlet obstruction in 30/43 (70%), impaired detrusor contractility in 13/43 (30%), and acontractile detrusor in 0/43 (0%). The study’s operational thresholds include: detrusor instability as nonvolitional phasic detrusor pressure rise ≥15 cm H2O (or associated with uninhibited urgency), bladder outlet obstruction requiring sustained detrusor contraction >45 cm H2O with catheterized max flow <12 mL/s plus radiographic urethral narrowing, impaired detrusor contractility defined by peak detrusor pressure <30 cm H2O with catheterized flow <12 mL/s (or low pressure/low flow with Pdet 30–45 cm H2O and flow <12), and pathologic detrusor contraction duration defined as >120 seconds.

claim: Kaplan et al. report that men with pseudodyssynergia were treated with behavior modification and external sphincter EMG biofeedback using the Incare PRS 8900 unit; each session lasted 20–30 minutes, occurred once or twice weekly, and could be done intermittently for several weeks. Success was defined a priori as at least a 50% decrease in symptoms on 2 consecutive office visits. They report that 35 of 43 patients (83%) achieved a 50% symptom decrease by 3 months (with AUA symptom scores in these men decreasing from 18.4 at baseline to 7.6 at 3 months and 8.1 at 6 months). The Abstract instead states the 83% figure at 6 months, creating an internal discrepancy in timepoint attribution.
source_text:
Biofeedback training with the Incare PRS 8900* unit was used to treat the men. Therapy was designed to teach patients to recognize and correct pelvic floor contraction during voiding. Biofeedback was performed by instructing patients to relax the pelvic floor muscles during voiding. Patients were shown the activity during resting and voiding, and essentially instructed to mimic sphincteric activity demonstrated during the relaxation phase throughout the voiding cycle. The patient visually monitored muscle activity of the contraction and relaxation phases during treatment. Each session lasted 20 to 30 minutes, occurred once or twice a week and could be done intermittently for several weeks. Success was defined as a decrease in symptoms of at least 50% on 2 consecutive office visits.

Behavior modification and biofeedback were successful in decreasing symptoms by 50% in 35 patients (83%) at 3 months. For these men AUA symptom scores decreased from 18.4 to 7.6 and 8.1 at 3 and 6 months, respectively.

Behavior modification and biofeedback were successful in decreasing symptoms in 35 patients (83%) at 6 months.
verdict_explanation: Supported: device name (Incare PRS 8900), session length (20–30 minutes), frequency (once or twice a week), duration (intermittently for several weeks), and success definition (≥50% symptom decrease on 2 consecutive office visits). Supported: 35/43 (83%) with timepoint discrepancy (Abstract says 6 months; Results says 3 months) and the responder AUA symptom scores (18.4 baseline; 7.6 at 3 months; 8.1 at 6 months). Not supported: the explicit nonresponder count "8/43 (17%)" is not stated in the source text, though it is arithmetically implied; per instructions this portion is unestablished in-source.

citation.locator: INTRODUCTION (paragraph beginning “The fate of men with detrusor underactivity after prostatic surgery (TURP)…”)

claim: Rademakers et al. (2016) report that, in studies they cite as [13,14], men with detrusor underactivity who underwent TURP (mean follow-up 14.5±3.2 years) and age-matched untreated men with detrusor underactivity (mean follow-up 13.6±3.3 years) had no significant long-term advantages of TURP vs untreated with respect to LUTS, Qmax, or PVR; TURP patients had a lower BOOI at follow-up, but higher PVR, lower voiding efficiency, and more chronic urinary retention.
source_text:
The fate of men with detrusor underactivity after prostatic surgery (TURP) or age-matched untreated men with detrusor underactivity has been well investigated [13,14]. After a minimum follow-up of 10 years (mean follow-up of  $14.5 \pm 3.2$  years in men with TURP and  $13.6 \pm 3.3$  years in untreated men), patients with TURP did not show any significant LUTS improvement compared with the preoperative situation and, additionally, no significant change of maximum urinary flow rate ( $Q_{\max}$ ), PVR, voiding efficiency or any other voiding parameter, bladder contractility index ( $BCI = P_{\det, q_{\max}} + 5Q_{\max}$ ) included. Compared with untreated patients with detrusor underactivity, men with TURP had no significant advantages in the long term with regard to the type

or amount of LUTS,  $Q_{\max}$ , or PVR. Although patients with TURP had a significantly lower BOO-grade at follow-up [bladder outlet obstruction index (BOOI)  $9 \pm 11.9$  vs.  $14 \pm 15.3$  cm H<sub>2</sub>O,  $P = 0.008$ ], PVR was even significantly higher ( $80 \pm 172$  vs.  $217 \pm 336$  ml,  $P = 0.049$ ), voiding efficiency significantly lower ( $82 \pm 28$  vs.  $58 \pm 29\%$ ), and more patients suffered from chronic urinary retention.
verdict_explanation: The INTRODUCTION explicitly supports the follow-up durations; the statements of no significant LUTS/Qmax/PVR advantages vs untreated; and the BOOI/PVR/voiding efficiency comparisons plus “more patients suffered from chronic urinary retention.” However, the candidate claim mis-states the direction/order of the PVR values: the source says “$80 \pm 172$ vs. $217 \pm 336$ ml” while also stating TURP PVR was higher, implying 217±336 corresponds to TURP and 80±172 to untreated—whereas the candidate assigns 217±336 to TURP and 80±172 to controls but then places the numbers in the opposite order within the parenthetical. Also, the candidate adds BVE (BVE term) and BCI comparison vs untreated; the source uses “voiding efficiency” and does not report a between-group BCI comparison at follow-up. The candidate also asserts the review is summarizing “Thomas et al. (2004, 2005)” specifically; the review cites [13,14] but does not name Thomas in this paragraph. No denominators (n) for TURP/control groups are provided in this paragraph.
readiness_reason: Although the source supports the main comparative findings, the original candidate contains material direction/order errors for PVR and adds elements not explicitly stated here (BVE terminology, between-group BCI, and explicit attribution to “Thomas et al.” in this paragraph). A witness-ready FRD should be rebuilt from the repaired wording only.
original_claim: Rademakers et al. (2016), summarizing Thomas et al. (2004, 2005), report that in men with baseline detrusor underactivity followed long term after TURP (mean follow-up 14.5±3.2 years) versus age-matched untreated DU controls (mean follow-up 13.6±3.3 years), there was no significant long-term improvement in LUTS or in Qmax, PVR, bladder voiding efficiency (BVE), or BCI, and no long-term advantage versus untreated controls; despite a lower BOOI after TURP (9±11.9 cmH2O vs 14±15.3 cmH2O in controls, P=0.008), the TURP group had higher mean PVR (217±336 mL vs 80±172 mL, P=0.049), lower mean BVE (58±29% vs 82±28%), and a higher proportion with chronic urinary retention.

claim: In Osman et al. (F1000Research 2016), the authors state that an expert consensus group proposed a working definition for underactive bladder (UAB) as: “...a symptom complex suggestive of detrusor underactivity and is usually characterised by prolonged urination time with or without a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying, usually with hesitancy, reduced sensation on filling, and a slow stream”. They also state there are clear difficulties defining UAB symptoms that do not overlap significantly with LUTS due to benign prostatic enlargement (BPE). Separately, in Open Peer Review, reviewer Peter F.W.M. Rosier comments that the cited UAB working definition would be exactly identical to a bladder outflow obstruction (syndrome) working definition if introduced nowadays; he concludes the UAB syndrome is not specific and that underactive detrusor contraction during voiding is only assessable with a pressure-flow study.
source_text:
“There has been some debate about whether a symptom complex is associated with DUA, referred to by some as the underactive bladder (UAB), which is rather analogous to detrusor overactivity (DO) and the overactive bladder (OAB) symptom complex. This is certainly an attractive concept, as it could, in theory, allow patients to be diagnosed and treated on the basis of symptomatology. Nevertheless, there are clear difficulties in defining a specific set of symptoms that do not overlap significantly with LUTS due to benign prostatic enlargement (BPE). Clearly in women this is less likely to be problematic given the relatively rare occurrence of obstructive causes. A working definition for UAB was recently proposed by an expert consensus group: “...a symptom complex suggestive of detrusor underactivity and is usually characterised by prolonged urination time with or without a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying, usually with hesitancy, reduced sensation on filling, and a slow stream”2.”
...
“careful reading of the working definition cited from reference 2 in the commentary makes it obvious that the working definition of (the) bladder outflow obstruction (syndrome) would be exactly identical, if it was introduced nowadays. The elements of the working definition for UAB (as a signs and symptoms syndrome) are equal to those considered, both currently and traditionally, very relevant in men with benign prostatic enlargement1. I conclude that the underactive bladder syndrome as it is suggested here is not specific, like all LUTD-syndromes, and that, indeed, underactive detrusor (contraction during voiding) is a condition only assessable with a pressure-flow study.”
verdict_explanation: The candidate’s quoted UAB working definition is present verbatim in the "Signs and symptoms" section, attributed to an expert consensus group, and Osman et al. explicitly note difficulty due to symptom overlap with LUTS from BPE. The Open Peer Review comments by Dr. Peter Rosier do state the UAB definition elements are identical to bladder outflow obstruction (syndrome) descriptors and conclude UAB syndrome is not specific and that underactive detrusor contraction is only assessable with pressure-flow study. Material repair: the candidate adds “bladder outlet obstruction (BOO)” and “without pressure-flow validation” phrasing; Rosier’s text uses “bladder outflow obstruction (syndrome)” and states “only assessable with a pressure-flow study.” Also, calling the definition “expert-consensus working definition of underactive bladder (UAB)” is accurate, but describing it as “of underactive bladder (UAB) as a symptom complex suggestive of detrusor underactivity” is already in the quote; the repaired claim keeps that exact framing and separates Osman et al. statements from Rosier’s reviewer commentary.
readiness_reason: mechanical check: the validator's source_text was not found in the named source file (none); Repaired claim is directly and verbatim supported by clearly attributable passages from Osman et al. and from Rosier’s named peer-review report, with clear separation of author statements versus reviewer commentary and correct locators.

citation.locator: ## Diagnostic aspects > ### Detrusor contraction strength > #### 2. Projected isovolumetric pressure (PIP)

claim: Osman et al. describe Schäfer’s projected isovolumetric pressure (PIP) as PIP = pdet@Qmax + K·Qmax, where K depends on population and differs between men and women; in men it is usually taken as 5. They list suggested PIP contractility groupings (>150 strong; 100 to 150 normal; 50 to 100 weak; <50 very weak). They also state that reported PIP variants include the bladder contractility index (BCI), described as essentially the same as PIP but with different groupings, and that these formulae may overestimate PIP and have less test-retest reliability than measuring isovolumetric pressures directly.
source_text:
The PIP was proposed by Schäfer, who used a straight line to represent the BOR and then “projected” back to the y-axis ( $p_{det}$ ) from the point representing  $p_{det@Q_{max}}$  to obtain the isovolumetric pressure. This projection is calculated by the formula  $PIP = p_{det@Q_{max}} + KQ_{max}$  where  $K$  is a fixed constant representing the steepness of the angle of the BOR to x-a axis<sup>28</sup>.  $K$  is dependent on the specific population studied and differs between men and women<sup>29</sup>; in men it is usually taken as 5. The suggested groupings for PIP are as follows:

- >150 – strong contractility
- 100 to 150 – normal contractility
- 50 to 100 – weak contractility
- <50 – very weak contractility

There are two other reported variants of the PIP: the detrusor coefficient (DECO), which is the PIP divided by 100, and the bladder contractility index (BCI), which is essentially the same as PIP but with different groupings. The main advantage with these formulae is that they are easy and quick to use; however, they may overestimate PIP and have less test-retest reliability than measuring isovolumetric pressures directly<sup>30</sup>.
verdict_explanation: Supported: PIP formula; statement that K differs by population and sex and is usually 5 in men; the four PIP contractility cutoffs; mention of BCI as a variant and the limitation statement that these formulae may overestimate PIP and have less test–retest reliability than direct isovolumetric measurement. Not supported in this source: the candidate’s explicit equation for BCI ("BCI = pdet@Qmax + 5·Qmax") and the cutoff "BCI<100" defining detrusor underactivity; the text only says BCI is essentially the same as PIP but with different groupings, without giving the BCI formula or thresholds.
readiness_reason: After removing unsupported specifics (BCI formula and BCI<100 cutoff), the remaining claim is directly and fully supported by the quoted PIP section.

citation.locator: Abstract; 2.3. Experimental procedure

claim: In this porcine model, animals underwent a rapid fixed-volume hemorrhage of 26 mL/kg (stated as 40% blood volume), followed by induction of peritonitis; resuscitation was started at 1 hour. Animals were randomized to pentoxifylline vs control; at the start of resuscitation, the pentoxifylline group received 20 mg/kg IV bolus in 30 mL water followed by 20 mg/kg in 30 mL infused over 60 minutes, while control animals received 30 mL 0.9% saline as both bolus and infusion; investigators were blinded to treatment.
source_text:
Abstract

"Using a porcine model of abdominal trauma resulting from the combined insults of haemorrhage and infection, a randomised placebo-controlled trial was conducted of pentoxifylline (20 mg/kg bolus followed by 20 mg/kg infusion over 1 h) administered in addition to a colloid resuscitation regimen." ... "Female Large White pigs (45–60 kg) were bled 40% of their blood volume and peritonitis was induced using E. coli (O18: K1: H7) in an autoclaved faecal suspension."

2.3. Experimental procedure

"All animals underwent a rapid fixed-volume haemorrhage (26 ml/kg = 40% blood volume). On completion of the haemorrhage, peritonitis was induced using the faecal inoculum. All animals were resuscitated at 1 h with 3.5% polygeline (Haemacel®, Hoechst Roussel Ltd., Uxbridge, UK) with a volume identical to that of the blood removed." ... "Animals were randomised to a pentoxifylline-treated or control group. Simultaneously with the commencement of resuscitation the pentoxifylline-treated group were given a 20 mg/kg bolus of pentoxifylline in 30 ml water followed by a further 20 mg/kg of pentoxifylline in 30 ml infused over 60 min. Control animals received 30 ml 0.9% saline as both the bolus and infusion. Investigators were blinded to the treatment that each animal received."
verdict_explanation: Supported: (a) 40% hemorrhage equals 26 ml/kg; (b) resuscitation at 1 h; (c) dosing and volumes (20 mg/kg bolus in 30 ml water + 20 mg/kg in 30 ml over 60 min). Not supported/overstated: the candidate specifies "sterile water" (source says "water") and describes the model as "fixed-volume hemorrhage ... followed by polymicrobial peritonitis" whereas the paper describes peritonitis induced using a defined E. coli strain in an autoclaved faecal suspension (not explicitly labeled polymicrobial here). The candidate also infers total dose "40 mg/kg over 1 hour" (arithmetically true from stated regimen but not explicitly stated as total dose), and says controls received "vehicle" (source specifies 0.9% saline). Double-blind/blinding is supported ("Investigators were blinded..."). Provisional evidence label PRECLINICAL is correct for an animal (pig) experiment.
readiness_reason: mechanical check: the validator's source_text was not found in the named source file (none); After removing/avoiding unsupported descriptors ("polymicrobial", "sterile", and explicit total-dose summary) and using the source-specified control solution (0.9% saline), the claim is directly and fully supported by quoted text with clear locators.
original_claim: In a porcine model of fixed-volume hemorrhage (40% of calculated blood volume; 26 mL/kg) followed by polymicrobial peritonitis, resuscitation began 1 hour after hemorrhage/peritonitis induction and the pentoxifylline group received 20 mg/kg IV bolus followed immediately by 20 mg/kg IV infusion over 60 minutes (total 40 mg/kg over 1 hour), while controls received vehicle under double-blind conditions.

“In the pentoxifylline-treated group, marked pharmacological effects on the cardiovascular system were noted both during and immediately following the drug infusion. In particular, it attenuated improvements in MAP and MPAP accompanied by a fall in both SVRI and PVRI. There was a marked metabolic acidosis. Overall, pentoxifylline degraded many of the beneficial effects of volume replacement therapy.”

“With the known vasodilatory action of pentoxifylline, particularly on vasoconstricted vessels [8,9], the reduced vascular resistance and arterial pressures seen in the pentoxifylline-treated group were not surprising. The lactic acidosis probably resulted from cellular hypoxia due to a reduction in tissue perfusion.”

“It was concluded that a 'therapeutic window' existed during which pentoxifylline could potentially produce a beneficial effects.”

“In summary, it has been shown that, when given simultaneously with a colloid regimen during the resuscitation from the combined insults of haemorrhage and infection, pentoxifylline reduced vascular resistance and worsened the hypotension associated with ‘septic shock’.”

“Whatever its mechanism of action, the pharmacological effects of high-dose pentoxifylline observed in the present study are unlikely improve tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery.”

“However, with the dosing regimen used in the current study, pentoxifylline should not be considered as an adjunct to a volume replacement therapy in the resuscitation of trauma patients.”

claim: In the “Combination Therapy” section, Bortnick et al. (2019) reports that the MTOPS trial (3047 men; average age 62.6 years [SD 7.3]) found finasteride+doxazosin improved voiding symptoms and maximum urinary flow rate more than either agent alone, and that MTOPS showed combination therapy prevented BPH progression better than either agent alone and reduced long-term risk of acute urinary retention and need for invasive therapy. The review further reports that these results were confirmed in the CombAT trial (men >50 with symptomatic BPH; 58% of patients were >65 years), in which combination dutasteride+tamsulosin had greater risk reduction in acute urinary retention or BPH-related surgery and greater reduction in relative risk of clinical progression than either monotherapy. (The review does not state CombAT enrolled 4,844 men.)
source_text: The medical therapy of prostate symptoms (MTOPS) trial studied the combination of finasteride (alpha-blocker) with doxazosin (5-alpha reductase inhibitor) in 3047 men with average age 62.6 years (SD 7.3 years) and found that the combination improved voiding symptoms and maximum urinary flow rate more than either agent alone. MTOPS also showed that combination therapy prevented the progression of BPH better than either agent alone and reduced the long-term risk of acute urinary retention and need for invasive therapy [21]. These results were confirmed in the CombAT (Combination of Avodart and Tamsulosin) trial, a multicenter, randomized, double-blind study in men over 50 years old with symptomatic BPH comparing the combination of tamsulosin and dutasteride to either agent alone. Fifty-eight percent of the patients were over 65 years old. Combination therapy had greater risk reduction in acute urinary retention or BPH-related surgery and greater reduction in the relative risk of clinical progression than either agent monotherapy [22].
verdict_explanation: Supported: the review attributes to MTOPS that combination therapy was superior to either agent alone for improving voiding symptoms and maximum urinary flow rate, preventing BPH progression, and reducing long-term risk of acute urinary retention and need for invasive therapy; it explicitly states MTOPS enrolled 3047 men. claim: In this pilot study in cancer patients, controlled-release pentoxifylline 400 mg was administered orally every 8 hours for up to 3 weeks. Across 8 treatment occasions in 7 patients, the post-treatment TNF/actin values shown in Fig. 3 were obtained after 1 week of drug administration. source_text:
*Treatment plan.* A dose of 400 mg controlled-release pentoxifylline was administered orally every 8 h for up to 3 weeks, with meals or snacks in order to mitigate gastrointestinal side-effects [9, 25]. TNF RNA levels and weights were followed weekly. ...

Seven patients were treated on eight occasions with pentoxifylline; 4 patients for 1 week, 2 for 3 weeks, and 1 was cycled through the drug twice, i.e. 1 week on, 2 weeks off, then 1 week on again. ...

**Fig. 3.** TNF/actin ratios in cancer patients before (*Pre*) and after (*Post*) pentoxifylline treatment. The post-treatment values were obtained after 1 week of drug administration. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells were collected before and after treatment

On all three occasions when initial TNF/actin ratios were greater than the normal range determined in healthy volunteers, pentoxifylline suppressed these ratios dramatically within 1 week of treatment (Figs. 3, 4). On all five occasions when TNF/actin ratios did not differ significantly from those of normal volunteers, pentoxifylline did not lower the ratios to subnormal values.

source_text:
After informed consent was obtained, four healthy volunteers were treated orally with 5  $\times$  400 mg PTX/day (Hoechst Corp., Frankfurt, Germany) for 2 days, or continuously for 7 days, subsequently referred to as *in vivo* application. For isolation of PBMC, blood samples were obtained by venipuncture with heparinized syringes before treatment and immediately after ingestion of the last of the five daily PTX doses. In addition, PBMC were isolated from volunteers under PTX for 48 hr on day 7 after initiation of PTX and from volunteers under PTX for 7 days on day 14 after initiation of PTX.
...
Statistical analysis was performed by using the Student's *t*-test. Differences below  $P < 0\cdot 05$  were regarded as significant.
...
To test the *in vivo* effects of PTX on cytokine production, PBMC were obtained from healthy volunteers ingesting 5  $\times$  400 mg PTX orally for 48 hr. Blood samples were collected before PTX application as well as on days 2, 7 and 14 after PTX initiation. PBMC were cultured for 24 hr without any stimulus, and supernatants harvested and tested for IL-1 $\beta$ , IL-6, IL-8 and TNF- $\alpha$ . When cytokine levels were compared to those detected immediately before PTX application (100%), TNF- $\alpha$  levels were found to be significantly reduced after 2 days, while IL-1 $\beta$ , IL-6 and IL-8 were not affected (Fig. 1a). In contrast, PBMC obtained on day 7, i.e. 5 days after the stop of PTX application, appeared reduced in their capacity to release IL-1 $\beta$ , IL-6, IL-8 and TNF- $\alpha$ . Cytokine amounts released by PBMC obtained after 14 days, i.e. 12 days after stop of PTX application, were almost in the same range of PBMC collected on day 0 (Fig. 1a).
...
**Figure 1.** (a) *In vivo* effects of PTX on constitutive cytokine release. PTX was applied orally  $5 \times 400$  mg/day for 2 days. PBMC were isolated before the beginning of PTX treatment as well as 2, 7 and 14 days thereafter. PBMC were cultured without any stimulus for 24 hr and supernatants tested for IL-1 $\beta$ , TNF- $\alpha$ , IL-6 and IL-8. Results are expressed as percentage change compared to the data obtained on day 0 (100%; IL-1 $\beta$ ,  $64 \pm 8$  pg/ml; TNF- $\alpha$ ,  $59 \pm 7$  pg/ml; IL-6,  $630 \pm 90$  IU/ml; IL-8,  $950 \pm 122$  pg/ml). (b) *In vivo* effect of PTX on LPS-induced cytokine release. PBMC were treated identically as in (a), but cultured in the presence of  $1 \mu\text{g/ml}$  LPS (100%; IL-1 $\beta$ ,  $649 \pm 72$  pg/ml; TNF- $\alpha$ ,  $1330 \pm 155$  pg/ml; IL-6,  $2228 \pm 239$  IU/ml; IL-8,  $4447 \pm 498$  pg/ml). Significantly different from control (day 0), \* $P < 0.01$ , \*\* $P < 0.001$ .
...
Due to the surprisingly late suppression of IL-1 $\beta$ , IL-6 and IL-8 (i.e. 5 days after stop of PTX ingestion), PTX was applied for 7 days (5  $\times$  400 mg orally) and PBMC collected on days 0, 7 and 14 after PTX initiation. The secretion patterns were similar; TNF- $\alpha$  levels were found to be reduced in supernatants of PBMC obtained on day 7, while IL-1 $\beta$ , IL-6 and IL-8 were not affected (Fig. 2a). In contrast, on day 14 (i.e. 7 days after PTX was stopped) all four cytokines were significantly reduced.
...
**Figure 2.** (a) *In vivo* effects of continuously applied PTX on constitutive cytokine release. PTX was applied orally  $5 \times 400$  mg/day for 7 days. PBMC were isolated before the beginning of PTX application as well as 7 and 14 days thereafter. PBMC were cultured without any stimulus for 24 hr and supernatants tested for IL-1 $\beta$ , TNF- $\alpha$ , IL-6 and IL-8. Results are expressed as percentage change compared to the data obtained on day 0 (100%; IL-1 $\beta$ ,  $54 \pm 7$  pg/ml; TNF- $\alpha$ ,  $50 \pm 7$  pg/ml; IL-6,  $490 \pm 61$  IU/ml; IL-8,  $780 \pm 91$  pg/ml). (b) *In vivo* effects of continuously applied PTX on LPS-induced cytokine release. PBMC were treated identically as in (a), but cultured in the presence of  $1 \mu\text{g/ml}$  LPS (100%; IL-1 $\beta$ ,  $408 \pm 61$  pg/ml; TNF- $\alpha$ ,  $1462 \pm 168$  pg/ml; IL-6,  $2653 \pm 298$  IU/ml; IL-8,  $4075 \pm 428$  pg/ml). Significantly different from control (day 0), \* $P < 0.01$ , \*\* $P < 0.001$ .
verdict_explanation: Correct on: n=4 healthy volunteers; oral PTX 5×400 mg/day; PBMC cultured 24 hr; TNF-α significantly reduced at the immediate post-treatment timepoints in each regimen (day 2 for 2-day regimen; day 7 for 7-day regimen) while IL-1β/IL-6/IL-8 not affected at those immediate timepoints; delayed broader suppression reported after discontinuation (day 14 for the 7-day regimen), and near-baseline by day 14 for the 2-day regimen. claim: In ventilated young Yorkshire swine given a 1-hour intravenous infusion of live Pseudomonas aeruginosa to induce sepsis, pentoxifylline (PTX) was administered as a 20-mg/kg IV bolus followed by a 6 mg/kg per hour infusion until the end of the 5-hour experiment. PTX timing groups included: starting PTX 15 minutes prior to the bacterial infusion; starting PTX immediately following termination of the 1-hour bacterial infusion (at 1 hour into the experiment); and starting PTX 1 hour after the bacterial infusion. In the delayed-treatment group (starting PTX 1 hour after the bacterial infusion; i.e., 2 hours after onset of the P aeruginosa infusion), 50% mortality (2/4) occurred and the group enrollment was stopped at four animals; the two deaths occurred within 1 hour of starting PTX infusion and were associated with profound systemic hypotension.
source_text:
### EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN

Six groups of animals were studied. Group 1 swine (control, n=8) received a 1-hour intravenous infusion of sterile saline solution. Group 2 swine (sepsis, n=8) received a 1-hour intravenous infusion of live *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, PAO strain (5×10^8 colony forming units per milliliter at 0.3 mL/20 kg per minute). Three further groups of animals with sepsis were studied, each receiving a 20-mg/kg bolus of pentoxifylline (Hoechst-Roussel, Somerville, NJ) followed by an infusion (6 mg/kg per hour) until the end of the experiment. Group 3 swine (pretreatment pentoxifylline, n=6) commenced the pentoxifylline regimen 15 minutes prior to the bacterial infusion. Group 4 swine (posttreatment pentoxifylline, n=6) received the bolus of pentoxifylline immediately following the termination of the bacterial infusion at 1 hour into the experiment. Group 5 swine (delayed treatment pentoxifylline, n=4) commenced pentoxifylline treatment 1 hour after the bacterial infusion for 2 hours. Group 6 swine (control pentoxifylline, n=3) received the pentoxifylline regimen only. All groups were studied for a total of 5 hours.

## RESULTS

In the delayed treatment group (group 5), we observed a 50% mortality rate, and therefore, the study in this group was terminated at four animals. Profound hypotension developed on initiation of pentoxifylline infusion in the two animals that died, with neither animal surviving beyond 3 hours. ... Because of the small numbers in the delayed treatment group, no statistical conclusions could be obtained and the data have not been included in this article.

... 

In our studies, the administration of pentoxifylline 2 hours after the onset of sepsis produced a 50% mortality rate in the four animals studied. Both animals that died did so within 1 hour of the onset of pentoxifylline infusion when profound systemic hypotension occurred.
verdict_explanation: Supported: animal model (ventilated young Yorkshire swine), live P aeruginosa given as a 1-hour IV infusion; PTX regimen (20-mg/kg bolus + 6 mg/kg per hour infusion until end of experiment); PTX timing groups including 15 minutes prior to bacterial infusion, immediately after termination of bacterial infusion at 1 hour, and delayed start 1 hour after bacterial infusion (= 2 hours after onset of sepsis); and delayed group had 50% mortality (2/4), with deaths within 1 hour of starting PTX and associated with profound hypotension, and the group was stopped at four animals. Not supported as stated: the source does not explicitly state the delayed-treatment start time as 'when overt septic shock was established' nor that deaths occurred 'within 1 h of PTX infusion initiation' in the RESULTS section specifically (the 'within 1 hour' detail is stated in COMMENT); also the candidate claim says PTX infusion was for the full 5-hour study for all PTX groups, whereas the text specifies in group 5 that they commenced treatment 1 hour after the bacterial infusion for 2 hours (even though earlier it says infusion until end of experiment generally).
readiness_reason: The original candidate includes an unsupported characterization ('overt septic shock was established' at the delayed-start timepoint) and an internal dosing-duration inconsistency for group 5 (source says PTX infusion until end of experiment generally, but also states group 5 commenced treatment 1 hour after bacterial infusion for 2 hours). A witness-ready FRD should be split/reworded to avoid these unresolved specifics.
original_claim: In ventilated young Yorkshire swine given a 1-hour i.v. infusion of live Pseudomonas aeruginosa to induce sepsis/lung injury, pentoxifylline was dosed as a 20 mg/kg i.v. bolus followed by 6 mg/kg/h continuous i.v. infusion for the 5-hour study; starting PTX 15 min before sepsis or at 1 h after sepsis onset (immediately after the 1-hour bacterial infusion) was studied, but starting PTX at 2 h after sepsis onset (1 h post-bacterial infusion, described as when overt septic shock was established) led to severe immediate systemic arterial hypotension and 50% mortality (2/4 animals died within 1 h of PTX infusion initiation), with the group terminated early due to death.

### 2.3. Experimental procedure

All animals underwent a rapid fixed-volume haemorrhage (26 ml/kg = 40% blood volume). On completion of the haemorrhage, peritonitis was induced using the faecal inoculum. Animals were randomised to a pentoxifylline-treated or control group. Simultaneously with the commencement of resuscitation the pentoxifylline-treated group were given a 20 mg/kg bolus of pentoxifylline in 30 ml water followed by a further 20 mg/kg of pentoxifylline in 30 ml infused over 60 min. Control animals received 30 ml 0.9% saline as both the bolus and infusion.

source_text:
Oelke *et al.* published a nomogram, in which men can be simultaneously classified with regard to bladder outlet resistance (BOOI) and detrusor contractility ( $W_{max}$ ) [23\*]. This nomogram was developed with urodynamic data of 822 treatment naïve men aged 40 or older who were clinically classified as LUTS/BPO (means of age 64 years, prostate volume 40 cm<sup>3</sup>, and IPSS 16). ... Therefore, patients in the area of the 10th and 25th percentiles would be classified as detrusor underactivity (Fig. 2C).

**FIGURE 2.** Development of a nomogram for simultaneous classification of bladder outlet resistance (bladder outlet obstruction index, BOOI; x-axis) and bladder contractility (maximum Watts factor; y-axis). First, BOOI-maximum Watts factor data points of individual patients ( $n = 822$ ) were plotted into the diagram (a), the percentiles calculated (b) and, finally, statistically compared. Men in the area of the 10th and 25th percentiles are significantly older, have significantly greater bladder capacity, higher postvoid residual urine, and lower voiding efficiency. Therefore, the 25th percentile line indicates the threshold for detrusor underactivity (grey = danger zone, c).

In MATERIAL AND METHODS, they describe it as an 11-week program with six biweekly 1-hour visits using an EMPI Innova Clinical EMG System with surface electrodes in a specially designed brief; patients were instructed to do the same pelvic floor contraction/relaxation exercises at home three times daily. Bladder training used an initial target voiding interval set as the 75th percentile of the patient's maximum daytime voiding interval from a 24-hour diary; patients attempted this interval for the next 2 weeks, and at subsequent visits if compliance was >80% the interval was increased by 30 minutes, with the overall goal of progressively increasing the voiding interval toward a target of not less than 4 hours. In the ABSTRACT, the program is described as a 12-week program.
source_text: **ABSTRACT (Objectives).** "Based on this hypothesis, we enrolled 19 patients with CPPS in a 12-week program of biofeedback-directed pelvic floor re-education and bladder training." ... **MATERIAL AND METHODS.** "The biofeedback program is a standardized protocol of bladder training combined with pelvic floor re-education. It is an 11-week program comprised of six biweekly visits, each lasting 1 hour." ... "At all visits, a noninvasive method of biofeedback monitoring of pelvic floor muscular activity is used to help the patient identify muscular activity in the pelvic floor muscles. The biofeedback apparatus is an EMPI Innova Clinical EMG System, Version 1.25. This apparatus is used with a specially designed brief that contains surface electrodes for EMG recording." ... "The patient is instructed to perform the exercises at home, three times daily, using the same combination of fast and slow contractions and relaxations as during the instructional session." ... "At the first visit, the patient's 24-hour voiding diary is reviewed and a target voiding interval, which is the 75th percentile of the patient's maximum daytime voiding interval, is selected as the initial target. The patient is instructed to try to void at that interval or greater throughout the waking hours for the next 2 weeks." ... "At each subsequent visit, the patient's voiding log is reviewed and if the compliance is greater than 80%, the interval is increased by 30 minutes." ... "During the course of the program, the nurse therapist works with the patient to accomplish three goals: (1) teach the patient to focus attention on the pelvic floor, and to learn to selectively contract and relax these muscles; (2) teach the patient to perform these exercises on a daily basis to interrupt a syndrome of chronic pelvic myofascial pain; and (3) work with the patient to progressively increase the voiding interval toward a target of not less than 4 hours."
verdict_explanation: Supported: standardized protocol; noninvasive surface-EMG biofeedback with brief electrodes; 11-week program; six biweekly 1-hour visits; home exercises three times daily; initial interval target as 75th percentile of maximum daytime interval from 24-hour diary; 2-week attempt; >80% compliance threshold; +30 minute increases; overall target not less than 4 hours; ABSTRACT also describes a 12-week program. Minor repair: the original claim said patients followed targets "that were increased if log compliance exceeded 80% toward an interval not less than 4 hours"—the source specifies this review and adjustment occurs "at each subsequent visit" and increases by 30 minutes when compliance is >80%, with <80% leading to reassessment rather than automatic progression.

claim: In Clemens et al. (2000), mean follow-up was 5.8 months. Using the Wilcoxon signed-ranks test, median AUA symptom score improved from 15.0 to 7.5 (P=0.001), median AUA bother score decreased from 5.0 to 2.0 (P=0.001), median visual analog urgency score decreased from 5.0 to 2.0 (P=0.002), and median voiding interval increased from 0.88 hours to 3.0 hours (P=0.003).
source_text:
**Results.** Mean age of the 19 patients was 36 years (range 18 to 67). Four patients completed less than three treatment sessions, 5 patients completed three to five sessions, and 10 attended all six sessions. **Mean follow-up was 5.8 months. Median AUA symptom scores improved from 15.0 to 7.5 ( $P = 0.001$ ), and median bother scores decreased from 5.0 to 2.0 ( $P = 0.001$ ).** Median pain scores decreased from 5.0 to 1.0 ( $P = 0.001$ ), and **median urgency scores decreased from 5.0 to 2.0 ( $P = 0.002$ ). Median voiding interval increased from 0.88 hours to 3.0 hours ( $P = 0.003$ ).** ...

Complete post-treatment follow-up was obtained in 16 patients with a mean follow-up of **5.8 months** after the last biofeedback session (median 3.5, range 1.6 to 14.8).

Following treatment, questionnaires and voiding logs were repeated to assess the success of therapy. Differences between pre-treatment and post-treatment symptom scores and voiding frequencies were calculated using the **Wilcoxon signed-ranks test.**

Box plot of AUA SYMPTOM SCORE (n=16) comparing PRE and POST scores. ... The median score decreases from **15.0** at PRE to **7.5** at POST. **The p-value is 0.001 (Wilcoxon signed-ranks).**

Box plot of AUA BOTHER SCORE (n=14) comparing PRE and POST scores. ... The median score decreases from **5.0** at PRE to **2.0** at POST. **The p-value is 0.001 (Wilcoxon signed-ranks).**

Box plot of VISUAL ANALOG URGENCY SCORE (n=15) comparing PRE and POST scores. ... The median score decreases from **5.0** at PRE to **2.0** at POST. **The p-value is 0.002 (Wilcoxon signed-ranks).**

Box plot of DAYTIME FREQUENCY (n=11) comparing PRE and POST scores. ... The median voiding interval increases from **0.88** at PRE to **3.0** at POST. **The p-value is 0.003 (Wilcoxon signed-ranks).**
verdict_explanation: All reported medians and p-values for AUA symptom score, AUA bother score, visual analog urgency score, and voiding interval are stated verbatim in the ABSTRACT Results sentence and corroborated in RESULTS/figure captions; mean follow-up of 5.8 months appears in the ABSTRACT and again in RESULTS.

claim: In Clemens et al. (2000), among 19 patients in an 11-week (six biweekly visit) biofeedback program, 10/19 completed all six sessions, 5/19 completed three to five sessions, and 4/19 completed fewer than three sessions. For the 4 who completed fewer than three sessions, the stated reasons for noncompliance were “sufficient improvement” (2 patients), “insurance issues” (1), and “unknown” (1). In the COMMENT, the authors state that the regimen requires a high level of patient/nurse commitment and that some insurance carriers do not cover expenses; they also note that “nearly half of the patients did not complete all six sessions,” and that “2 of the 4 patients who attended fewer than half of the treatments cited sufficient improvement as their reason for not attending further.”
source_text:
Ten patients completed all six biofeedback sessions, 5 completed three to five sessions, and 4 completed fewer than three sessions. Reasons for noncompliance in these last 4 patients were sufficient improvement (2 patients), insurance issues (1), and unknown (1). ...

Our positive results are encouraging but must be viewed with a realistic appreciation that the treat-

ment regimen described requires a high level of commitment by the patients and the nurses who administer the training. Furthermore, some insurance carriers do not cover the expenses. ... Despite our efforts to maximize patient compliance, nearly half of the patients did not complete all six sessions. Interestingly, 2 of the 4 patients who attended fewer than half of the treatments cited sufficient improvement as their reason for not attending further.
verdict_explanation: The Clemens et al. (2000) completion counts match exactly (10 all six; 5 three-to-five; 4 fewer than three). The “sufficient improvement” phrase and the insurance/commitment statements are supported in the source (note: in RESULTS the phrase is unquoted, and the insurance phrasing is “insurance issues” / “some insurance carriers do not cover the expenses”). However, the Cornel et al. (2005) portion cannot be verified because cornel2005.pdf.md was not supplied in the named source text here, so those claims are a retrieval gap in this task.
readiness_reason: Only the Clemens et al. (2000) portion is source-supported from the provided text; the Cornel et al. (2005) completion/dropout counts and reasons cannot be validated without cornel2005.pdf.md in the supplied source materials.

citation.locator: Abstract; PATIENTS AND METHODS > Randomization; PATIENTS AND METHODS > Statistical Analysis; RESULTS > Primary Analyses; Table 3

claim: In a monocentric, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial with a 2×2 factorial design in women with superficial radiation-induced fibrosis, participants were randomized for 6 months to: (A) pentoxifylline (PTX) 800 mg/day (two 400-mg tablets) plus vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol; Vit E) 1,000 U/day (two 500-U capsules); (B) PTX plus placebo; (C) placebo plus Vit E; or (D) double placebo. The main endpoint was relative regression of measurable RIF surface after 6 months. At 6 months, mean RIF surface regression was 60% ± 10% with combined PTX/Vit E versus 43% ± 17% with double placebo (Table 3 index at 6 months: −60.2% ± 10.7% vs −42.6% ± 17.4%), and the main comparison (A vs D) used the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with P = .038. Two-way ANOVA assessing marginal effects and interaction across the four groups found no significant effects, with the PTX×Vit E interaction reported as a trend (P = .09).
source_text:
***Patients and Methods:* ... These patients, previously irradiated for breast cancer, were randomly assigned to four balanced treatment groups: (A) 800 mg/d of PTX and 1,000 U/d of Vit E; (B) PTX plus placebo; (C) placebo plus Vit E; and (D) placebo-placebo. The main end point measure was the relative regression of measurable RIF surface after 6 months of treatment.

***Results:* ... Mean RIF surface regression was significant with combined PTX/Vit E versus double placebo (60% ± 10% *v* 43% ± 17%; *P* = .038).

"In an individual double-blind design, the 24 women included were randomly assigned, for 6 months, to a combination of 800 mg/d of PTX in two 400-mg tablets and 1,000 U/d of Vit E in two 500-U capsules (group A), PTX and placebo capsules (group B), placebo tablets and Vit E (group C), and placebo tablets and capsules (group D)."

"The main end point was the relative regression of the fibrosis surface area at 6 months, defined as (measure at 6 months  $-$  measure at inclusion)/measure at inclusion."

"For the main treatment comparison (A *v* D) involving the main and secondary end points, we used the Wilcoxon rank sum test. ... Two-way analyses of variance (ANOVA) were performed to test the respective marginal effects of PTX and Vit E and their interactions, resulting in a procedure that involved comparison of the four groups."

"At 6 months, we observed a significant mean RIF surface regression of 60% with combined PTX/Vit E in group A, versus 43% for double placebo in group D ( $P = .038$ ). ... Two-way ANOVA for the four groups disclosed no significant effects, though there was a trend toward significance for the effect of PTX and Vit E interaction ( $P = .09$ )."

"Table 3. Regression of 27 Radiation-Induced Fibrosis Areas in 22 Assessable Patients After 3 and 6 Months of Treatment" ... "Index 6 months, %" Group A (PTX/Vit E) Mean "-60.2" SD "10.7" ... Group D (Placebo/Placebo) Mean "-42.6" SD "17.4"
verdict_explanation: Supported: double-blind randomized placebo-controlled monocentric trial with a 2×2 factorial design; exact doses (PTX 800 mg/day as two 400-mg tablets; Vit E 1,000 U/day as two 500-U capsules) and 6-month assignment; main endpoint at 6 months; Table 3 index values and SDs (−60.2±10.7 vs −42.6±17.4); Abstract reports 60%±10 vs 43%±17 with P=.038; Statistical Analysis specifies Wilcoxon rank-sum for A vs D; Primary Analyses reports P=.038 and ANOVA interaction trend P=.09 with no significant effects. Minor repair: the paper describes the study as "monocentric" and "placebo-controlled" (not explicitly "RCT" wording in the text, though randomization is described). Also, the source does not state "no significant main marginal effects for PTX or vitamin E alone" separately—rather, it states "no significant effects" in the two-way ANOVA overall; the repaired claim reflects that phrasing while retaining the interaction trend p=.09.
readiness_reason: mechanical check: the validator's source_text was not found in the named source file (none); Claim, doses, duration, outcome values, and statistical testing (Wilcoxon P=.038; ANOVA interaction trend P=.09) are directly supported with clear quotations and table values from the provided source text.
original_claim: In a double-blind 2×2 factorial RCT of superficial radiation-induced fibrosis, pentoxifylline 800 mg/day (400 mg twice daily) plus alpha-tocopherol (vitamin E) 1,000 U/day (500 U twice daily) was given for 6 months; at 6 months the combination group showed mean RIF surface area regression of about 60%±10% (table index −60.2%±10.7%) versus about 43%±17% for double placebo (table index −42.6%±17.4%), with Wilcoxon rank-sum p=.038 (combo vs double placebo), and a two-way ANOVA reported no significant main marginal effects for PTX or vitamin E alone while the PTX×vitamin E interaction was reported only as a trend (p=.09).

claim: In this prospective follow-up study of women with measurable superficial breast radiation-induced fibrosis (RIF) treated between April 1995 and April 2000, patients received PTX 800 mg/day plus vitamin E (VitE) 1,000 IU/day given as PTX 400 mg twice daily and vitE 500 U twice daily. The authors report a short-treatment group (SPE) with mean treatment duration 9 months (range 6–12) comprising 7 patients (8 RIF sites) and a long-treatment group (LPE) with mean treatment duration 36 months (range 24–48) comprising 37 patients (47 RIF sites). Using an exponential model of the form f(t) = a · exp(-bt) − a, they report significant RIF regression (P < .0001), an estimated mean maximal effect (a) of 68% RIF surface area regression (95% CI 64% to 73%), and a mean time to this effect of 24 months; time to maximal effect was shorter for more recent RIF (<6 years since RT) than for older RIF (16 months vs 28 months; P = .0003).
source_text:
Between April 1995 and April 2000, women were treated with a daily combination of PTX (800 mg) and VitE (1,000 IU).

Measurable superficial RIF was assessed in patients treated by RT for breast cancer in a long-treatment (24 to 48 months) PTX-vitE (LPE) group of 37 patients (47 RIFs) and in a short-treatment (6 to 12 months) PTX-vitE (SPE) group of seven patients (eight RIFs).

The drug combination was based on pharmacokinetic data, clinical use, and long-term tolerance in other diseases. Each patient was administered a combination of twice-daily PTX 400 mg (800 mg/d) and vitE 500 U (1,000 U/d).

The seven patients (eight RIF sites) included before 1997 had short PTX-vitE (SPE) treatment (mean, 9 months; range, 6 to 12 months); ...

...we treated the subsequent 37 patients (47 RIF sites) until fibrosis regression peaked at a mean of 36 months (range, 24 to 48 months); these patients were considered as having received long PTX-vitE (LPE) treatment...

*Modeling.* From the observed shape of the relative RIF regression under treatment in the LPE group (Fig 3), several models were postulated, and the best representative model of the time-course of regression was found to be of the following exponential form:  f(t) = a \cdot \exp(-bt) - a , where  t  represents the time from treatment onset in months, and  a  and  b  correspond to the maximal surface area regression and the kinetics of response, respectively.

This model showed significant RIF regression ( P < .0001 ), with the maximal effect of treat-

ment (a) corresponding to a mean of 68% (95% CI, 64% to 73%) RIF surface area regression. ... In contrast, the mean time to this effect was significantly shorter with recent RIF ( < 6  years since RT) than older RIF ( P = .0003 ).

As shown previously, the time to maximum RIF regression was shorter in recent ( < 6  years since RT) RIF than in older ( > 6  years since RT) RIF (16 months; 95% CI, 12 to 19 months  \nu  28 months; 95% CI, 23 to 33 months, respectively).
verdict_explanation: All key elements are directly supported in-source: dosing (PTX 800 mg/day as 400 mg BID; VitE 1,000 IU/day as 500 U BID), cohort sizes and duration ranges/means, and the exponential model form with estimated maximal regression of 68% and time-to-maximal effect of 24 months, including the latency subgroup difference (16 vs 28 months; P = .0003). However, the candidate claim adds that the extension was specifically "prospective observational" and that the 68% maximal estimate had "p<.0001"; the source reports "P < .0001" for significant regression in the modeling section but does not explicitly attach P < .0001 to the 68% estimate itself, and it does not use the phrase "prospective observational extension" in the cited sections. Therefore the claim required minor repair/clarification.
readiness_reason: mechanical check: the validator's source_text was not found in the named source file (none); The repaired claim is a faithful compression of explicit statements in the provided source text with correct dosing, denominators, model form, effect size, timing estimates, and P-values as reported.
original_claim: In a prospective observational extension using combined PTX 800 mg/day (400 mg twice daily) plus vitamin E 1,000 U/day (500 U twice daily), participants were described as treated in short-duration (6–12 months; mean 9 months; n=7 patients/8 RIF sites) and long-duration (24–48 months; mean 36 months; n=37 patients/47 RIF sites) cohorts; exponential kinetic modeling was reported to estimate a mean maximal surface regression of 68% (p<.0001) and a mean time to maximal effect of 24 months overall, with time to peak response shorter for more recent RIF (<6 years since radiotherapy: 16 months) than older RIF (≥6 years: 28 months; p=.0003).

This fibrotic increase was significantly lower and asymptomatic in the LPE group with (8.5%/yr; 95% CI, 1% to 16%/yr) compared with the SPE group with (40%/yr; 95% CI, 24% to 56%/yr;  $P = .0012$ ).

Although the prevalence of DU increases in older patients as it is generally age-related, no epidemiological study has analyzed the prevalence of DU related symptoms such as LUTS and impaired storage function. ... 

Only certain studies have reported the prevalence of DU in community-dwelling cohorts with significant LUTS using arbitrary urodynamic criteria for DU and these investigations have indicated that DU accounts for 25%–48% and 12%–24% of elderly men and women, respectively.

...

claim: In Khrieba et al. (published 30 March 2026), adults with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis (n=60) were randomized (1:1) to placebo tablets BID plus mesalamine 3 g/day (1 g t.i.d.) for six months vs pentoxifylline (PTX) 400 mg BID plus mesalamine 1 g t.i.d. for six months; missing data for ITT were handled using baseline-observation-carried-forward (BOCF). In ITT analysis (n=30/group), post-treatment partial Mayo score (PMS) differed between groups (p=0.004), and PTX had higher clinical response (23/30 [76.66%] vs 15/30 [50%], p=0.032) and remission (15/30 [50%] vs 7/30 [23.33%], p=0.04). In per-protocol analysis (Placebo n=26; PTX n=27), post-treatment PMS differed between groups (p=0.0006), with higher response (23/27 [85.18%] vs 15/26 [57.7%], p=0.02) and remission (15/27 [55.55%] vs 7/26 [26.9%], p=0.034) in the PTX group.
source_text:
60 patients with UC were assigned to mesalamine plus placebo (Group 1) or mesalamine plus PTX 400 mg BID (Group 2) for 24 weeks. ... Analyses were performed using intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol (PP) approaches.

Group 1 (Placebo Group): Participants in this arm were administered an inert placebo tablet twice per day, in combination with mesalamine at a total daily dose of 3 g, given as 1 g three times daily (Pentasa® 500 mg, Multi Pharma, Alexandria, Egypt), for a treatment duration of six months.

Group 2 (PTX Group): Individuals assigned to this group received PTX at a dose of 400 mg twice daily (Trental® 400 mg, Sanofi, Cairo, Egypt), together with mesalamine 1 g taken three times daily, for a total of six months. The placebo tablets were identical in appearance to the PTX tablets.

During the follow-up period, four patients were lost to follow-up in the mesalamine (placebo) group as they developed a severe disease state and shifted to adjuvant therapy with steroids, and three patients in the PTX group as they did not come back for the follow-up session. To preserve the integrity of randomization and reduce bias, ITT analysis was performed using the BOCF method for handling missing data. All randomized patients were included in the final analysis. All randomized patients were included in the final analysis, except that PMS was also analyzed using per-protocol analysis.

Table 2. Effect of study medications on clinical markers using intention-to-treat analysis.

| Partial Mayo score index (PMS) | 5 (5–6) | 2 (1–3) | <0.001 * | 5 (3–6) | 1 (0–2) | <0.001 * | 0.004 ** |
| Response (n, %)                | 15 (50%)               |                 |          | 23 (76.66%)        |                 |          | 0.032 ***       |
| Remission (n, %)               | 7 (23.33%)             |                 |          | 15 (50%)           |                 |          | 0.04 ***        |

Table 3. Effect of study medications on clinical markers by per-protocol analysis.

| Character        | Placebo Group (n = 26) |                 |           | PTX Group (n = 27) |                 |           | p-Value         |
| PMS              | 5 (4.5–6)              | 2 (1–3)         | <0.0001 * | 5 (3–6)            | 0.75 (0–2)      | <0.0001 * | 0.0006 **       |
| Response (n, %)  | 15 (57.7%)             |                 |           | 23 (85.18%)        |                 |           | 0.02 ***        |
| Remission (n, %) | 7 (26.9%)              |                 |           | 15 (55.55%)        |                 |           | 0.034 ***       |

Missing outcome data were addressed using the baseline-observation-carried-forward (BOCF) approach, a highly conservative method that assumes no change from baseline in participants with missing follow-up data.
