claim: In male Wistar rats studied with the split hydronephrotic kidney preparation, pentoxifylline (PTX) given as an IV bolus of 25 mg/kg in 1 ml over 5 min immediately followed by 12.5 mg/kg in a 1.5-ml infusion over 90 min, with live E. coli (1 × 10^9 bacteria in 1 ml over 5 min) infused 15 min after the beginning of PTX administration, reportedly prevented E. coli–induced preglomerular vasoconstriction and maintained vasodilation/near-baseline ILA diameter and flow; ILA flow in the PTX + E. coli group peaked at +26.8 ± 4.4% above baseline at 30 min, and the figures indicate this group differed from E. coli alone at P < 0.05 (PTX + E. coli vs E. coli). The text also reports, for PTX alone, AFF diameter +21.9 ± 3.1% at 120 min and EFF diameter +11.5 ± 3.3% (maximum at 30 min) and +8.6 ± 1.8% at 120 min; the figures indicate PTX alone differs from saline at P < 0.05 and PTX + E. coli differs from E. coli at P < 0.05, but the text does not explicitly attach P-values to those specific AFF/EFF summary values.
source_text:
Male Wistar rats were acclimated for 10 days at an animal care facility with free access to water and Purina rat chow (Purina, Rich-

mond, IN). ...

Group III ( $n = 7$ ) was used to study the effects of pentoxifylline on the renal microcirculation. After baseline measurements, PTX was administered as a bolus of 25 mg/kg in 1 ml over 5 min, immediately followed by 12.5 mg/kg in a 1.5-ml infusion over 90 min. Fifteen minutes after the beginning of PTX administration, 1 ml of saline was given over 5 min to control for the volume of *E. coli* given in Group II.

Group IV ( $n = 7$ ) was used to study the effects of pentoxifylline on the vascular sequelae of *E. coli*. Pentoxifylline was infused at the dose and rate described for Group III. Fifteen minutes after the beginning of PTX administration, 1 ml of saline was given over 5 min to control for the volume of *E. coli* given in Group II.

... Serial dilutions were measured spectrophotometrically at a 500- $\mu\text{m}$ wavelength to provide  $1 \times 10^9$  bacteria per milliliter. This dose was administered through the femoral vein catheter over 5 min.

...

*E. coli* infusion produced rapid and progressive preglomerular vasoconstriction (Fig. 2). ...

Pentoxifylline infusion in the third group produced pre- and postglomerular vasodilation, also affecting ILA diameters significantly. ILA flow increased throughout the experiment, remaining 12–16% above baseline. Afferent arterioles dilated considerably to  $21.9 \pm 3.1\%$  above baseline at 120 min and efferent arterioles dilated to a lesser extent ( $+11.5 \pm 3.3\%$ ), with a maximum at 30 min, and remained dilated at 120 min ( $+8.6 \pm 1.8\%$ ).

Pentoxifylline infusion prevented vasoconstriction during bacteremia; indeed, vasodilation was maintained. ILA diameter and blood flow remained above or near baseline throughout the experimental period. ILA flow peaked at  $26.8 \pm 4.4\%$  above baseline at 30 min (Figs. 2 and 3).

...

FIG. 2. ILA diameter and ILA flow changes for Group I (●, saline;  $n = 8$ ), Group II (■, *E. coli*;  $n = 7$ ), Group III (▲, PTX;  $n = 7$ ), and Group IV (▼, PTX + *E. coli*;  $n = 7$ ). \* $P < 0.05$  *E. coli* vs saline; + $P < 0.05$  PTX + *E. coli* vs *E. coli*; by ANOVA and Tukey's HSD test.

FIG. 3. AFF and EFF diameter changes for Group I (●, saline;  $n = 8$ ), Group II (■, *E. coli*;  $n = 7$ ), Group III (▲, PTX;  $n = 7$ ), and Group IV (▼, PTX + *E. coli*;  $n = 7$ ). \* $P < 0.05$  *E. coli* vs saline; + $P < 0.05$  PTX + *E. coli* vs *E. coli*; # $P < 0.05$  PTX vs saline; by ANOVA and Tukey's HSD test.
verdict_explanation: Supported: split hydronephrotic kidney model; E. coli dose/volume/infusion duration (1×10^9 in 1 ml over 5 min); PTX bolus and infusion regimen (25 mg/kg in 1 ml over 5 min then 12.5 mg/kg in 1.5 ml over 90 min) and timing (15 min after beginning PTX); statement that PTX prevented bacteremia-associated preglomerular vasoconstriction; ILA flow peak +26.8 ± 4.4% at 30 min; and that the statistical comparator for the PTX+E. coli group in Figs. 2–3 is “PTX + E. coli vs E. coli” at P<0.05. Not supported/needs repair: the candidate specifies “male Sprague-Dawley rats” (source says “Male Wistar rats”); and it attributes P<0.05 vs E. coli alone to specific AFF/EFF percentage values summarized in the text (the source text gives those values for PTX alone and does not explicitly attach P-values to those specific summary numbers, although Fig. 3 provides general significance markers for PTX vs saline and PTX+E. coli vs E. coli).
readiness_reason: As written, the candidate contains an animal-strain error (Sprague-Dawley vs Wistar) and over-precise/statistical attributions for AFF/EFF values (P-value comparator not explicitly tied in the text to those specific numerical summaries). A repaired claim is supportable, but the original is not witness-ready.
original_claim: In male Sprague-Dawley rats using the split hydronephrotic kidney preparation, IV pentoxifylline pretreatment (25 mg/kg bolus over 5 min followed immediately by 12.5 mg/kg infusion over 90 min, started 15 min before IV live E. coli 1×10^9 in 1 mL over 5 min) reportedly abolished E. coli–induced preglomerular vasoconstriction and preserved/dilated vessels, including ILA flow peaking at +26.8 ± 4.4% at 30 min (P < 0.05 vs E. coli alone), AFF diameter +21.9 ± 3.1% at 120 min (P < 0.05 vs E. coli alone), and EFF diameter max +11.5 ± 3.3% at 30 min and +8.6 ± 1.8% at 120 min (P < 0.05 vs E. coli alone).

original_claim: In an isolated single-pass perfused rat kidney model after in vivo bacteremia, E. coli alone reportedly increased ex vivo renal vascular resistance (RVR) versus saline controls (~1450 vs ~550 mmHg·mL⁻¹·min⁻¹·g⁻¹ at 60 min; P < 0.05 by ANOVA and Tukey-Kramer HSD) with elevated values also reported at 75 min (~850 vs ~350), 90 min (~950 vs ~350), and 105 min (~1100 vs ~550); IV PTX pretreatment (25 mg/kg bolus 15 min pre-bacteremia plus 12.5 mg/kg infusion over 60 min) reportedly suppressed the RVR surge (~900 at 60 min; P < 0.05 vs E. coli alone) and was described as returning RVR to control levels by ~105 min (~800).

claim: In venous effluent from an isolated rat kidney single-pass perfusion model, E. coli bacteremia increased 6-keto-PGF1α and TXB2 at 60 min versus normal saline controls (both reported as statistically significant in the figures/Results text for 60 min vs normal saline). Pentoxifylline (PTX) pretreatment had only a small effect on TXB2 and did not significantly affect 6-keto-PGF1α production after bacteremia; PTX significantly reduced TXB2 only at the 60-min time point versus E. coli alone. Bacteremia increased peptido-leukotriene production, and PTX significantly reduced peptido-leukotriene production versus E. coli over the course of the experiment. Bacteremia increased 8-iso-PGF2α (8-isoprostane) production, while PTX caused a small, non-statistically-significant reduction versus E. coli.

In the non-corrected analysis, IL-8 increased significantly after remission for C. albicans and S. aureus (p<0.05). In the non-corrected analysis, IL-1Ra decreased significantly after remission for all four stimuli (LPS 1 ng/mL, LPS 10 ng/mL, C. albicans, S. aureus) (p<0.05), and IL-10 decreased significantly after remission for LPS 1 ng/mL (p<0.05; approximately 1100 to 400 pg/mL). The candidate claim’s additional specifics (e.g., IL-8 significance for S. aureus in the monocyte-normalized analysis; IL-6 significance; p-values for specific IL-8 comparisons in the monocyte-normalized analysis; calling Fig. 4 values “cumulative output”; asserting corrected/uncorrected status beyond what is stated) are not fully supported as written.
source_text: Flowchart (Fig. 1): “PBMC stimulation available for 7 CS patients” Materials and methods > Statistical analysis: “Cell counts, steroid hormone concentrations and cytokine concentrations were compared using the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test. In order to correctly assess the cytokine production capacity, taking into account the changes in PBMC composition, monocyte-derived cytokine production after 24 h of stimulation was normalized by dividing the cytokine concentration (in pg/mL) by monocyte counts (as per $1 \times 10^5$ monocytes).” Results > Increased production of IL-8 and IL-6 after remission of CS: “Monocyte-derived cytokines were measured in supernatants from 24 h stimulated PBMCs that were obtained at baseline and after achieving remission and tapering off glucocorticoid replacement therapy (Fig. 3). Because percentages of monocytes within the PBMC fraction significantly changed after achieving remission from CS, the cytokine production per $1.0 \times 10^5$ monocytes was calculated as well. This way, cytokine production capacity of stimulated PBMCs could be compared between baseline and after achieving remission. PBMCs produced significantly more IL-8 after stimulation after achieving remission from CS (Fig. 3A). The same trend could be observed for IL-6, however this was not statistically significant (Fig. 3B). In contrast, for anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-1Ra and IL-10, a trend towards lower production after achieving remission could be observed (Fig. 3C & D).” Results (immediately after the above paragraph): “The non-corrected cytokine concentrations, which more accurately represent the cumulative *in vivo* effects, are shown in Fig. 4. Like in the monocyte-percentage corrected analysis, concentrations of IL-8 and IL-6 were higher after achieving remission and concentrations of IL-1Ra were lower after achieving remission of CS. For IL-10, production capacity was lower after achieving remission for stimulations with LPS 1 ng/mL, but not for the other stimulations.” Fig. 3 caption: “Fig. 3. Increased proinflammatory and decreased antiinflammatory cytokine production capacity in monocytes from Cushing's patients after achieving remission. ... The y-axis for all panels represents cytokine concentration (pg/mL per 100,000 monocytes). ... \* indicates $p < 0.05$ .” Fig. 4 caption: “Fig. 4. Cytokine production capacity in PBMCs without correction for monocyte percentages. Concentrations of cytokines IL-8 (A), IL-6 (B), IL-1Ra (C), IL-10 (D), TNF (E) and IL-1 $\beta$ (F) after 24 h of PBMC stimulation at diagnosis and after achieving remission, not corrected for percentages of monocytes. \* indicates $p < 0.05$ .” Fig. 4 (tabled values in provided source rendering), IL-8 and IL-1Ra and IL-10 excerpts: “| A: IL-8 | C. albicans | 100,000 | 200,000 | * | | | S. aureus | 110,000 | 130,000 | * |” “| C: IL-1Ra | LPS 1ng/ml | 15,000 | 7,000 | * | | | LPS 10ng/ml | 17,000 | 10,000 | * | | | C. albicans | 18,000 | 10,000 | * | | | S. aureus | 22,000 | 11,000 | * |” “| D: IL-10 | LPS 1ng/ml | 1100 | 400 | * |”
verdict_explanation: Correct: paired PBMC stimulation availability n=7 (Fig. 1); monocyte-normalization basis “as per 1 × 10^5 monocytes”; IL-8 increases significantly after remission in some conditions; IL-1Ra decreases significantly across all four stimuli in the non-corrected analysis (Fig. 4); IL-10 decreases significantly for LPS 1 ng/mL in the monocyte-normalized analysis (Fig. 3D shows *). claim: Roerink et al. state that because the patient/matched-control ratio for each measured skeletal muscle variable was close to 1.0 (Tables 4 and 5), they conclude that the reduced VO2peak in patients must be due to impairments in blood supply to exercising muscle or reduced efficiency of mitochondrial respiration (lower ATP/O ratio), rather than differences in the measured muscle mitochondrial content, capillary measures, or microvascular eNOS/NAD(P)H-oxidase-related protein measures.
source_text: To investigate whether this lower VO2peak is the result of 1) a reduced mitochondrial content, 2) differences in the structure and density of the muscle capillary network and/or 3) an increased imbalance between the protein content and phosphorylation state of eNOS and of the subunits of the NAD(P)H-oxidase protein complex in the muscle microvasculature, muscle biopsies were collected to make these measurements in 7-8 patient/matched control pairs. As the patient/matched control ratio for each of the measured variables was close to 1.0 (Table 4 and Table 5) this leads to the conclusion that the reduction in VO2peak in the patients must be the result of impairments in the blood supply to the exercising muscle or of a reduction in the efficiency of mitochondrial respiration (lower ATP/O ratio) in the exercising muscle.
verdict_explanation: Supported: In the Discussion, the authors explicitly tie their conclusion to the finding that the patient/matched-control ratios for measured variables were close to 1.0 in Tables 4 and 5, and conclude VO2peak reduction "must" reflect impaired blood supply or reduced mitochondrial efficiency. Not supported as written: the candidate claim says VO2peak reduction "cannot be explained by peripheral skeletal muscle pathology such as fiber atrophy, microvascular rarefaction, capillary structural defects, or endothelial enzymatic imbalance" and specifies "with P>0.05". The Discussion passage provided does not use the exact "cannot be explained" phrasing nor explicitly lists those specific pathologies; it also relies on ratios close to 1.0 rather than explicitly stating a P-value criterion in that sentence (though the tables show non-significant P values). Therefore the claim needs narrowing to match the authors' stated conclusion.
readiness_reason: The repaired claim is directly supported by an explicit Discussion statement that references Tables 4 and 5 and states a causal/interpretive conclusion about mechanisms of reduced VO2peak.
original_claim: Roerink et al. conclude that because measured skeletal muscle variables (e.g., fiber cross-sectional area, capillarization indices, mitochondrial COXIV content, eNOS/eNOS Ser1177 measures, and NOX2 complex subunits) were near a patient/control ratio of 1.0 with P>0.05, the observed VO2peak reduction cannot be explained by peripheral skeletal muscle pathology such as fiber atrophy, microvascular rarefaction, capillary structural defects, or endothelial enzymatic imbalance.

MCAS may be diagnosed when the symptoms of MC activation are systemic (involving more than one organ system), severe, and recurrent and the MCAS criteria are fulfilled [17••, 18••]. There are three sets of criteria required for an MCAS diagnosis as illustrated in Fig. 1: (1) the presence of typical, severe, episodic MC activation symptoms in  $\geq 2$  organ systems; (2) the detection of a substantial transient increase in a validated marker of MC activation during the symptomatic event; (3) the control of symptoms with MC mediator–targeting drugs.

... 

The clinical criterion of MCAS requires the simultaneous involvement of  $\geq 2$  organ systems [17••, 18••].

... 

Secondly, the diagnosis of MCAS requires laboratory proof. ... 

Thirdly, the MCAS diagnosis requires a favorable response to agents that act as MC stabilizers or inhibitors of MC mediators, such as histamine receptor antagonists (H1- and H2-antihistamines), leukotriene blockers, MC stabilizers, and aspirin or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs) [15•, 58, 59•].

readiness_reason: Exact kinetics language is directly quoted from the source.

claim: In Siu et al. The patients were instructed to perform the exercise 30 times in three intervals each day: in the morning, afternoon, and before retiring. ... Compliance was recorded as the number of sessions and contractions the patient logged each day.

Abstract

"Complete ischemia in the left hindlimb was maintained for 3.5 h in 16 rats randomized into two equal groups. One group served as control, the other was treated with pentoxifylline before, during and after the ischemic period. The animals were killed 72 h later, and the anterior tibial muscles were prepared for histological investigation. ... The total areas of necrosis and the areas of no resorption were measured as percent of the cross-sectional area of each muscle. There was extensive necrosis in both groups. The infarcted area was 93% in the control group and 89% in the treated group (NS). The corresponding areas of no resorption were 23 and 6% (p = 0.01)."

Material and Methods

Induction of Ischemia

"Sixteen male Wistar/Han/Mol SPF rats, weighing 250–300 g, were anesthetized ..." ... "The tourniquets and clamps were released after 3.5 h of ischemia, ..."

Experimental Groups

"Sixteen animals were randomized into two equal groups. One group was treated with pentoxifylline (Trental® 20 mg/ml; Hoechst, FRG) and the other served as control. The animals treated with pentoxifylline received 5 mg (20 mg/kg) i.p. 1 h prior to the ischemia, 5 mg 15 min before release of the occlusions, 5 mg after 5 h of reperfusion, and thereafter 5 mg at 12-hour intervals. The total doses were 60 mg/kg during the first day and then 40 mg/kg/day until the animals were killed after 3 days."

Statistics

"The total areas of necrosis and the areas of no resorption will be given as means and standard deviations (SD). The areas in the two groups were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test, and  $p < 0.05$  was considered significant."

claim: In male Sprague-Dawley rats given an intravenous injection of live Escherichia coli (7×10^8 CFU), pentoxifylline (PX) pretreatment (100 mg/kg intraperitoneally 1 h before infection) was associated with lower plasma TNF-α at 90 min, and lower plasma IL-1β and IL-6-like bioactivity at 3 h, compared with infected (INF) rats; PX treatment also reduced plasma α1-acid glycoprotein (AGP) at days 2 and 6 and reduced plasma α2-macroglobulin (A2M) and fibrinogen at day 6 (but not day 2), while it did not significantly modify the infection-associated decrease in plasma albumin (no † marker vs INF).
source_text:
To explore the regulation of the acute phase response in vivo, the effects of pentoxifylline (PX) treatment (100 mg/kg ip 1 h before infection) were investigated in infected and pair-fed rats 2 and 6 days after an intravenous injection of live bacteria (Escherichia coli). PX treatment prevented the increase in plasma tumor necrosis factor (TNF)- α (peak 1.5 h after the infection) and resulted in an 84 and 61% inhibition of plasma interleukin (IL)-1 β and IL-6, respectively (peaks at 3 h). ... PX significantly reduced AGP plasma concentration as early as day 2 in infected animals but reduced A2M and fibrinogen plasma levels only at day 6. The treatment had no effect on the albumin plasma concentration.

"The INF group received saline intraperitoneally 1 h before injection of Escherichia coli (serotype 0153-K- -H-; 7 \times 10^8 colony-forming units) into a lateral tail vein. ... In the PX-INF group, PX (100 mg/kg) was injected intraperitoneally 1 h before bacteria administration."

"Thus blood samples were collected in a lateral tail vein 1.5 and 3 h after the infection ..."

"Administration of PX 1 h before infection suppressed the rise of the plasma TNF- α level (by 99%; Table 2). PX treatment induced a reduction of 84 and 61% of plasma IL-1 β- and IL-6-like bioactivity concentrations, respectively, 3 h after infection (Table 2)."

|--------------|-------------|--------------|
| TNF-α, ng/ml | 71.9 ± 4.6  | 0.6 ± 0.1*   |
| IL-1β, ng/ml | 1.38 ± 0.48 | 0.22 ± 0.05* |
| IL-6, μg/ml  | 5.09 ± 0.56 | 1.98 ± 0.40* |

Values are means ± SE for 12–14 animals. ... *P < 0.05 vs. infected animals."

claim: In conscious ICR mice (28–35 g) given E. coli LPS 60 mg/kg intraperitoneally, therapeutic pentoxifylline 3 mg/kg intraperitoneally administered at 0, 6, 15, and 24 hours after LPS increased 36-hour survival from 10% (LPS group; n=20) to 35% (PTX+LPS group; n=20).
source_text:
Abstract
"Treatment of conscious mice with a high dose of endotoxin (60 mg/kg, i.p.) resulted in a survival rate of only 10% at 36 h ( $n = 20$ ). However, therapeutic application of pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, i.p. at 0, 6, 15 and 24 h after lipopolysaccharide) increased the 36-h survival to 35% ( $n = 20$ )."

### 2.5. Survival studies
"Survival studies were performed with mice (28–35 g), whose stock originated from the Institute of Cancer Research of National Institute of Health, USA, were purchased from the National Animal Centre (Taipei, Taiwan, R.O.C.). Lipopolysaccharide (60 mg/kg, i.p.) was injected in the presence of vehicle or drugs and survival was monitored every 6 up to 36 h. Different groups of animals received vehicle (saline) together with lipopolysaccharide ( $n = 20$ ) or lipopolysaccharide plus pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, i.p. at 0, 6, 15 and 24 h after lipopolysaccharide,  $n = 20$ )."

### 3.5. Effects of pentoxifylline on the survival rate of mice treated with lipopolysaccharide
"The administration of a high dose (60 mg/kg, i.p.) of lipopolysaccharide to mice was associated with a 36-h survival rate of only 10% of the animals. In contrast, lipopolysaccharide-mice treated with pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, i.p. at 0, 6, 15 and 24 h after lipopolysaccharide,  $n = 20$ ) had a higher survival rate, 35%, at 36 h (Fig. 5)."

Fig. 5 caption
"Fig. 5. Effects of pentoxifylline (PTF) on the survival rate of mice treated with endotoxin. Depicted are the changes in survival during the experimental period of different groups of ICR mice which received intraperitoneal injection of *E. coli* LPS (60 mg/kg; solid triangles;  $n = 20$ ) or PTF (3 mg/kg; at time 0, 6, 15 and 24 h after LPS,  $n = 20$ ) plus LPS."
verdict_explanation: Supported: ICR mice (28–35 g), LPS 60 mg/kg i.p., PTX 3 mg/kg i.p. at 0/6/15/24 h after LPS, n=20 per group, 36-h survival 10% vs 35%. claim: In 12 pigs (25–35 kg) given fecal peritonitis induced by intraperitoneal spread of 35 mL aspirated cecal content, six animals received a pentoxifylline (PTF) infusion of 60 mg/h started 120 minutes before peritonitis induction and maintained for the study duration; animals were killed 300 minutes after peritonitis induction. In hemodynamic results, the peritonitis (test/untreated) group had SVR increase to 133% above baseline at 300 minutes versus 36% above baseline in the PTF group at 300 minutes, with significant differences between groups at all points from baseline to 300 minutes except at 30 minutes; PVR reached 462% above baseline (test) versus 140% above baseline (PTF) at 300 minutes, with significant between-group differences at 270 and 300 minutes; MAP decreased to 65% of baseline (test) and 71% of baseline (PTF) at 300 minutes, with a significant difference between groups at 180 and 210 minutes.
source_text:
Anesthesia was induced in 12 pigs (25 to 35 kg) with azaperone (2.0 mg/kg im) and metomidate (10 mg/kg ip). ... A laparotomy was performed and 35 ml of aspirated cecal content was spread in the peritoneum to induce peritonitis (PI). In six animals an infusion of PTF (60 mg/h) was started 120 min before PI and maintained for the study duration. ... The animals were killed 300 min after PI.

In the test group, MAP decreased progressively to 65% of baseline at 300 min (Fig. 1). The baseline value was not significantly lower in the PTF group and after PI there was a similar pattern with MAP decreasing to 71% of baseline at 300 min. There was a significant difference between the two groups at 180 and 210 min.

In the test group there was a progressive increase in SVR to 133% above baseline at 300 min. In marked contrast, SVR increased only to 36% above baseline in the PTF group at 300 min. There were significant differences between the two groups at all points from baseline to 300 min other than at 30 min.

In both groups, PVR increased progressively, reaching a maximum 462% above baseline in the test group and 140% above baseline in the PTF group at 300 min. There were significant differences between the two groups at 270 and 300 min.
verdict_explanation: Supported: species/weight range; fecal peritonitis induction method and volume; PTF infusion rate (60 mg/h), start time (120 min before PI), and maintained for study duration; animals killed 300 min after PI; SVR and PVR percent-above-baseline values at 300 min and which time points showed significant between-group differences; MAP percent-of-baseline at 300 min and significant between-group differences at 180 and 210 min. Not supported as written: (1) the claim that MAP was "higher" in the PTF-pretreated group at 180 and 210 min (the source states only that there was a significant difference, and also reports overall similar MAP pattern with no significant differences in MAP in the abstract/summary statement: "No significant differences were seen in MAP..."); (2) explicit p-values of p<0.05 for those specific MAP/SVR/PVR time points are not stated in the Hemodynamics text (significance is described without giving exact p-values); (3) the observation period is described as animals killed 300 min after PI, but the source does not explicitly phrase this as a "300-minute post-induction observation period"; (4) "untreated peritonitis pigs" group size is not explicitly stated in the methods text (it states 12 pigs total and 6 with PTF; the remaining peritonitis test group size is inferable but not explicitly stated). Provisional label corrected from PRECLINICAL (already appropriate) and maintained.
readiness_reason: After repair, the claim is directly supported by explicit methods and hemodynamics text with no unresolved attributions; removed/avoided unsupported directions about MAP being higher and exact p-values, and avoided unstated group size for the untreated peritonitis group.
original_claim: In domestic pigs (25–35 kg) with fecal peritonitis, pentoxifylline was infused IV continuously at 60 mg/h starting 120 minutes before peritonitis induction and continued through a 300-minute post-induction observation period; compared with untreated peritonitis pigs, the PTX-pretreated group had higher MAP at 180 and 210 minutes (p<0.05), lower SVR increases at 300 minutes (+36% vs +133% above baseline; p<0.05 at all time points except 30 min), and lower PVR increases at 300 minutes (+140% vs +462% above baseline; significant at 270 and 300 min, p<0.05).

citation.locator: RESULTS > Neutrophil Adhesiveness; MATERIALS AND METHODS (neutrophil adhesiveness assay); RESULTS > Histology; Fig. 3 caption; Fig. 4 caption; DISCUSSION (histology summary)

claim: Support is only partial for the candidate as written. The source reports that neutrophil adhesiveness was measured using a whole-blood glass cover-slip clearance assay (half clearance time), that neutrophil adhesiveness did not change significantly in untreated (test) pigs, and that pentoxifylline (PTF) pretreatment significantly reduced neutrophil adhesiveness as reflected by a 100% increase in half clearance time before peritonitis induction and a further 238% increase at 30 min after induction; the source also reports that TEM performed on postmortem tissues taken 5 h after peritonitis induction showed severe ultrastructural damage/leukostasis in test pigs and that PTF pretreatment attenuated these changes (improved capillary/sinusoidal patency; reduced occlusion and degranulating cells). The source does not provide the absolute half-clearance-time values in the text (only percent changes) and does not state the exact p-value comparators claimed (e.g., 'p<0.05 vs baseline' at both time points); it only states significance within group and between groups, without specifying baseline comparator in the prose.
source_text:
Measurements of neutrophil adhesiveness were undertaken using the technique of Boghossian (10). In the PTF group blood was obtained in heparinized tubes before the drug infusion was begun. Further blood samples were taken from both groups before PI and after 30 min. ... Thirty-five milliliters of blood was circulated in a temperature-controlled chamber at 37°C containing glass cover slips to which the neutrophils adhered. Neutrophil counts were made on samples taken from the chamber at 0, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 min. The time for the neutrophil count to decline to 50% of the baseline value was calculated and expressed as the half clearance time. A decrease in neutrophil adhesiveness is thus expressed as an increase in the half clearance time.

### *Neutrophil Adhesiveness*

In the test group there was no significant change in neutrophil adhesiveness (Fig. 2). However, pretreatment with PTF caused reduction in neutrophil adhesiveness reflected by a significant increase of 100% in half clearance time before PI, increasing by a further 238% 30 min after PI. There was a significant difference between the two groups both before and at 30 min after PI.

Postmortem samples of lung, liver, and spleen were taken for transmission electron microscopy (TEM).

### *Histology*

In the test group, lung tissue showed reduced alveolar capillary patency with occlusion by degranulating neutrophils and lymphocytes. There was disruption of the capillary endothelium and alveolar epithelium and the type II pneumocytes showed loss of their lamellar bodies. The liver demonstrated sinusoidal occlusion by degranulating neutrophils, lymphocytes, and activated Kupffer cells with endothelial hypertrophy and obliteration of the space of Disse. The spleen showed increased numbers of degranulating neutrophils, lymphocytes, and aggregations of platelets in the the red pulp, arterioles, and venous sinuses. Macrophages showed evidence of activation and contained large amounts of phagocytosed cell debris.

When compared to the test group, lung tissue from the PTF group showed almost normal capillary patency and only small numbers of neutrophils and lymphocytes. Capillary endothelium, alveolar epithelium, and type II pneumocytes appeared normal. Similarly, liver tissue showed relatively normal sinusoidal patency and a smaller number of neutrophils and lymphocytes. Endothelial damage was reduced, Kupffer cells were normal, and the space of Disse present. The spleen showed less neutrophils, lymphocytes, and platelet aggregates. Increased numbers of erythrocytes were seen in the red pulp with less occlusion of venous sinuses.

Fig 3. A) Transmission electron micrograph (TEM) of part of the alveolar wall from a pig lung taken 5 h after peritonitis induction. There is loss of capillary patency, with occlusion by PMN, lymphocytes, and platelets. ... B) Micrograph of the alveolar wall from a pig lung taken 5 h after peritonitis induction, but pretreated with PTF, showing improved capillary patency with little occlusion by PMN, lymphocytes, and platelets. ... D) TEM of a part of a pig liver taken 5 h after peritonitis induction, showing a sinusoid occluded by hypertrophic endothelial cells, erythrocytes, platelets, and cell debris. The space of Disse cannot be clearly seen. ... E) Micrograph of pig liver taken 5 h after peritonitis induction, but pretreated with PTF, showing improved sinusoidal patency, with little occlusion by PMN, lymphocytes, and platelets or cell debris. The endothelium shows normal architecture and easily defined space of Disse (arrowhead).

FIG. 4. A) TEM of pig spleen taken 5 h after peritonitis induction, showing part of the red pulp area but with few erythrocytes present. ... B) TEM of pig spleen 5 h after peritonitis induction, but pretreated with PTF. This shows the increased numbers of erythrocytes present within the red pulp area.

The histology of the test group shows severe damage to the lungs, liver, and spleen with aggregation of a large number of lymphocytes and degranulated neutrophils. ... In contrast, pretreatment with PTF prevented much of the ultrastructural damage, leukocyte aggregation, and neutrophil degranulation that occurred in the organs of the test animals.
verdict_explanation: Neutrophil adhesiveness assay description is supported (whole blood circulated over glass cover slips; half clearance time defined as time for count to decline to 50%). The directionality for untreated vs PTF is wrong: the source says untreated group had no significant change, while PTF reduced adhesiveness (increased half clearance time) with +100% before PI and +238% further increase 30 min after PI. The candidate's statement that PTF 'increased half-clearance time' matches the source, but its claim that untreated was 'unchanged' is supported; however, the candidate adds unsupported details about p-value comparators ('p<0.05 vs baseline' and 'p<0.05 vs untreated at both time points'); the source only states significant increases and significant differences between groups, without specifying baseline comparator in the prose. The TEM timepoint '5 hours' is supported via figure captions and the animals being killed at 300 min; descriptive organ findings (occlusion/leukostasis/degranulation; attenuation with PTF and improved patency) are supported, though some candidate specifics (e.g., 'largely prevented', 'maintained sinusoidal patency', 'prevented degranulation') should be phrased as 'attenuated'/'reduced' per source wording.
readiness_reason: As written, the candidate includes unsupported quantitative/p-value comparator detail and misstates the direction of the group difference implied by Fig. 2 rendering; it must be split and repaired into supported subclaims without adding unstated p-value comparators or absolute values not given in the text.

In experiment 1 (rats killed 53 h after infection), PTX pretreatment was associated with higher food intake on postinfection days 1 and 2 (13.5±3.0 vs 6.5±5.2 g dry matter/day; and 21.9±0.7 vs 13.8±5.8), less body weight loss at day 1 (2.4±2.7 vs 12.6±6.2 g lost) and a more favorable cumulative weight change over days 1–2 (+10.5±3.0 vs −4.1±8.0 g), higher gastrocnemius muscle weight (1.17±0.07 vs 1.03±0.03 g) and gastrocnemius protein mass (239±20 vs 208±7 mg), and higher gastrocnemius absolute protein synthesis rate (ASR; 22.9±2.4 vs 17.3±2.8 mg/day; P<0.05 vs INF-C); gastrocnemius fractional synthesis rate (Ks) was 9.72±1.04 vs 8.27±1.39 %/day with P<0.06 vs INF-C. In experiment 2 (10× higher E. coli dose than experiment 1), food intake was higher in PTX-INF than INF-C on days 1–3 and cumulative weight change on day 6 was −10.5 g (INF-C) vs +11.0 g (PTX-INF), with Fig. 3 indicating P<0.001 vs INF-C.
source_text:
At 200–210 g body wt, rats were divided into three groups. The infected control group of rats (INF-C,  n = 5 ) was injected intraperitoneally with saline 30 min before the injection of  5.4 ± 0.4 × 10^7  live Escherichia coli into a lateral tail vein. ... In this group, PTX was injected intraperitoneally (100 mg/kg) 30 min before E. coli administration. ... Rats were killed 53 h after infection for measurement of protein synthesis rates and protein mass in the gastrocnemius muscle and liver.

In experiment 1, the intake of INF-C rats on postinfection days 1 and 2 was, respectively, 30 and 63% of their intake before the infection. This anorexia was significantly limited by pretreatment with PTX since intakes were  13.5 ± 3.0  and  21.9 ± 0.7  g dry matter/day in the PTX-INF group on days 1 and 2, respectively, vs.  6.5 ± 5.2  and  13.8 ± 5.8  in the INF-C group.

During the 1st day after infection, the PTX-INF group lost significantly less body weight than the INF-C group ( 2.4 ± 2.7  and  12.6 ± 6.2  g, respectively). This difference increased during the 2nd day since the cumulative weight change of days 1 and 2 was  10.5 ± 3.0  g in the PTX-INF group and  -4.1 ± 8.0  g in the INF-C rats (expt 1, Fig. 2).

claim: In 14 anesthetized, ventilated (and paralyzed) mongrel dogs given an IV bolus of 2 mg/kg Escherichia coli endotoxin and then subjected 30 minutes later to progressive cardiac tamponade, pretreatment with IV pentoxifylline (20 mg/kg bolus followed by 20 mg/kg·h continuous infusion) resulted in lower DO2crit (9.1 ± 1.8 vs 11.6 ± 2.4 ml/kg·min; p < .05), higher O2ERcrit (70.6 ± 14.0% vs 49.3 ± 14.6%; p < .05), and a steeper VO2/DO2 dependency slope (0.80 ± 0.28 vs 0.43 ± 0.19; p < .05) compared with controls; VO2 at DO2crit was 6.3 ± 1.1 vs 5.3 ± 1.0 ml/kg·min (p = NS).
source_text:
Fourteen anesthetized, ventilated, and paralyzed dogs, received intravenous 2 mg/kg of Escherichia coli endotoxin followed by a continuous infusion of 20 ml/kg·h of saline. 30 min later tamponade was induced by repeated bolus injections of warm saline into the pericardial space. Seven dogs were pretreated with PTX as an intravenous bolus of 20 mg/kg, followed by a continuous infusion at 20 mg/kg·h, and the other seven dogs served as a control group. ... In addition, the critical Do2 (Do2crit) was lower and the critical oxygen extraction ratio was higher in the PTX treated than in the control group (9.1 ± 1.8 vs. 11.6 ± 2.4 ml/kg·min, and 70.6 ± 14.0 vs. 49.3 ± 14.6%, both p < .05). The VO2/Do2 dependency slope was also steeper in the PTX-treated than in the control group (.80 ± .28 vs. .43 ± .19, p < .05). ...

"The dogs were randomly divided into two groups. The PTX group (seven dogs) received PTX (Pentoxifylline, Trental; Hoechst AG, Frankfurt/Main, Germany) as an intravenous bolus of 20 mg/kg (20 mg/ml solution) followed by a continuous infusion of 20 mg/kg·h (10 mg/ml) until the end of the study. The other seven dogs served as a control group. After second baseline measurements (baseline 2) 30 min later, each dog received a slow intravenous bolus of 2 mg/kg of Escherichia coli endotoxin (055B5; Difco Laboratories, Detroit, MI), and followed by a saline infusion at 20 ml/kg·h throughout the study. Third measurements were performed 30 min after endotoxin administration (baseline 3).

Cardiac tamponade was then induced by repeated bolus injections of normal saline heated to 37°C into the pericardial space." ...

"\dot{V}O2 at Do2crit was slightly higher in the PTX than in the control group (6.3 ± 1.1 vs. 5.3 ± 1.0 ml/kg·min, p = NS). The Do2crit was significantly lower and O2ERcrit higher in the PTX treated than in the control group (9.1 ± 1.8 vs. 11.6 ± 2.4 ml/kg·min and 70.6 ± 14.0 vs. 49.3 ± 14.6%, respectively, both p < .05). The slope of \dot{V}O2/Do2-dependent line was also steeper in the PTX than in the control group (.80 ± .28 vs. .43 ± .19, p < .05)"
verdict_explanation: All requested numeric outcomes and p-values (DO2crit, O2ERcrit, VO2/DO2 dependency slope, and VO2 at DO2crit with p = NS) and group sizes (7 vs 7; total 14) are explicitly supported in the source. claim: In male Sprague–Dawley rats given endotoxin (Salmonella typhimurium, 20 mg/kg ip), concurrent pentoxifylline (PTX, 50 mg/kg ip) attenuated endotoxin-associated impairment of pulmonary artery ring vasorelaxation measured ex vivo 6 hr later: with ACh 10^-6 M, remaining PE-induced ring tension was 86 ± 21 mg (PTX+endotoxin) vs 216 ± 16 mg (endotoxin alone) vs 11 ± 4 mg (saline controls); with A23187 10^-6 M, remaining tension was 93 ± 11 mg vs 185 ± 26 mg vs 11 ± 6 mg; with SNP 10^-6 M, remaining tension was 7 ± 4 mg vs 54 ± 10 mg vs 0 mg. The study reports n=10 rings/5 rats per group; the ACh figure caption indicates *P<0.05 vs control and +P<0.05 vs endotoxin at the same concentration; the A23187 and SNP figure captions state the same annotation scheme, while the RESULTS text states endotoxin alone differs from control at P<0.05 and that PTX+endotoxin is less impaired than endotoxin alone at P<0.05; the RESULTS text states PTX+endotoxin is impaired vs controls at P<0.05 for ACh and A23187, and states PTX+endotoxin response to SNP is similar to controls (no p-value given).
source_text:
METHODS: "Awake, fed rats were administered endotoxin (Salmonella typhimurium, 20 mg/kg ip) ... Control rats received an equal volume of saline. A third group received concurrent injections of pentoxifylline (50 mg/kg ip) and endotoxin. Pulmonary vasomotor control mechanisms were studied in isolated pulmonary arterial rings 6 hr after treatment." ... "The ring tension remaining in the rings in response to each dose of vasorelaxing agent was expressed in milligrams of PE-induced tension. Five rats/10 rings were studied in all groups."

RESULTS (ACh): "Pulmonary artery rings from saline-injected rats were precontracted to 277 ± 15 mg of PE-induced tension and relaxed to 11 ± 4 mg tension with ACh 10-6 M. Rings from endotoxin-treated rats were precontracted to 274 ± 15 mg tension, and 216 ± 16 mg of PE-induced tension remained in response to ACh 10-6 M (P < 0.05 versus control). Rings from PTX plus endotoxin-treated rats were precontracted with PE to 290 ± 18 mg tension with 86 ± 21 mg of tension remaining in response to ACh 10-6 M." ... "PTX plus endotoxin-treated rats had an impaired response to ACh compared to controls (P < 0.05). However, PTX plus endotoxin-treated rats had significantly less impairment ... than endotoxin (alone)-treated rats (P < 0.05)." 
FIG. 1 caption: "Values are means ± SEM (n = 10 rings/5 rats for each group). * P < 0.05 vs control and + P < 0.05 vs endotoxin (alone) at same concentration of agonist." 
FIG. 1 table row for 6: "6 | 11 ± 4 | 216 ± 16 | 86 ± 21*+"

RESULTS (A23187): "Controls were precontracted to 303 ± 23 mg of PE-induced tension and relaxed to 11 ± 6 mg tension with A23187 10-6 M. In endotoxin-treated rats precontracted to 281 ± 15 mg tension, 185 ± 26 mg of PE-induced tension remained in response to A23187 10-6 M (P < 0.05 versus control). Rings from PTX plus endotoxin-treated rats were precontracted with PE to 283 ± 19 mg tension with 93 ± 11 mg of tension remaining in response to A23187 10-6 M." ... "Thus, PTX plus endotoxin-treated rats had an impaired response to A23187 compared to controls (P < 0.05). However, PTX plus endotoxin-treated rats had significantly less impairment ... than endotoxin (alone)-treated rats (P < 0.05)."
FIG. 2 caption: "Values are means ± SEM (n = 10 rings/5 rats for each group). * P < 0.05 vs control and +P < 0.05 vs endotoxin (alone) at same concentration of agonist." 
FIG. 2 table row for 6: "6 | 11 ± 6 | 185 ± 26 | 93 ± 11"

RESULTS (SNP): "As shown in Fig. 3, controls were precontracted to 298 ± 14 mg of PE-induced tension and relaxed to 0 mg tension with SNP 10-6 M. In endotoxin-treated rats precontracted to 299 ± 24 mg tension, 54 ± 10 mg of PE-induced tension remained in response to SNP 10-6 M (P < 0.05 versus control). Rings from PTX plus endotoxin-treated rats were precontracted with PE to 270 ± 16 mg tension with 7 ± 4 mg of tension remaining in response to SNP 10-6 M. Thus, PTX plus endotoxin-treated rats had a response to SNP that was similar to that of controls and less impaired than endotoxin (alone)-treated rats (P < 0.05)."
FIG. 3 caption: "Values are means ± SEM (n = 10 rings/5 rats for each group). * P < 0.05 vs control and +P < 0.05 vs endotoxin (alone) at same concentration of agonist." 
FIG. 3 table row for 6: "6 | 0 | 54 ± 10 | 7 ± 4"
verdict_explanation: Group structure (5 rats/10 rings per group), dosing (endotoxin 20 mg/kg ip; PTX 50 mg/kg ip concurrent), timing (6 hr), and the reported remaining-tension values at 10^-6 M for ACh, A23187, and SNP are supported. However, the candidate’s specific p-value statement for SNP vs control as "p=NS" is not stated in the source; the RESULTS only says the PTX+endotoxin response to SNP was "similar" to controls (no p-value provided). Also, in the A23187 table provided here, the 10^-6 M row lacks the *+ symbols even though the figure caption defines them; therefore significance at that exact concentration is clearly asserted in RESULTS text but the table markup as shown is inconsistent. The candidate’s significance assertions for ACh and A23187 (improved vs endotoxin alone p<0.05; still impaired vs control p<0.05) are supported by the RESULTS text and (for ACh) by the Fig. 1 table/caption.

claim: In Vogel et al. (2023), inflammatory status was evaluated using CRP and IL-6 (and, in a 25-patient subgroup with matched controls, also total IgG). CRP increased from median 0.10 mg dL−1 (IQR 0.06–0.39) during active CS (n=80) to median 0.48 mg dL−1 (IQR 0.14–0.90) at 1 month after surgery (n=66; P≤.001 vs active CS). In the 25-patient subgroup, IL-6 increased from median 1.7 pg mL−1 (IQR 1.5–2.5) during active CS to median 7.2 pg mL−1 (IQR 3.3–11.7) at 1 month after surgery (P≤.001 vs active CS) and was higher than matched controls (median 2.0 pg mL−1 [1.5–3.6], P≤.001). In a post-hoc analysis dividing the 25-patient subgroup by BMI at the time of active CS, patients with BMI >30 kg m−2 had higher 1-month IL-6 (median 9.2 pg mL−1 [6.1–13.7]) than those with BMI <30 kg m−2 (median 4.0 pg mL−1 [2.5–9.1], P=.03).
source_text:
### Laboratory analyses

Venous blood samples were drawn following overnight fasting at the time of diagnosis and as part of the follow-up visits after successful surgery. The biochemical analyses were performed in the laboratory of the Endocrine Department and in the Institute of Laboratory Medicine of Ludwig-Maximilians-University Hospital Munich using standard methods. Measurements of interleukin-6 (IL-6), C-reactive protein (CRP) and total immunoglobulin G (IgG) of the subgroup of 25 patients with CS and 25 age-, gender-, and BMI-matched control subjects were made in one run at the end of the observation period using a Cobas 8000 analyzer (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany).
...
### Remission phase after surgery for CS is characterized by a state of low-grade inflammation

In the cohort of 80 patients, early remission 1 month after surgery was characterized by a 4.8-fold increase in CRP concentrations compared with the time of active CS [median CRP 0.48 mg dL<sup>-1</sup> (0.14–0.90) vs 0.10 mg dL<sup>-1</sup> (0.06–0.39),  $P \leq .001$ ].
...
**Figure 1.** C-reactive protein (mg dL<sup>-1</sup>; reference ≤0.5 mg dL<sup>-1</sup>, dashed line) during active Cushing's syndrome (CS) and after successful operation (OP) up to 24 months (mo). Active CS *n* = 80, 1 mo *n* = 66, 3 mo *n* = 61, 6 mo *n* = 75, 12 mo *n* = 73, 24 mo *n* = 65.
...
Interleukin-6 levels showed a 4.2-fold increase 1 month after surgery compared with the time point of active CS [median IL-6 7.2 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (3.3–11.7) vs 1.7 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (1.5–2.5),  $P \leq .001$ ], and an elevation of more than 3-fold compared with the 25 matched control subjects [median IL-6 7.2 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (3.3–11.7) vs 2.0 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (1.5–3.6),  $P \leq .001$ ].
...
When dividing the patient subgroup in a post-hoc analysis according to BMI < 30 kg m<sup>-2</sup> and BMI > 30 kg m<sup>-2</sup> at the time of active CS, inflammatory markers revealed significant differences between the groups (Figure 3), with a median IL-6 of 9.2 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (6.1–13.7) in BMI > 30 kg m<sup>-2</sup> at 1 month follow-up compared with 4.0 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (2.5–9.1) in BMI < 30 kg m<sup>-2</sup> ( $P = .03$ ; Figure 3A).

Differential blood count/platelets are discussed elsewhere in Results/Discussion, but the candidate’s framing as part of the inflammatory-status evaluation set in the Methods section is not supported as written. claim: Vogel et al. (2023) report that CRP concentrations 3 months after successful surgery for Cushing's syndrome correlated inversely with (i) normalized grip strength at 12 months (N=50, Spearman's coefficient −0.371, R2=0.155, P=.008) and (ii) SF-36 Physical Component Summary at 12 months (N=38, Spearman's coefficient −0.356, R2=0.127, P=.028). They also report group-wise comparisons based on CRP at 3 months after surgery (CRP-low <0.2 mg/dL; CRP-medium ≥0.2 and ≤0.5 mg/dL; CRP-high >0.5 mg/dL) in which 12-month muscle function differed between CRP groups (normalized grip strength p=0.044; chair rising test p=0.050). They further state that after adjustment for age and BMI, the influence of 3-month CRP on 12-month muscle function remained significant in multivariable linear regression (Table S6), whereas CRP no longer had a significant influence on quality of life, with age and BMI suggested as possible confounders.
source_text:
### Association between low-grade inflammation during the early remission and patient outcome

C-reactive protein and IL-6 concentrations during early remission showed an inverse correlation with muscle function and QoL during follow-up in the univariate analysis (Figure 4 and Table S5). In group-wise comparisons, muscle function outcome 1 year after surgery was better in patients with CRP concentrations  $< 0.2 \text{ mg dL}^{-1}$  (CRP-low group) at 3-month follow-up, with less muscular impairments compared with patients with CRP concentrations between 0.2 and  $0.5 \text{ mg dL}^{-1}$  (CRP-medium group) or  $> 0.5 \text{ mg dL}^{-1}$  (CRP-high group; Figure 5A). ... After adjustment for age and BMI, the influence of CRP levels 3 months after surgery on muscle

function 1 year in remission remained significant in the multi-variable linear regression analysis (Table S6). However, CRP no longer had a significant influence on QoL, making age and BMI possible confounders for this relationship.

**Figure 4.** (A) Relationship between C-reactive protein concentrations (mg dL<sup>-1</sup>) 3 months after successful surgery for Cushing's syndrome and age- and gender-corrected grip strength (normalized grip strength, % of normal controls) 12 months after surgery. Line indicates estimated linear regression line.  $N$  = 50, Spearman's coefficient  $-0.371$ ,  $R^2$  = 0.155,  $P$  = .008. (B) Relationship between C-reactive protein concentrations (mg dL<sup>-1</sup>) 3 months after successful surgery for Cushing's syndrome and Short Form 36 health survey (SF-36) Physical Component Summary 12 months after surgery. Line indicates estimated linear regression line.  $N$  = 38, Spearman's coefficient  $-0.356$ ,  $R^2$  = 0.127,  $P$  = .028.

**Figure 5.** (A) Muscle function and (B) quality of life (QoL) in patients with Cushing's syndrome 12 months after successful surgery. Division into groups was made according to C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels at the time of 3 months after surgery (CRP-high group: CRP  $>0.5$  mg dL $^{-1}$ ,  $n = 22$ ; CRP-medium group: CRP  $\geq 0.2$  and  $\leq 0.5$  mg dL $^{-1}$ ,  $n = 19$ ; CRP-low group: CRP  $<0.2$  mg dL $^{-1}$ ,  $n = 20$ ; IL-6-high group: IL-6  $\geq 6.0$  pg mL $^{-1}$ ,  $n = 13$ ; IL-6-low group: IL-6  $<6.0$  pg mL $^{-1}$ ,  $n = 10$ ). Muscle function of the groups (CRP-high  $n = 19$ ; CRP-medium  $n = 14$ ; CRP-low  $n = 18$ ) is presented with age- and gender-corrected grip strength (normalized grip strength, % of normal controls) and chair rising test (s). Quality of life of the groups (CRP-high  $n = 16$ ; CRP-medium  $n = 10$ ; CRP-low  $n = 11$ ; IL-6-high  $n = 7$ ; IL-6-low  $n = 9$ ) is presented with the questionnaires Cushing's quality of life (CushingQoL; range 0 worst QoL,  100 best QoL), Tubingen Cushing's disease quality of life inventory (Tubingen CD-25; range 0 best QoL, 100 worst QoL) and the Short Form 36 health survey (SF-36) Physical Component Summary ( $>50$  better QoL than reference population,  $<50$  poorer QoL than reference population). Comparisons were performed by Kruskal–Wallis test or Mann–Whitney *U* test.

[Discussion]
"We further investigated whether CRP concentrations correlated with clinical features of glucocorticoid withdrawal such as impaired muscle function5 and low QoL.27 Indeed, inflammatory markers were inversely correlated with muscle function in the further postoperative course. This effect was also evident after adjustment for age and BMI in the multivariable linear regression analysis. ... Inflammatory markers also showed an inverse correlation with QoL in the univariate analysis, but this relationship was no longer significant after adjusting for age and BMI, indicating possible confounding variables."

claim: In this retrospective observational study of postoperative remission in Cushing’s syndrome, Vogel et al. (2023) report that CRP and IL-6 during early remission correlated inversely with muscle function during follow-up, and state that CRP and IL-6 could serve as easily measurable biomarkers/surrogate parameters for clinical features of glucocorticoid withdrawal syndrome (with potential use for monitoring glucocorticoid replacement adjustments), while emphasizing that the observational design demonstrates associations, not causation, and noting it is unclear whether the inflammation–myopathy relationship is associative or causal.
source_text:
Thus, our study provides evidence that easily measurable quantitative biomarkers—CRP and IL-6—could serve as surrogate parameters for the clinical features of glucocorticoid withdrawal syndrome and could potentially be used to monitor adjustments of the glucocorticoid replacement dose. However, this has yet to be shown in a prospective study with specific assessment of glucocorticoid

withdrawal syndrome. ... Nevertheless, it is unclear whether this is an association or causally related given that the molecular processes underlying glucocorticoid-induced myopathy are poorly understood.

...

This is an observational study and therefore demonstrates only associations and not causation.

...

C-reactive protein and IL-6 could serve as biomarkers to monitor patients during the glucocorticoid withdrawal phase.
verdict_explanation: Supported that the authors describe CRP/IL-6 as potential surrogate parameters/biomarkers to monitor glucocorticoid withdrawal phase and report inverse correlations with muscle function during follow-up, including 12 months (1 year) outcomes. The limitation language is explicitly stated by the authors (“observational… only associations and not causation”), and the Discussion explicitly says it is unclear whether the relationship is association vs causal. However, the candidate over-specifies timing and directionality as “early post-operative CRP and IL-6 elevations” being “predictive biomarkers” for “prolonged glucocorticoid withdrawal symptoms” and “delayed functional muscle recovery”: the paper frames these as correlations/associations and potential surrogate parameters/biomarkers; it does not explicitly claim prediction, does not explicitly state “prolonged symptoms,” and does not present CRP/IL-6 as validated surrogate endpoints. Also, the muscle-function association is described for CRP and IL-6 together in univariate analysis; multivariable significance is stated specifically for CRP (3 months) and muscle function (1 year).
readiness_reason: Key elements (biomarker/surrogate language; association with muscle function; non-causation limitation; unclear association vs causality statement) are directly supported by quoted source text with clear locators and can be faithfully compressed without adding prediction/validation claims.

claim: Pucheu-Haston et al. (2014) used 6 healthy sexually intact adult mixed-breed dogs (mean age, 4.6 years). In a nonsensitized model of IgE-mediated cutaneous hypersensitivity, each dog received intradermal injections (0.1 mL each) of PBS solution, histamine phosphate (0.275 mg/mL), and rabbit-origin IgG polyclonal anti-canine IgE antibodies (0.1 mg/mL) on day 0, then the same injection/measurement procedures were repeated on day 30 (2 hours after discontinuation of pentoxifylline treatment) and on day 37 (after discontinuation of pentoxifylline administration). Pentoxifylline was given orally, compounded into a liquid, at 20 mg/kg every 8 hours (3 times daily) from day 2 through day 30 (29 days).
source_text:
**Animals**—6 healthy adult mixed-breed dogs.

**Dogs**—Six healthy sexually intact male and female mixed-breed dogs (mean age, 4.6 years) were used for the study.

**Procedures**—Intradermal injections (0.1 mL each) of PBS solution, histamine phosphate, and cross-linking rabbit-origin anti-canine IgE antibodies (3 injections/dog) were administered at 0 hours on day 0; wheal sizes were evaluated at 20 minutes, 6 hours, and 24 hours. ... On day 2, treatment with pentoxifylline (20 mg/kg, PO, q 8 h) was initiated and continued until day 30. For each dog, injection, measurement, and biopsy procedures were repeated on days 30 to 31 and on days 37 to 38 (ie, after discontinuation of pentoxifylline administration).

**Experimental design**—... intradermal injections (0.1 mL each) of PBS solution, histamine phosphate (0.275 mg/mL), and rabbit-origin IgG polyclonal anti-canine IgE antibodies (0.1 mg/mL) were administered; time of injection was designated as 0 hours. ...

On day 2, oral treatment with pentoxifylline was initiated at a dosage of 20 mg/kg (compounded into a liquid to allow precise dosing) 3 times daily. Treatment continued for 29 days (until day 30). Two hours after discontinuation of drug treatment on day 30, each dog was sedated with dexmedetomidine and again administered the intradermal injections, as performed on day 0, this time on the right side of the thorax. ...

On day 37, the sedation and intradermal injection procedures were repeated for each dog ...

**Treatment with pentoxifylline**—Treatment with pentoxifylline (20 mg/kg, PO, q 8 h) was initiated on day 2 and continued until 2 hours before the dogs were sedated on day 30.
verdict_explanation: Supported: n=6; healthy sexually intact adult mixed-breed dogs with mean age 4.6 years; intradermal injection volume 0.1 mL each; concentrations for histamine phosphate (0.275 mg/mL) and anti-canine IgE antibodies (0.1 mg/mL); PTX oral dosing 20 mg/kg PO q8h/3 times daily; PTX compounded into a liquid; PTX given day 2 through day 30 (29 days); day-30 repeat injections performed 2 hours after discontinuation; another repeat on day 37 after discontinuation (7 days later). Not supported as written: the candidate specifies a challenge at baseline 'Day 0', on-treatment 'Day 30, 2 hours post-dose' and washout 'Day 37 after a 7-day washout'—the source states 'Two hours after discontinuation of drug treatment on day 30' (not 2 hours post-dose), and it does not explicitly use the term 'washout' (though day 37 is 7 days after day 30).

claim: In 6 healthy adult mixed-breed dogs given intradermal anti-canine IgE, oral pentoxifylline (20 mg/kg PO q8h) given from day 2 through day 30 (29 days) had no significant effect (P > 0.05) on the immediate (20-minute) macroscopic reaction (subjective erythema/induration features and measured wheal area) compared with pretreatment findings.
source_text:
“Treatment with pentoxifylline from day 2 through day 30 had no effects on the subjective features of the macroscopic immediate reaction (erythema and induration), and there was no significant ( P > 0.05 ) effect on wheal area, compared with findings prior to the administration of pentoxifylline (Figures 1 and 2).”
...
“In the present study, we investigated the effects of orally administered pentoxifylline on the development of immediate and late-phase cutaneous reactions in response to intradermal injections of anti-canine IgE antibodies (equivalent to IgE-mediated responses) in healthy adult dogs. We determined that treatment with pentoxifylline for 29 days did not result in significant inhibition of immediate reactivity to anti-IgE antibodies.”
...
“Pentoxifylline administered orally at a dosage of 20 mg/kg 3 times daily for 29 days failed to induce significant suppression of the immediate wheal-and-flare reaction in the study dogs.”
...
“Figure 1—Mean ± SE wheal area measurements in 6 healthy adult mixed-breed dogs obtained 20 minutes, 6 hours, and 24 hours after separate intradermal injections of cross-linking rabbit-origin anti-canine IgE antibodies (0.1 mL [gray column]) and PBS solution (0.1 mL [white column]) administered prior to treatment with pentoxifylline (injection procedures on day 0 with measurement procedures on days 0 and 1; A), after oral administration of 20 mg of pentoxifylline/kg 3 times daily beginning day 2 to day 30 (injection procedures on day 30 with measurement procedures on days 30 and 31; B), and 7 days after discontinuation of pentoxifylline administration (injection procedures on day 37 with measurement procedures on days 37 and 38; C).”
...
“Figure 2—Mean ± SE wheal area measurements in 6 healthy adult mixed-breed dogs obtained 20 minutes (A), 6 hours (B), and 24 hours (C) after an intradermal injection of anti-canine IgE antibodies (0.1 mL) administered prior to treatment with pentoxifylline (injection procedure on day 0 with measurement procedures on days 0 and 1), after oral administration of 20 mg of pentoxifylline/kg 3 times daily beginning day 2 to day 30 (injection procedure on day 30 with measurement procedures on days 30 and 31), and 7 days after discontinuation of pentoxifylline administration (injection procedure on day 37 with measurement procedures on days 37 and 38).”
verdict_explanation: Supported: the study states pentoxifylline (20 mg/kg PO q8h; given day 2 through day 30, i.e., 29 days) had no effect on subjective immediate features (erythema/induration) and no significant effect on wheal area versus pretreatment, with P > 0.05 explicitly reported. Not fully supported: the candidate’s approximate 20-minute anti-IgE wheal areas “~180 mm² at baseline vs ~200 mm² on-treatment and ~180 mm² after washout” are not provided as exact numbers in the text; the figures shown in the supplied source are graphical and any numeric values are approximate readings rather than reported exact values. Also, the claim’s phrase “compared with pretreatment baseline” is supported generally, but the candidate’s three specific ~180/~200/~180 values should be treated as non-verbatim approximations from figures and are not stated as exact values elsewhere in the provided source text.
readiness_reason: Although the non-significance (P > 0.05) for 20-minute wheal area and the lack of subjective erythema/induration effects are directly supported, the candidate includes specific approximate wheal-area values (~180/~200/~180 mm²) that are not reported as exact numeric results in the text; they appear to be reader-estimates from figures. To determine the duration of pentoxifylline-mediated inhibition of the macroscopic cutaneous late-phase reaction, the injection and measurement procedure was repeated on day 37 (1 week after cessation of pentoxifylline administration) with further measurement of wheal area at 24 hours after injection (day 38). On day 38, the 6-hour late-phase reaction was not significantly ( $P < 0.05$ ) different from the pretreatment wheal area (Figure 2), whereas the 24-hour reaction was somewhat larger than the pretreatment wheal area.

claim: In adult male Sprague–Dawley rats subjected to CLP sepsis, PTX (50 mg/kg body wt in 1 mL normal saline) was infused intravenously over 90 min starting 1 h after CLP. At 20 h after CLP or sham operation, plasma ADM was increased in CLP vs sham (673 ± 142 vs 164 ± 12.7 pg/mL; P < 0.05) and was unaffected by PTX treatment (661 ± 95 pg/mL). Plasma TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 were significantly elevated at 20 h after CLP, and PTX significantly attenuated these cytokine increases (Fig. 3); cytokine levels in PTX-treated animals were slightly elevated vs sham but not statistically significantly different from sham. At 20 h after CLP, ADM-induced relaxation to rat ADM (10^-7 M) was reduced in NE-preconstricted aortic rings and intestinal resistance vessels; PTX treatment prevented this reduction such that there was no significant reduction vs sham (aorta: sham 76.4 ± 2.6%, CLP 56.8 ± 4.2%, CLP+PTX 73.2 ± 5.3%; intestine: sham 94.5 ± 2.4%, CLP 78.4 ± 2.9%, CLP+PTX 87.8 ± 1.9%). In the methods, the NE concentrations were 5 × 10^-9 M for aortic rings and 2.4 × 10^-7 M for the isolated intestine preparation.
source_text:
*Administration of PTX.* One hour after CLP, animals were re-anesthetized with methoxyflurane inhalation and the femoral vein was cannulated using PE-50 tubing. PTX (50 mg/kg body wt in 1 mL normal saline solution; Sigma, St. Louis, MO) was infused through the venous catheter at a constant infusion rate over a period of 90 min. ... Vehicle-treated septic animals received 1 mL normal saline solution intravenously for 90 min. Sham-operated animals received neither PTX nor saline.

**Determination of plasma ADM and inflammatory cytokines.** Twenty hours after CLP or sham operation, whole blood was drawn from a femoral artery catheter into a syringe. ...

**Effects of PTX on plasma ADM and inflammatory cytokines.** Twenty hours after CLP, the plasma level of ADM was increased from  $164 \pm 12.7$  to  $673 \pm 142$  pg/mL ( $P < 0.05$ ) and the level was unaffected by treatment with PTX ( $661 \pm 95$  pg/mL) (Fig. 2). Plasma levels of TNF- $\alpha$ , IL-1 $\beta$ , and IL-6 were all significantly elevated 20 h after the onset of sepsis. However, treatment with PTX significantly attenuated the increase in inflammatory cytokines in septic animals (Fig. 3). Although the plasma cytokine levels in PTX-treated animals were slightly elevated when compared with those of sham-operated animals, there were no statistically significant differences between these two groups (Fig. 3).

*Isolation of aortic rings and determination of ADM-induced relaxation.* ... When the basal tension became stable, a submaximal contraction of ~400 mg was induced by  $5 imes 10^{-9}$  M norepinephrine (Sigma). Synthetic rat ADM (Peninsula Labs, Belmont, CA) at a concentration of  $10^{-7}$  M was then applied ...

*Isolation of the small intestine and determination of ADM-induced relaxation.* ... blood vessels in the isolated gut were constricted with  $2.4 imes 10^{-7}$  M NE ... On pressure stabilization, synthetic rat ADM ( $10^{-7}$  M) was then applied ...

**Effects of PTX on ADM-induced relaxation.** Application of ADM to vessels from sham-operated animals induced  $76.4 \pm 2.6\%$  relaxation in NE-preconstricted aortic rings (Fig. 1A) and  $94.5 \pm 2.4\%$  relaxation in intestinal vessels (Fig. 1B). Vascular responsiveness to ADM 20 h after CLP was significantly reduced in both the aortic rings ( $56.8 \pm 4.2\%$ ) and intestinal vessels ( $78.4 \pm 2.9\%$ ). However, vessels isolated from septic animals that received PTX treatment displayed no significant reduction in ADM responsiveness 20 h after CLP (aortic rings,  $73.2 \pm 5.3\%$ ; intestinal vessels,  $87.8 \pm 1.9\%$ ) as compared with vessels from sham-operated animals (Fig. 1).
verdict_explanation: Correct on model/species/sex, PTX dose (50 mg/kg), vehicle volume (1 mL saline), route (IV), timing (1 h post-CLP), infusion duration (90 min), endpoint timing (20 h), ADM values (164 ± 12.7; 673 ± 142; 661 ± 95) and P<0.05 vs sham for CLP (and figure indicates CLP+PTX also vs sham), and on ex vivo relaxation percentages and ADM concentration (10^-7 M) plus NE concentration for intestine (2.4 × 10^-7 M). However: (1) the claim says cytokine numeric values and P-value attributions versus vehicle and sham; the paper’s Fig. 3 in the provided text gives only approximate bar heights without exact means±SEM, and the Results text does not state the numeric cytokine concentrations, so those specific ~15/~30, ~20/~90, ~600/~2000 values are not directly supported here; (2) for aortic rings, the NE concentration in Methods is 5 × 10^-9 M (the candidate incorrectly states 2.4 × 10^-7 M for aorta); (3) the candidate states plasma ADM was “not significantly changed vs CLP+vehicle (661±95 vs 673±142 pg/mL; both P<0.05 vs sham)”: the source states ADM level was “unaffected by treatment with PTX” and provides P<0.05 only for the increase to 673±142 vs sham; the star in Fig. 2 indicates significance vs sham but the Results text does not explicitly report a P-value for CLP+PTX vs sham.
readiness_reason: As written, the candidate includes specific cytokine concentration values and some P-value attributions that are not explicitly reported in the supplied source text (Fig. 3 shown only as approximate bar heights; no exact cytokine means±SEM stated). The aortic NE concentration is also misstated in the candidate. A witness-ready FRD requires splitting and limiting to supported elements.
original_claim: In adult male Sprague-Dawley rats with CLP sepsis, pentoxifylline 50 mg/kg in 1 mL saline given as a continuous IV infusion over 90 minutes starting 1 hour post-CLP reduced plasma TNF-α (~15 vs ~30 pg/mL), IL-1β (~20 vs ~90 pg/mL), and IL-6 (~600 vs ~2000 pg/mL) versus CLP+vehicle at 20 hours (P<0.05 vs CLP+vehicle; reported as non-significant vs sham), while plasma adrenomedullin was not significantly changed versus CLP+vehicle (661±95 vs 673±142 pg/mL; both P<0.05 vs sham). In the same study, PTX restored ADM-induced relaxation ex vivo after norepinephrine preconstriction (ADM 10^-7 M; norepinephrine 2.4×10^-7 M) in thoracic aorta (73.2±5.3% vs 56.8±4.2%; P<0.05) and small intestine resistance vessels (87.8±1.9% vs 78.4±2.9%; P<0.05) compared with CLP+vehicle (reported as non-significant vs sham).

claim: Support is established that, in a Wistar rat caecal ligation and puncture (CLP) sepsis model using two 21-gauge needle holes, animals were allocated to CLP-only or pentoxifylline (PTF) timing groups (1 hour before CLP; 1, 10, or 16 hours after CLP), and 10 animals per group were reanaesthetised and sacrificed at 6, 12, or 18 hours postoperatively. Resting membrane potential was measured and used (with the Nernst equation and chloride space assumptions) to calculate intracellular/extracellular water and electrolyte partition, including intracellular Na, K, and Cl concentrations. Two-way ANOVA showed between-group differences for intracellular sodium (P<.001), intracellular potassium (P<.05), and intracellular chloride (P<.001), but not for intracellular water. Figure-embedded tables report intracellular Na (Normal 10.0 at time 0; CLP 11.7 at 6h, 15.2 at 12h, 17.9 at 18h), intracellular Cl (Normal 4.5 at time 0; CLP 5.5 at 6h, 6.2 at 12h, 7.0 at 18h), intracellular K (Normal 155 at time 0; CLP 145 at 6h, 135 at 12h, 125 at 18h), and intracellular water (Normal 0.285 at time 0; CLP 0.285 at 6h, 0.300 at 12h, 0.315 at 18h). The Results text also states Bonferroni tests were used to compare PTF groups to CLP at each time point and describes specific significant reductions for intracellular sodium, chloride, and potassium at stated timepoints; however, the provided text does not include a complete Table 1 with all Bonferroni significance statements in tabular form.
source_text:
A previously reported caecal ligation and puncture (CLP) model of hyperdynamic sepsis in Wistar rats was used. ...

The animals were randomly allocated to 5 groups. Group 1 had CLP. Group 2 was given PTF 1 hour before CLP. Groups 3, 4, and 5 had PTF administered after CLP, at 1, 10, or 16 hours, respectively. ...

Ten animals from each group were reanaesthetised and sacrificed at 6, 12, or 18 hours postoperatively. Before sacrifice, the resting membrane potential was measured and a muscle sample taken for direct measurement of total muscle sodium, chloride potassium, and water content. ...

At each time point, the intracellular distribution of electrolytes and water was calculated from the striated muscle cell membrane potential, total water, and the plasma and muscle concentration of sodium, potassium, and chloride by applying the Nernst equation.

### *Sepsis Model*

The animals underwent a midline laparotomy. The caecum was mobilised, ligated distal to the ileocaecal valve, and two 21-gauge needle holes were made in the antimesenteric border. ...

### *Intracellular and Extracellular Water and Electrolyte Partition*

The partition of water and electrolytes between the intracellular and extracellular phases was calculated on the basis of the chloride space as the estimate of extracellular fluid volume. Intracellular and extracellular chloride distribution was considered to be a passive phenomenon, related to the measured resting membrane potential of skeletal muscle in a manner predicted by the Nernst equation. ...

Intracellular chloride was calculated as follows:

$$\text{PD} = -61.5 \log \frac{\text{CLo}}{\text{CLi}} \quad \text{CLi} = \frac{\text{CLo}}{\text{antilog } \text{PD}/-61.5}$$

... Extracellular water (ECW) was calculated as follows:

$$\text{ECW} = \frac{\text{TW} \times ([\text{CLts}] - [\text{CLi}])}{[\text{CLo}] - [\text{CLi}]}$$

... Intracellular water (ICW) was calculated from the formula  $\text{ICW} = \text{TW} - \text{ECW}$ .

... allows computation of the [Nai] and [Ki] intracellular concentrations, as follows:

$$[\text{Nai}] = \frac{\text{Nats} - (\text{ECW} \times [\text{Nao}])}{\text{ICW}} \quad [\text{Ki}] = \frac{\text{Kts} - (\text{ECW} \times [\text{Ko}])}{\text{ICW}}$$

## RESULTS

ANOVA showed a significant difference between the study groups for intracellular sodium, potassium, and chloride concentrations (*P* < .001, *P* < .05, and *P* < .001, respectively), but not for intracellular water. The Bonferroni test was used to compare the means of the groups receiving PTF to those of the CLP group, at each time point.

claim: Intracellular and extracellular water/electrolyte partition was calculated using chloride space as extracellular fluid estimate and assuming passive chloride distribution related to measured resting membrane potential as predicted by the Nernst equation; intracellular chloride was calculated using the Nernst equation, and intracellular sodium and potassium concentrations were computed from total muscle ion content and water partitioning.
source_text:
At each time point, the intracellular distribution of electrolytes and water was calculated from the striated muscle cell membrane potential, total water, and the plasma and muscle concentration of sodium, potassium, and chloride by applying the Nernst equation.

### *Intracellular and Extracellular Water and Electrolyte Partition*

The partition of water and electrolytes between the intracellular and extracellular phases was calculated on the basis of the chloride space as the estimate of extracellular fluid volume. Intracellular and extracellular chloride distribution was considered to be a passive phenomenon, related to the measured resting membrane potential of skeletal muscle in a manner predicted by the Nernst equation.

Intracellular chloride was calculated as follows:

$$\text{PD} = -61.5 \log \frac{\text{CLo}}{\text{CLi}} \quad \text{CLi} = \frac{\text{CLo}}{\text{antilog } \text{PD}/-61.5}$$

... allows computation of the [Nai] and [Ki] intracellular concentrations, as follows:

$$[\text{Nai}] = \frac{\text{Nats} - (\text{ECW} \times [\text{Nao}])}{\text{ICW}} \quad [\text{Ki}] = \frac{\text{Kts} - (\text{ECW} \times [\text{Ko}])}{\text{ICW}}$$

source_text:
We studied 24 patients (16 women and 8 men; mean [ \pm SD] age,  $38\pm 12$  years), each of whom had Cushing's syndrome due to a hyperfunctioning adrenocortical adenoma. ... During this two-year period, symptomatic thyroid dysfunction developed in 3 of the 24 patients; they are described in detail in Results. The other 21 patients had no thyroid dysfunction at any time after adrenalectomy.

In 3 of the 24 patients who had Cushing's syndrome due to a hyperfunctioning adrenocortical adenoma, thyroid dysfunction developed after unilateral adrenalectomy.

Of the remaining 21 patients with a hyperfunctioning adrenocortical adenoma, 2 had positive antimicrosomal-antibody titers (1:100 in both) and negative antithyroglobulin-antibody titers at first. After surgery, the antimicrosomal-antibody titers for these patients did not change, and their thyroid function remained normal. The remaining 19 patients had no symptoms or signs of thyroid disease, no abnormalities in thyroid-function tests, and no thyroid autoantibodies at any time after the operation.

source_text:
During this two-year period, symptomatic thyroid dysfunction developed in 3 of the 24 patients; they are described in detail in Results. ...

Another possible mechanism for the exacerbation of autoimmune thyroid dysfunction may be exposure to large amounts of iodine during the workup for Cushing's syndrome. All three patients had CT scanning and scintigraphy with 131I-labeled cholesterol; thus, they received iodinated organic compounds. To protect their thyroid glands, they also received sodium iodide (30 mg per day) for 10 days before the scintigraphy. Although iodide administration may have contributed to the triggering of thyroid dysfunction, we think this possibility unlikely, because the dysfunction developed several months later, and in two patients it seemed to be permanent.
