claim: Support is PARTLY established. Luo et al. (2023) report developing a 12-item rehabilitation training compliance scale for patients with urinary incontinence with 3 dimensions (items 1–5 PFMT compliance; items 6–10 bladder training compliance; items 11–12 urination diary recording). The scale uses 5-point Likert scoring (1–5 per item) with total score 12–60; “high compliance” is defined as total score ≥ (total score × 80%) (i.e., ≥48/60) and “poor compliance” as < (total score × 80%). In 123 UI patients, they report reliability (overall Cronbach’s α=0.95; subscales α=0.93/0.91/0.94; split-half reliability 0.89; test–retest reliability for full scale 0.86 with P<0.05; test–retest for items 0.82–0.87). They report content validity (S-CVI=0.93; I-CVI=0.87–1.0; CVR for the scale=0.96; Kappa coefficient for the scale=0.86). They report factorability/construct tests (KMO=0.90; Bartlett χ2=851.130, df=66, P<0.001), EFA (3-factor solution explaining 85.99% variance; rotation sums of squared loadings variance %: 33.186%, 32.703%, 20.098%), and CFA fit indices (χ2=134.964, df=51, p<0.001; CMIN/DF=2.646; RMSEA=0.116; CFI=0.94; NFI=0.91; TLI=0.92; IFI=0.94). Criterion-related validity vs Chen PFMSE is reported as 0.89 (P<0.05).
source_text:
“Our research team members read the references and guidelines and extracted the three dimensions of the scale, namely pelvic floor muscle training, bladder training, and urination diary recording... Items 1 to 5 of the scale were used to assess compliance with pelvic floor muscle training, items 6 to 10 were used to assess compliance with bladder training, and items 11 to 12 were used to assess urinary diary recording.”

“The scale developed in this study was scored on a 5-point Likert scale. The total score of the scale ranged from 12 to 60 points. Every item in this scale was assigned a score of 5, 4, 3, 2, or 1 point, indicating 'always', 'usually', 'sometimes', 'occasionally', and 'never', respectively. The evaluation criteria were as follows: a score  $\geq$  total score of the scale  $\times$  80% indicated high compliance, and a score  $<$  total score of the scale  $\times$  80% indicated poor compliance [54].”

“In total, 132 questionnaires were dispatched during this study, and 123 validated questionnaires were recovered...”

“Cronbach's  $\alpha$  was 0.95 for the overall scale, and the Cronbach's  $\alpha$  values for the three factors were 0.93 of pelvic floor muscle training compliance, 0.91 of compliance of bladder training, and 0.94 of urination diary recording. The test–retest reliability was 0.82–0.87 for the items and 0.86 of the full scale ( $P < 0.05$ ). The split-half reliability of this scale was 0.89 ( $P < 0.05$ ).”

“The S-CVI was 0.93 and the I-CVI was 0.87–1.0, indicating that the scale had good content validity (Table 7). ... The CVR was 0.92, indicating that the experts recognised all of the items in the scale as essential. Kappa coefficient of the scale was 0.86 indicating that the items consistency in the scale were good [56].”

“**Table 7** Kappa coefficient, CVI and CVR of items in the rehabilitation training compliance scale for patients with UI ...
| Scale for compliance evaluation | 0.86 | 0.93 | 0.96 |”

“The KMO value was 0.90, indicating that factor analysis was appropriate for the data. Bartlett's test of sphericity was significant ( $\chi^2 = 851.130$ ,  $df = 66$ ,  $P < 0.001$ )... EFA with varimax rotation yielded a three-factor solution that explained 85.99% of the variance in the data (Table 8).”

“**Table 8** Factor analysis: total variance explained ...
| 1 | ... | Rotation sums of squared loadings ... Variance (%) 33.186 ... |
| 2 | ... | Rotation sums of squared loadings ... Variance (%) 32.703 ... Accumulation (%) 65.889 |
| 3 | ... | Rotation sums of squared loadings ... Variance (%) 20.098 ... Accumulation (%) 85.987 |”

“The goodness-of-fit indices were as follows:  $\chi^2 = 134.964$ ;  $df = 51$ ;  $p < 0.001$ ; CMIN/DF = 2.646; RMSEA = 0.116; CFI = 0.94; NFI = 0.91; TLI = 0.92; and IFI = 0.94 [49, 57].”

“The criterion-related validity of the scale with the Chen PFMSE scale was 0.89 ( $P < 0.05$ ), indicating that the scale had high calibration correlation validity.”
verdict_explanation: Most psychometric results, sample size (N=123), 12-item/3-dimension structure (items 1–5, 6–10, 11–12), Likert scoring (12–60) and ≥80% threshold, KMO/Bartlett, EFA total variance, CFA indices (including RMSEA=0.116), reliability (Cronbach’s α overall/subscales; split-half; test–retest full scale r=0.86; items 0.82–0.87), and criterion correlation vs Chen PFMSE (0.89, P<0.05) are supported in the source. However, the candidate claim incorrectly states CVR=0.92 and implies this is the scale-level CVR; Table 7 reports “Scale for compliance evaluation” CVR=0.96, while 0.92 appears only in narrative text (“The CVR was 0.92...”), creating an internal inconsistency; the most specific tabulated value is 0.96. Also, the candidate claim asserts test–retest details “n=30 at 2 weeks r=0.86”; the source states the 2-week re-assessment involved 30 patients, but does not restate n=30 in the Results sentence reporting r=0.86, so the linkage must be made cautiously (it is described in Methods but not repeated in the Results reliability statement).
readiness_reason: The source contains an internal inconsistency for CVR (narrative: 0.92; Table 7 scale-level CVR: 0.96). The candidate claim also over-specifies that the full-scale test–retest r=0.86 is explicitly tied to n=30 at 2 weeks in the Results; that linkage is only explicit across Methods + Results. A witness-ready FRD should split and present only unambiguous, precisely attributable values (e.g., report both CVR values with their locations or prefer the table value) and avoid overstating what the Results section alone specifies.
original_claim: Luo et al. (2023) report developing a 12-item Rehabilitation Training Compliance Scale for urinary incontinence patients with 3 dimensions (PFMT compliance items 1–5; bladder training compliance items 6–10; urination diary recording items 11–12), scored on a 5-point Likert scale for a total score range 12–60 and defining “high compliance” as ≥48 points (≥80% of maximum). In their validation sample (N=123 UI patients), they report content validity (S-CVI=0.93; I-CVI=0.87–1.00; CVR=0.92; kappa=0.86), factorability/construct tests (KMO=0.90; Bartlett χ2=851.130, df=66, P<0.001), EFA (3 factors explaining 85.99% cumulative variance) and CFA fit indices (χ2=134.964, df=51, p<0.001; CMIN/DF=2.646; RMSEA=0.116; CFI=0.94; NFI=0.91; TLI=0.92; IFI=0.94), plus reliability (overall Cronbach’s α=0.95; subscales α=0.93/0.91/0.94; split-half=0.89; test-retest n=30 at 2 weeks r=0.86) and criterion correlation vs Chen’s PFMSE r=0.89 (P<0.05).

Not supported as written: the candidate claim asserts specific denominators for Glazener (2011) as 'men N=853 (411 RP, 442 TURP)' and for Glazener (2001) as 'postpartum women N=747 (n=692 analyzed)', and gives detailed adherence framing for Glazener (2001) including '78% overall adherence'; while parts of these numbers appear elsewhere (Table 1 shows n=853 and Table 3 shows n=747 and n=692 completed), the candidate also attributes several specific adherence figures/interpretations for Glazener (2001) that are not present in Table 5/Table 7 in the detailed form claimed (Table 5 reports PFMT performance 79%/48% and questionnaire response rates 75%/65%, but does not state '78% overall adherence' as a computed overall rate). readiness_reason: The candidate bundles multiple trial-specific denominator and adherence claims; several are supported, but some trial-specific details (especially the phrasing and computed '78% overall adherence' for Glazener 2001 and certain denominator/analysis wording) are not stated as claimed in the source. Splitting into supported children is required for witness construction.
original_claim: Villa-Del-Pino et al. (2025) (systematic review/meta-analysis) summarize adherence/compliance and denominators across included RCTs, reporting (as presented in their tables) examples such as: Sacomori (2020) postpartum women N=202 (n=132 analyzed) with 85.1% general adherence in the exercise group; Sahin (2022) SUI women N=60 (n=51 analyzed) with 83% adherence (PFMT) and 91% (EES+PFMT); Kaya (2015) UI women N=132 (n=108 analyzed) with median compliance 85% (IQR 75–100%); Glazener (2011) men N=853 (411 RP, 442 TURP) with RP 67% EG vs 50% CG (RR 1.30) and TURP 65% EG vs 20% CG (RR 3.20); and Glazener (2001) postpartum women N=747 (n=692 analyzed) with 79% EG vs 48% CG performing PFMT (78% overall adherence). The review further frames these findings using a “Nagpal four-scenario interpretation,” stating that across published trials all four scenarios can be fulfilled and that >80% adherence does not consistently correspond to superior efficacy versus controls, while some low-adherence cohorts can still show benefit.

claim: In a pilot experiment in male rats (n=6), 45 minutes before induction of hemorrhage, rats received an intravenous infusion of pentoxifylline (PTX) 40 mg/kg over 15 minutes. During PTX infusion, mean arterial pressure decreased (112 ± 2.0 to 84.4 ± 14.0 mmHg; p<0.05) and heart rate increased (365 ± 79 to 437 ± 38 beats/min; p<0.05). Total circulating leukocytes increased (7,140 ± 1,460 to 12,700 ± 2,980 cells/mm3; p<0.05), circulating PMNs increased (1,825 ± 280 to 4,055 ± 225 cells/mm3; p<0.05), and the absolute number of circulating NBT-positive PMNs increased (220 ± 218 to 609 ± 635 cells/mm3; p<0.05). When rats with such high NBT-positive PMN counts were subjected to the shock protocol, they all died.
source_text: 1) In this set of pilot experiments (n = 6), 45 minutes before the induction of hemorrhage the rats received an intravenous infusion of 40 mg/kg of PTX over a period of 15 minutes. During the PTX infusion, the animals showed a decrease in mean arterial pressure (MAP); from  $112 \pm 2.0$  mmHg to  $84.4 \pm 14.0$  mmHg ( $p < 0.05$ ). Throughout this period the heart rate was increased from  $365 \pm 79$  beats/min to  $437 \pm 38$  beats/min ( $p < 0.05$ ). The total number of circulating leukocytes was increased in all rats after this mode of PTX administration; from  $7,140 \pm 1,460$  cells/mm<sup>3</sup> before infusion to  $12,700 \pm 2,980$  cells/mm<sup>3</sup> at 45 minutes after infusion ( $p < 0.05$ ). The number of circulating PMNs was also increased with an average of  $1,825 \pm 280$  cells/mm<sup>3</sup> before the PTX infusion to  $4,055 \pm 225$  cells/mm<sup>3</sup> at 45 minutes after PTX infusion ( $p < 0.05$ ). This was not associated with a significant increase in the percent of circulating NBT-positive PMNs; from  $12.0 \pm 9.7\%$  to  $15.0 \pm 12.3\%$ . As a consequence, the absolute number of circulating NBT-positive PMNs appeared was higher after the acute PTX treatment, on average to  $609 \pm 635$  cells/mm<sup>3</sup> compared with  $220 \pm 218$  cells/mm<sup>3</sup> before the PTX infusion ( $p < 0.05$ ). When rats with such high NBT-positive PMN count were subjected to the current shock protocol, they all died.
verdict_explanation: The source supports the species/sex (male rats), acute IV infusion dose (40 mg/kg over 15 minutes) given 45 minutes before induction of hemorrhage, n=6, and the reported MAP/HR/WBC/PMN/absolute NBT(+) PMN values with p<0.05. However, the candidate claim adds details not stated in the source: it labels the post-infusion changes explicitly as "hypotension, tachycardia, leukocytosis, neutrophilia" (interpretive but consistent), and it states "100% mortality (0/6 survival)" after hemorrhagic shock; the source only states, without providing a denominator at the shock stage, "they all died" when subjected to the shock protocol. Also, the source notes there was not a significant increase in the *percent* NBT-positive PMNs (12.0±9.7% to 15.0±12.3%), which the candidate omits; the candidate focuses on the absolute NBT(+) count increase, which is supported.
readiness_reason: A repaired claim can be faithfully constructed from the quoted passage, with mortality phrased as "they all died" rather than asserting an explicit 0/6 denominator.
original_claim: In male rats, an acute PTX IV regimen (40 mg/kg over 15 minutes) given 45 minutes prior to hemorrhage caused significant hypotension (MAP 112±2.0 to 84.4±14.0 mmHg, P<0.05), tachycardia (HR 365±79 to 437±38 bpm, P<0.05), leukocytosis (WBC 7,140±1,460 to 12,700±2,980 cells/mm3, P<0.05), neutrophilia (PMNs 1,825±280 to 4,055±225 cells/mm3, P<0.05), increased activated NBT+ PMNs (220±218 to 609±635 cells/mm3, P<0.05), and when subsequently subjected to hemorrhagic shock resulted in 100% mortality (0/6 survival).

citation.locator: Pentoxifylline Pretreatment section; TABLE I; ABSTRACT; RESULTS > (b) Hemorrhagic Shock > Survival Rate

claim: In male rats, chronic oral pentoxifylline (PTX) pretreatment in drinking water at 40 mg/kg/day for at least 6 days (mean 9 ± 2 days) did not produce significant differences versus controls in mean arterial pressure (MAP), heart rate, hematocrit, circulating leukocytes (WBC), or circulating polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs), but significantly reduced the proportion and absolute number of circulating nitroblue tetrazolium positive (NBT+) PMNs (control 13.8 ± 10.2% and 220 ± 205 cells/mm3 vs PTX 2.3 ± 2.0% and 35 ± 40 cells/mm3; p < 0.001). In a Wiggers-type hemorrhagic shock protocol, 24-hour survival was 50% in untreated controls (n=30) and 91% in PTX-pretreated rats (n=22).
source_text:
PTX was administered orally in a second pilot group of 6 rats to determine whether this mode of administration affected the level of circulating PMN activation. PTX was mixed in drinking water at a dose of 40 mg/kg/day for at least 6 days ( 9 ± 2 days), which had no effect on the daily drinking volume of the animals. After this pharmacological pretreatment, there were no significant differences in MAP, heart rate, hematocrit, circulating leukocytes and circulating PMNs between the PTX-treated and the control group. On the other hand, the percent of circulating NBT-positive PMNs was found to be consistently lower in the PTX than in the control group (Table I).

+ Oral treatment for at least 6 days with pentoxifylline (40 mg/kg/day).

* p < 0.001 Control vs. PTX group.

ABSTRACT
... it was possible to reduce significantly the spontaneous PMN activation in rats pretreated with PTX orally for at least 6 days (40 mg/kg per day). Although there were no significant differences in the PMN count between the PTX and the control group, the number of circulating NBT-positive PMNs before bleeding, as well as during the hypotensive period, was significantly lower in the PTX than in the control group. The 24-hour survival rate after hemorrhagic shock was improved from 50% in the untreated controls to 91% in the PTX group.

RESULTS
(b) Hemorrhagic Shock
Survival Rate
The survival rate was improved from 50% in the untreated controls ( n=30 ) to 91% in the PTX treated group ( n=22 ).
verdict_explanation: Dose/timing (40 mg/kg/day in drinking water; at least 6 days; mean 9 ± 2 days) is supported. TABLE I supports that WBC and PMN counts are similar between control and PTX groups, and the text states there were no significant differences in those parameters; however TABLE I does not report 'P=NS' explicitly, so the candidate's specific 'P=NS' wording is not directly evidenced (it is only implied by the narrative statement). TABLE I supports the NBT+ PMN percent and absolute values with p < 0.001. Survival improvement and denominators are supported as 50% (n=30) vs 91% (n=22), but the source does not provide the 20/22 and 15/30 numerator counts nor an explicit 'p < 0.05' for survival; therefore those specific elements of the candidate claim are not supported in this source text.

claim: In male Wistar rats in a split hydronephrotic kidney model, pentoxifylline (PTX) administered as a 25 mg/kg bolus in 1 ml over 5 min immediately followed by 12.5 mg/kg in a 1.5-ml infusion over 90 min, with the second infusion (saline or E. coli) starting 15 min after beginning PTX administration, prevented E. coli–induced preglomerular vasoconstriction and reduction in interlobular artery (ILA) diameter and ILA flow; E. coli alone decreased ILA diameter to a nadir of −30.2 ± 2.4% at 90 min and ILA flow to a nadir of −60.4 ± 3.8% at 90 min, whereas with PTX + E. coli ILA diameter and blood flow remained above or near baseline and ILA flow peaked at +26.8 ± 4.4% at 30 min, with PTX + E. coli significantly different from E. coli (P < 0.05) per Fig. 2.
source_text:
**Experimental protocol.** ... Group III ( $n = 7$ ) was used to study the effects of pentoxifylline on the renal microcirculation. After baseline measurements, PTX was administered as a bolus of 25 mg/kg in 1 ml over 5 min, immediately followed by 12.5 mg/kg in a 1.5-ml infusion over 90 min. Fifteen minutes after the beginning of PTX administration, 1 ml of saline was given over 5 min to control for the volume of *E. coli* given in Group II.

Group IV ( $n = 7$ ) was used to study the effects of pentoxifylline on the vascular sequelae of *E. coli*. Pentoxifylline was infused at the dose and rate described for Group III. Fifteen minutes after the beginning of PTX administration, 1 ml of saline was given over 5 min to control for the volume of *E. coli* given in Group II.

**Preparation of bacteria.** ... Serial dilutions were measured spectrophotometrically ... to provide  $1 \times 10^9$  bacteria per milliliter. This dose was administered through the femoral vein catheter over 5 min.

### Renal Microvascular Variables

*E. coli* infusion produced rapid and progressive preglomerular vasoconstriction (Fig. 2). ILA diameter decreased over 120 min, reaching a nadir at 90 min ( $-30.2 \pm 2.4\%$ ). ILA flow was temporally related to ILA vasoconstriction, with a nadir at the same time point ( $-60.4 \pm 3.8\%$ ). ...

Pentoxifylline infusion prevented vasoconstriction during bacteremia; indeed, vasodilation was maintained. ILA diameter and blood flow remained above or near baseline throughout the experimental period. ILA flow peaked at  $26.8 \pm 4.4\%$  above baseline at 30 min (Figs. 2 and 3).

FIG. 2. ... \* $P < 0.05$  *E. coli* vs saline; + $P < 0.05$  PTX + *E. coli* vs *E. coli*; by ANOVA and Tukey's HSD test.
verdict_explanation: Dosing, bolus/infusion durations, and the “15 minutes after beginning PTX administration” timing are supported. E. coli dose (1×10^9 in 1 ml over 5 min) and the E. coli-alone nadirs for ILA diameter (−30.2±2.4% at 90 min) and ILA flow (−60.4±3.8% at 90 min) are supported, as is that PTX prevented vasoconstriction with ILA flow peaking at +26.8±4.4% at 30 min and that PTX+E. coli differed vs E. coli at P<0.05 (Fig. 2 legend). However, the candidate adds unsupported numeric detail that PTX+E. coli flow remained “12–16% above baseline through 120 min” (the 12–16% statement appears for PTX-alone group, not explicitly for PTX+E. coli), and it says PTX was started “15 minutes prior to IV E. coli challenge” (E. coli administration timing is implicit via protocol but not explicitly stated as E. coli in Group IV in the provided text; Group IV description in the supplied excerpt appears to contain a likely transcription error stating saline rather than E. coli). Also, “completely prevented” is stronger than the text (“prevented vasoconstriction... remained above or near baseline”).
readiness_reason: As written, the candidate includes unsupported/overstated elements (PTX+E. coli maintaining 12–16% above baseline through 120 min; “completely prevented”; and an explicit E. coli challenge timing statement not cleanly supported because Group IV wording in the supplied excerpt states saline rather than E. coli). A narrowed, source-faithful claim is needed.
original_claim: In male Wistar rats, PTX given as a 25 mg/kg IV bolus over 5 minutes followed immediately by IV infusion of 12.5 mg/kg over 90 minutes, started 15 minutes prior to IV E. coli challenge (1×109 over 5 min), reportedly completely prevented E. coli–induced preglomerular vasoconstriction and renal blood flow reduction in the split hydronephrotic kidney model (e.g., E. coli alone: interlobular artery diameter nadir −30.2±2.4% at 90 min and ILA flow nadir −60.4±3.8% at 90 min; PTX+E. coli: maintained diameter at/above baseline and prevented flow reduction, with flow +26.8±4.4% at 30 min and remaining 12–16% above baseline through 120 min; P<0.05 vs E. coli alone).

claim: Support is partially established in this source. Staubach et al. (1998) report that 51 surgical ICU patients with severe sepsis/septic shock were randomized within 12 hours of diagnosis to receive continuous IV pentoxifylline 1 mg/kg/hour (max 1800 mg/day) or placebo (saline) for up to 28 days (or until ICU discharge or death). The study reports no significant between-group differences over the study in serum endotoxin (LPS) and TNF-α/IL-6 bioactivity, nor in bilirubin, creatinine, or platelet count, and no significant differences in 28-day or in-hospital survival (log-rank P=.85 and P=.43, respectively). The MOD score decreased from day 4 onward in the pentoxifylline group vs placebo, reaching statistical significance on day 14 (P<.05; Student t test with Bonferroni correction). PaO2/FiO2 was significantly improved on days 14 and 17 (P<.05), and pressure-adjusted heart rate was significantly improved on day 6 (P<.05). Table 2 supports baseline (enrollment) comparability, not longitudinal 'no differences' claims; this source does not provide Table-based day-by-day P-values for those lab measures.
source_text:
**Patients:** Fifty-one surgical patients with severe sepsis were randomized to receive pentoxifylline continuously (27 patients) or saline infusion as placebo (24 patients).

**Interventions:** Patients received pentoxifylline (1 mg/kg of body weight per hour; maximum, 1800 mg/d) during 28 days or until they were discharged from the intensive care unit or died.

Fifty-one surgical patients were randomly assigned within 12 hours after diagnosis of sepsis to receive a continuous intravenous infusion of pentoxifylline (Rentyllin, Rentschler, Germany) 1 mg/kg of body weight per hour, to a maximum of 1800 mg/d or normal saline solution as placebo during 28 days or until patients were discharged from the ICU or died.

The 28-day mortality rate was 30% (8/27) in patients receiving pentoxifylline and 33% (8/24) in the placebo group. In-hospital mortality was 41% (11/27) in the pentoxifylline group and 54% (13/24) in the placebo group (**Figure 1**). There were no significant differences in the survival curves of the groups (log-rank analysis,  $P=.85$  for 28-day survival and  $P=.43$  for hospital survival).

At baseline, the multiple organ dysfunction score was not different between the groups. From day 4 after the diagnosis of sepsis, the score decreased in patients receiving pentoxifylline compared with placebo-infused patients (**Figure 2**). This difference reached significance on day 14 after the diagnosis of sepsis ( $P<.05$ ). The  $\text{PaO}_2/\text{FiO}_2$  ratio as a parameter for pulmonary dysfunction increased from day 7 in patients receiving pentoxifylline compared with patients receiving placebo (**Figure 3**). The difference was statistically significant on days 14 and 17 after the diagnosis of severe sepsis ( $P<.05$ ).

The pressure-adjusted heart rate characterizing cardiac function was significantly different on day 6 after diagnosis (*P*<.05) and remained decreased compared with the placebo group (**Figure 4**). The total bilirubin as a measure of hepatic dysfunction, serum creatinine as a measure of renal dysfunction, and the platelet count as a measure of hematologic dysfunction showed no differences throughout the evaluation. The serum endotoxin concentrations and IL-6 and TNF-α bioactivity were not significantly different in the groups during the study.

**Figure 2.** *Serial multiple organ dysfunction (MOD) score according to Marshall... Asterisk indicates* P*<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline (solid bars) vs patients receiving placebo (shaded bars); Student* t *test with Bonferroni correction.*

**Figure 3.** *Changes in  $\mathrm{PaO_2/FIO_2}$  (fraction of inspired oxygen) ratio... Asterisks indicate* P*<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline... vs patients receiving placebo...; Student* t *test with Bonferroni correction.*

**Figure 4.** *Changes in pressure-adjusted heart rate... Asterisk indicates* P*<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline... vs patients receiving placebo...; Student* t *test with Bonferroni correction.*
verdict_explanation: Correct on: population size and allocation (27 vs 24), setting (surgical ICU), severe sepsis/septic shock; dosing (1 mg/kg/h; max 1800 mg/d), duration (up to 28 days), and timing (randomized within 12 hours of diagnosis); mortality numerators/denominators and log-rank P-values; and which days showed P<.05 for MODS (day 14), PaO2/FiO2 (days 14 and 17), and PAHR (day 6), including use of Student t test with Bonferroni correction (as stated in figure captions and Statistical Analysis). Not fully correct: attributing the 'no significant differences' lab/organ-function findings specifically to 'Table 2' across the study. Table 2 reports enrollment (baseline) values only; the text (not Table 2) states that bilirubin/creatinine/platelets and endotoxin/cytokine bioactivity were not significantly different between groups during the study. Also, the source refers to "tumor necrosis factor α" and "interleukin 6 bioactivity" and does not mention 'serum TNF-α/IL-6' beyond bioactivity; and it reports PaO2/FiO2 significance on days 14 and 17 (not day 14 and 17 plus other unspecified later days).
readiness_reason: A repaired claim is fully supportable from this source when corrected to (a) cite Table 2 only for enrollment comparability and (b) cite the Results narrative/Figures for longitudinal 'no differences' and significant-day findings.

Abstract (Materials and Methods): "This randomized, double-blind clinical trial recruited 60 patients with BPH from a single center in 2022. Upon consent of patients meeting the eligibility criteria, they were randomly allocated to intervention (Pentoxifylline + tamsulosin) and control (placebo + tamsulosin) groups." ... "The patients were evaluated for international prostate symptom score (IPSS)... maximum urinary flow rate ( $Q_{max}$ ) ... and post-void residual volume (PVR) ... at the onset of the study and after the 12th week."

2.3 | Study design: "Afterward, 60 out of 75 patients were qualified and randomized with a random sequence generator into two groups: Pentoxifylline (Farabi company, Iran) and tamsulosin (Astellas international company). An equal number of patients received either fixed doses of Pentoxifylline 400 mg/Q8h plus tamsulosin 0.4 mg/day (Intervention Group)17 or tamsulosin 0.4 mg/day with placebo (Control Group) for 12 weeks."

claim: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 51 surgical ICU patients with severe sepsis (pentoxifylline n=27; placebo n=24), patients assigned to pentoxifylline received a continuous IV infusion of 1 mg/kg body weight per hour (maximum 1800 mg/day) for 28 days or until ICU discharge or death. The median serum concentration of pentoxifylline was 3628 ng/mL on day 1 after starting infusion and 1620 ng/mL on day 2; it reached a steady state from day 3 until the end of the 28-day study. The 28-day mortality rate was 30% (8/27) in the pentoxifylline group and 33% (8/24) in the placebo group; survival did not differ significantly between groups (log-rank P=.85 for 28-day survival).
source_text:
**Patients:** Fifty-one surgical patients with severe sepsis were randomized to receive pentoxifylline continuously (27 patients) or saline infusion as placebo (24 patients).

**Interventions:** Patients received pentoxifylline (1 mg/kg of body weight per hour; maximum, 1800 mg/d) during 28 days or until they were discharged from the intensive care unit or died.

Fifty-one surgical patients were randomly assigned within 12 hours after diagnosis of sepsis to receive a continuous intravenous infusion of pentoxifylline (Rentyllin, Rentschler, Germany) 1 mg/kg of body weight per hour, to a maximum of 1800 mg/d or normal saline solution as placebo during 28 days or until patients were discharged from the ICU or died.

The 28-day mortality rate was 30% (8/27) in patients receiving pentoxifylline and 33% (8/24) in the placebo group. In-hospital mortality was 41% (11/27) in the pentoxifylline group and 54% (13/24) in the placebo group (**Figure 1**). There were no significant differences in the survival curves of the groups (log-rank analysis,  $P=.85$  for 28-day survival and  $P=.43$  for hospital survival).

**Figure 1.** *Kaplan-Meier 28-day survival (top) and Kaplan-Meier hospital survival (bottom) analysis for all patients assigned to receive pentoxifylline (solid squares) or placebo (open squares). Survival did not differ significantly between patient groups (*P *= .85 for 28-day survival and* P *= .43 for hospital survival).*

The median serum concentration of pentoxifylline was 3628 ng/mL on the first day after starting infusion and 1620 ng/mL on day 2; it reached a steady state from day 3 until the end of the 28-day study. A similar pattern was demonstrated for the first metabolite of pentoxifylline (BL 194) with a 1.3- to 2.5-fold higher serum concentration than the parent drug (**Figure 5**).
verdict_explanation: Dosing, N=51 with group sizes (27 vs 24), day 1 and day 2 median serum pentoxifylline concentrations (3628 ng/mL; 1620 ng/mL), and the statement that steady state was reached from day 3 through the end of the 28-day study are supported. The 28-day mortality counts/percentages and log-rank P=.85 for 28-day survival are also supported. claim: In a study by Liao and Kuo, urethral injections of botulinum toxin A (BTX-A) had a reported success rate of 97% in 32 patients with idiopathic underactive bladder (UAB), and 76% in 33 patients with detrusor areflexia.
source_text:
#### 7.3.11. Botulinum toxin

Botulinum toxin is a powerful site-specific muscle relaxant. Botulinum toxin A (BTX-A) has been widely used in treatment of neurogenic bladder and showed efficacy in reduction of bladder outlet resistance and residual urine volume [116,117]. It is a promising alternative for treating refractory sphincter spasticity. It can decrease the need for lifelong CIC [116]. Injection of BTX-A into the urethral sphincter can relax the sphincter and thus reduce bladder outlet resistance and improve bladder emptying in UAB patients [6]. In a study by Liao and Kuo, a success rate of 97% was reported after urethral injections of BTX-A in 32 patients with idiopathic UAB. Also, a success rate of 76% was obtained in 33 patients with detrusor areflexia [118].
verdict_explanation: The source supports the denominators (32; 33) and success rates (97%; 76%) and attributes them to “a study by Liao and Kuo” involving urethral BTX-A injections. readiness_reason: Although the success rates and denominators are supported, the candidate’s added outcome details (voiding efficiency restoration; PVR reduction as study outcomes) and any definition of “success” are not supported in the cited section. claim: In a crossover study of ten healthy male volunteers studied on two occasions separated by at least 21 days, endotoxin (100 ng LPS from Salmonella abortus equi) was given as an IV bolus at 0800 h; on the first study day subjects received an IV saline infusion and on the second occasion received oxpentifylline 500 mg in 500 ml isotonic saline started 30 min before endotoxin and continued for 4 h. In the nine responders (≥1.0°C temperature rise), serum TNF increased at 1 h and 2 h after endotoxin during saline infusion (baseline 21 [4] pg/ml; 2 h 38 [11] pg/ml; p<0.007 vs baseline), but during oxpentifylline there was no rise (baseline 23 [7] pg/ml; 2 h 24 [5] pg/ml), and the between-period difference at 2 h was significant (p<0.02). Oxpentifylline did not affect IL-6 serum levels after endotoxin, and clinical responses to endotoxin (including fever) were not affected.
source_text:
***Summary*** Oxpentifylline (pentoxifylline) ... was tested in human beings after injection of endotoxin. Of ten healthy volunteers, nine met the inclusion criterion of a rise in body temperature of at least 1·0°C after 100 ng endotoxin (Salmonella abortus equi) as a bolus injection. Serum levels of tumour necrosis factor α (TNF) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) were both significantly higher than baseline levels 2 h and 3 h after endotoxin injection. 3 weeks later the nine volunteers were again injected with 100 ng endotoxin and oxpentifylline (500 mg over 4 h) was also infused. There was no rise in TNF levels, though IL-6 levels rose in parallel with body temperature.

"We studied ten male volunteers (26–38 years old) ... The subjects were admitted to the medical clinic of the Borstel research institute and studied on two occasions separated by at least 21 days. The endotoxin preparation (sodium salt of LPS from Salmonella abortus equi) was dissolved in isotonic saline and given as a bolus injection (100 ng) intravenously at 0800 h. ... infusion of saline (0·9%, 125 ml/h) on the first study day or oxpentifylline (500 mg in 500 ml isotonic saline; Hoechst AG Werk Albert) on the second occasion was started 30 min before endotoxin administration and continued for 4 h."

"In nine of the ten subjects there was a rise in body temperature of at least 1·0°C ... Since these responses were required for inclusion, the values for that individual were not included in the statistical analysis. ... None of the clinical responses to endotoxin were affected by oxpentifylline."

"The baseline serum TNF level was 21 (4) pg/ml. The level rose to 30 (6) pg/ml at 1 h and 38 (11) pg/ml at 2 h after endotoxin injection. These levels were both significantly (p < 0·007) higher than the baseline level, but no significant differences were found at any other time. In contrast, during oxpentifylline treatment there was no rise in serum TNF (baseline: 23 [7] pg/ml, 2 h after endotoxin 24 [5] pg/ml). The difference in TNF levels 2 h after endotoxin between the saline infusion and oxpentifylline infusion periods was significant (p < 0·02)."

"Oxpentifylline treatment did not affect IL-6 serum levels after endotoxin administration (fig 2)."

"We found that treatment with oxpentifylline caused selective inhibition of TNF without affecting IL-6 levels. ... clinical signs of endotoxaemia, such as fever and myalgia as well as high cortisol levels ... are not affected by oxpentifylline treatment."
verdict_explanation: Design, dosing, timing, washout (≥21 days/3 weeks), LPS type/dose/0800 h IV bolus, TNF values and statistics (baseline 21(4); 2 h 38(11); p<0.007 vs baseline; oxpentifylline baseline 23[7], 2 h 24[5]; between-period p<0.02), and lack of effect on IL-6 and clinical responses (including fever) are supported. However, the original claim overstates that pentoxifylline "abolished" the TNF rise (source: "there was no rise" during treatment, but TNF at 2 h was 24[5] vs baseline 23[7], and the key comparison is between periods) and it asserts an IL-6 rise "still rose significantly" plus a specific fever threshold statement in the treatment session; the source supports that IL-6 was not affected and rose after endotoxin, and that clinical responses (including fever) were not affected, but does not explicitly restate the ≥1.0°C criterion for the second session. The claim's infusion duration relative to LPS ("continuing 3.5 hours after") is implied by starting 30 min before and continuing 4 h, but not stated in that phrasing. Also, the numeric example "PTX vs saline" at 2 h matches the reported means but the saline session is described as 38(11) at 2 h after endotoxin, not explicitly labeled as "peak" in the candidate claim.
readiness_reason: mechanical check: the validator's source_text was not found in the named source file (none); After minor wording tightening (avoid overstated 'abolished' and avoid adding unstated qualifiers), the study design, dosing/timing, TNF statistics, and lack of effect on IL-6/clinical responses are directly supported by quoted source text with clear locators.
original_claim: In 10 healthy male volunteers given an IV bolus of 100 ng Salmonella abortus equi LPS at 8:00 AM, an IV infusion of pentoxifylline (oxpentifylline) 500 mg in 500 mL saline over 4 hours started 30 minutes before LPS (continuing 3.5 hours after) abolished the LPS-associated rise in serum TNF (e.g., 2-hour TNF 24±5 pg/mL with PTX vs 38±11 pg/mL at 2 hours in the saline session; P<0.02 for the 2-hour difference), while IL-6 still rose significantly and fever (≥1.0°C) was not blocked.

claim: In a prospective observational study at Haukeland University Hospital (June 2016–June 2021), 73 hypercortisolism patients (63 ACS, 2 adrenal CS, 8 pituitary CS) were compared with 120 healthy controls; 49/92 Olink (Proseek Multiplex Inflammation I Panel) serum inflammatory/cardiovascular biomarkers differed significantly between combined ACS/CS patients and controls after Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction and additional linear-regression adjustment for age, sex, BMI (when correlated) and smoking; 46 biomarkers were higher and 3 were lower in patients. Example effect sizes shown in Figure 2 include FGF21 mean difference 2.0 NPX (95% CI 1.8–2.2) and IL6 0.8 (0.6–1.0) higher in patients, while TRANCE −0.4 (−0.6 to −0.2), TNFB −0.3 (−0.5 to −0.1), and ST1A1 −0.5 (−0.7 to −0.3) were lower. Postoperative samples were available for 17 patients a median 24 months after surgery and biochemical cure, and the paper reports no significant postoperative normalization of biomarkers. The paper also reports that none of the biomarkers correlated with degree of hypercortisolism (post-DST cortisol, 24 h UFC, or morning serum cortisol).
source_text:
## Abstract

**Method:** Observational study including serum from prospectively included patients with ACS ( $n = 63$ ), adrenal CS ( $n = 2$ ), pituitary CS ( $n = 8$ ), and healthy subjects ( $n = 120$ ). Serum samples were analysed for 92 inflammatory biomarkers using proximity extension assay (OLINK).

**Results:** Combined, the ACS and CS patients displayed significant differences in levels of 49/92 inflammatory biomarkers (46 increased/3 decreased) compared with healthy controls. No differences in biomarker levels were found between ACS and overt CS, and none of the biomarkers correlated with the degree of hypercortisolism. Postoperative samples were available for 17 patients, median 24 months (range 6–40) after surgery and biochemical cure. There was no significant normalization of the biomarkers postoperatively.

...

### Study organization and participants

From June 2016 to June 2021, we consecutively included patients with adrenal incidentalomas diagnosed with ACS and adrenal CS and patients diagnosed with pituitary CS, in a prospective observational study at Haukeland University Hospital, Bergen, Norway ( $n = 73$ ). Healthy controls ( $n = 120$ ) were recruited from the hospital and university staff. ... Seventeen patients with ACS and CS successfully treated with adrenalectomy or pituitary surgery were sampled at least 6 months after having tapered off cortisone treatment.

...

### Statistical analyses

... Benjamin Hochberg procedure for adjustment of *P* value was used to correct for possible false discovery rate (FDR) due to multiple comparisons. ... When correlation was found, linear regression was used to adjust for the independent variables age, sex, and BMI (the biomarker data were set as the dependent variable). Linear regression was also used to correct for smoking habits for all significant biomarkers.

...

### Inflammatory biomarkers

Forty-nine of the 92 inflammatory and cardiovascular biomarkers differed significantly between patients with ACS/CS and healthy controls, after correction for possible FDR and smoking habits (for complete list, see Table S2). Forty-six biomarkers were upregulated in patients, and three were downregulated (Figures 1 and 2).

...

| Biomarker     | Mean Difference (NPX) | 95% CI      |
|---------------|-----------------------|-------------|
| FGF21         | 2.0                   | 1.8 - 2.2   |
| IL6           | 0.8                   | 0.6 - 1.0   |
...
| TNFB          | -0.3                  | -0.5 - -0.1 |
| TRANCE        | -0.4                  | -0.6 - -0.2 |
| ST1A1         | -0.5                  | -0.7 - -0.3 |

...

## Discussion

... the biomarker levels did not correlate with the post-DST cortisol levels, the 24 h UFC level, or the morning serum cortisol levels. ... Surprisingly, biomarker levels continued to be elevated even after biochemical cure. ...

...

**Figure 3.** Boxplot showing the distribution of biomarker levels ... All panels show significantly higher levels in ACS/CS patients compared with healthy controls and a lack of normalization postoperatively.
verdict_explanation: Supported: cohort sizes (73 patients; 120 controls; postoperative n=17; median 24 months; Abstract reports range 6–40), the general finding of 49/92 biomarkers differing with 46 increased/3 decreased, the use of Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction and regression adjustment (age/sex/BMI when correlated; smoking for significant biomarkers), the listed effect sizes/CIs for FGF21, IL6, TRANCE, TNFB, and ST1A1 (shown in Figure 2 table), and statements that biomarkers did not correlate with hypercortisolism degree and did not significantly normalize postoperatively. Not supported as stated: the candidate claim says postoperative median 24 months with range 6–40 (this range is in the Abstract), but the Results section states postoperative specimens were collected median 24 (range 11–61) months; also the claim says 'none of the 49 biomarkers correlated ...; P=NS' but the paper states 'none ... correlated' without specifying '0/49', without listing P=NS, and it does not explicitly tie the 'none correlated' statement to the subset of 49 (though it is strongly implied in Abstract/Discussion). Additionally, the statistical approach is somewhat overstated: the paper does not say the regression (age/sex/BMI) was applied uniformly to all biomarkers; it says regression was used when correlation was found in controls, and smoking correction was applied for significant biomarkers.

claim: Support is partially established. In this prospective longitudinal cohort, blood samples were collected from nine Cushing’s syndrome patients at diagnosis and after achieving remission (median 18 months between baseline and post-remission sample). Monocyte-derived cytokine production after 24 h PBMC stimulation was normalized by dividing cytokine concentration (pg/mL) by monocyte counts (per 1×10^5 monocytes). Fig. 3 shows IL-8 production capacity (pg/mL per 1×10^5 monocytes) was significantly higher post-remission for LPS 1 ng/mL, LPS 10 ng/mL, and C. albicans (p<0.05), and IL-10 production capacity was significantly lower post-remission for LPS 1 ng/mL (p<0.05). Proteomic analysis of plasma identified seven inflammation-related proteins increased and eleven decreased after achieving remission (18 total), with proteins compared by Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Circulating concentrations of IL-6, IL-8 and CRP did not change after remission.
source_text:
ABSTRACT
"Blood samples were collected from nine CS patients (six adrenal CS and three Cushing's disease) at diagnosis and after achieving remission and fully tapering off glucocorticoid suppletion." ... "Production of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and IL-8 by monocytes after 24 h of stimulation with microbial stimuli was higher after achieving remission, while production of anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-10 and IL-1Ra was lower." ... "Proteomic analysis of plasma identified seven inflammation-related proteins with increased expression and eleven proteins with decreased expression after achieving remission." ... "Concentrations of circulating IL-6, IL-8 and CRP did not change after remission."

Results > Patient characteristics
"Post remission samples were obtained in nine out of 19 patients with CS that were included at baseline." ... "Median time between baseline and post remission sample and between surgery and post remission sample were respectively 18 months (range: 13–27 months) and 14 months (range: 11–26 months)."

"Per well,  $5 \times 10^5$  PBMCs were stimulated in duplicate." ... claim: In this 12-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial in 60 medically stable outpatients with major depression and treatment resistance, participants received infliximab 5 mg/kg (n=30) or placebo (n=30) by intravenous infusion at baseline and weeks 2 and 6. The trial reported no overall difference between groups in HAM-D change over time (t58=0.10, P=.92) and no treatment×time interaction (t305=0.86, P=.39), and overall treatment response rates were 50% in each group (χ2=0.00, P=.99). When baseline hs-CRP (log) was included, there was a significant treatment×time×log(baseline hs-CRP) interaction (t302=2.65, P=.01). Exploratory analyses in those with baseline hs-CRP >5 mg/L reported response 62% (8/13) for infliximab vs 33% (3/9) for placebo (χ2=1.69, P=.19) and reported that the number needed to treat (NNT) was 3.45; the reported least-squares mean HAM-D change difference (infliximab minus placebo) from baseline to week 12 for the >5 mg/L subgroup (n=22) was −3.1 (95% CI, −7.7 to 1.5) (i.e., favoring infliximab) and the standardized effect size difference at 12 weeks was 0.41 favoring infliximab. For baseline hs-CRP ≤5 mg/L, response was 41% (7/17) for infliximab vs 57% (12/21) for placebo (χ2=0.96, P=.33) and the source reports the number needed to harm (NNH) as 6.25; the standardized effect size difference at 12 weeks was −0.82 favoring placebo. Longitudinal hs-CRP analyses reported a significant main effect of treatment on hs-CRP concentrations across treatment (t57=2.25, P=.03). Exploratory analyses reported that baseline TNF and both soluble TNF receptors (I and II) were significantly higher in infliximab responders than in infliximab nonresponders (all P<.05).
source_text:
**Interventions:** "Three infusions of the TNF antagonist infliximab (5 mg/kg) (n=30) or placebo (n=30) at baseline and weeks 2 and 6 of a 12-week trial." ...

"Following screening for inclusion and exclusion criteria, all participants reported to the infusion center ... on 3 separate occasions (baseline, 2 weeks, and 6 weeks) to receive an infusion of either infliximab (5 mg/kg) or placebo over 120 minutes through an indwelling catheter." ...

"No differences in change in HAM-D scores over time were found between treatment groups ( $t_{58} = 0.10, P = .92$ ), nor was there a significant interaction between treatment and time ( $t_{305} = 0.86, P = .39$ ) (**Figure 1**)." ...

"Interestingly, when the baseline hs-CRP concentration (log-linear and quadratic terms) was entered into the model, there was a significant interaction among treatment, time, and log hs-CRP concentration ( $t_{302} = 2.65, P = .01$ )." ...

"Treatment response rates did not differ between groups in the entire sample and were 50% for each group ( $\chi^2 = 0.00$ ,  $P = .99$ ). For participants with a baseline hs-CRP concentration greater than 5 mg/L, however, the treatment response rate was 62% (8 of 13 participants) in the infliximab group and 33% (3 of 9 participants) in the placebo group ( $\chi^2 = 1.69$ ,  $P = .19$ ) (**Figure 6**). Based on these percentages, the number of patients needed to be treated with infliximab in order to have one more responder (number needed to treat) for participants with a hs-CRP concentration greater than 5 was 3.45 ... In contrast, for participants with a hs-CRP concentration of 5 mg/L or less, the treatment response rate was 41% (7 of 17 participants) for the infliximab group and 57% (12 of 21 participants) for the placebo group ( $\chi^2 = 0.96$ ,  $P = .33$ ). In this case, the disadvantage to infliximab (number needed to harm) was calculated as 6.25." ...

Figure 3 table ("Baseline hs-CRP concentration >5 mg/L (n=22)" row): "-3.1 (95% CI, -7.7 to 1.5)" ...

"Consistent with these findings, the standardized effect size difference at 12 weeks (from mixed-effects models for repeated measures) was moderate to large, in opposite directions: 0.41 favoring infliximab in the group with a baseline hs-CRP concentration greater than 5 mg/L com- pared with  $-0.82$  favoring placebo in the group with a baseline hs-CRP concentration of 5 mg/L or less." ...

"Regarding the effect of infliximab and placebo on hs-CRP concentrations across treatment, there was a significant effect of treatment ( $t_{57} = 2.25$ ,  $P = .03$ ), but no effect of time ( $t_{433} = 0.10$ ,  $P = .92$ ) and no treatment  $\times$  time interaction ( $t_{433} = 0.27$ ,  $P = .78$ ) (**Figure 7**)." ...

"Exploratory analyses of TNF and its receptors revealed no significant interactions between treatment, time, and the log of any of the TNF markers. However, all 3 TNF markers were significantly higher in infliximab responders vs infliximab nonresponders (all  $P < .05$ ) (eFigure 4)."

Design/dosing/sample size, the overall null HAM-D statistics (t58=0.10, P=.92; treatment×time t305=0.86, P=.39), equal overall response (50% each; χ2=0.00, P=.99), the treatment×time×log(baseline hs-CRP) interaction (t302=2.65, P=.01), the >5 mg/L subgroup response numbers and χ2/P, the NNT=3.45, the ≤5 mg/L subgroup response numbers and χ2/P, the NNH=6.25, the hs-CRP main treatment effect (t57=2.25, P=.03), and the statement that baseline TNF and soluble receptors I and II were higher in infliximab responders vs nonresponders (all P<.05) are all directly supported. 
However, the candidate claim contains a subgroup size discrepancy: the source text states the ≤5 mg/L subgroup is n=38 in the response-rate paragraph, but Figure 4’s caption states n=48 for the ≤5 mg/L subgroup; therefore, the claim as written (≤5 mg/L n=38) cannot be fully confirmed without resolving this internal inconsistency, and it must be reported with that conflict noted. Also, the candidate’s wording "among participants with baseline hs-CRP >5 mg/L (n=22), infliximab vs placebo showed a 3.1-point greater HAM-D reduction" is directionally consistent with Figure 3’s −3.1 (infliximab minus placebo) but needed sign/direction clarification (it is −3.1 for infliximab minus placebo, favoring infliximab).

claim: Staubach et al. (1998) report a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical study in surgical ICU patients with severe sepsis/septic shock (pentoxifylline continuous IV infusion 1 mg/kg body weight per hour; maximum 1800 mg/day; 27 pentoxifylline vs 24 placebo). They report no baseline differences in MOD score or PaO2/FiO2 or PAHR; MOD score decreased from day 4 after diagnosis in the pentoxifylline group vs placebo with a significant difference on day 14 (P<.05); PaO2/FiO2 was significantly improved on days 14 and 17 (P<.05); PAHR was significantly different/improved on day 6 (P<.05). They report 28-day mortality 30% (8/27) vs 33% (8/24) with log-rank P=.85, and in-hospital mortality 41% (11/27) vs 54% (13/24) with log-rank P=.43.
source_text:
“Design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.”

“Patients: Fifty-one surgical patients with severe sepsis were randomized to receive pentoxifylline continuously (27 patients) or saline infusion as placebo (24 patients).”

“Interventions: Patients received pentoxifylline (1 mg/kg of body weight per hour; maximum, 1800 mg/d) during 28 days or until they were discharged from the intensive care unit or died.”

“Fifty-one surgical patients were randomly assigned within 12 hours after diagnosis of sepsis to receive a continuous intravenous infusion of pentoxifylline (Rentyllin, Rentschler, Germany) 1 mg/kg of body weight per hour, to a maximum of 1800 mg/d or normal saline solution as placebo during 28 days or until patients were discharged from the ICU or died.”

“There were no differences in characteristics of patients at diagnosis in the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) score (mean±SEM, 17±4 points for the pentoxifylline group and 18±5 points for the placebo group), the multiple organ dysfunction score (mean±SEM, 11.0±0.8 vs 11.8±1.0 points), tumor necrosis factor  α  and interleukin 6 bio-
activity, serum endotoxin levels, or organ dysfunction.”

“Table 2. Severity of Sepsis at Enrollment*
...
| MOD score | 11.0±0.8 | 11.8±1.0 | .50 |
...
| PaO2/FiO2 ratio | 167±15 | 151±19 | .41 |
...
| PAHR, beats/min | 15.3±1.7 | 16.4±1.5 | .62 |”

“At baseline, the multiple organ dysfunction score was not different between the groups. From day 4 after the diagnosis of sepsis, the score decreased in patients receiving pentoxifylline compared with placebo-infused patients (Figure 2). This difference reached significance on day 14 after the diagnosis of sepsis (P<.05).”

“Figure 2. Serial multiple organ dysfunction (MOD) score according to Marshall12 from surgical patients with severe sepsis. Asterisk indicates P<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline (solid bars) vs patients receiving placebo (shaded bars); Student t test with Bonferroni correction. Values are mean±SEM.”

“The PaO2/FiO2 ratio as a parameter for pulmonary dysfunction increased from day 7 in patients receiving pentoxifylline compared with patients receiving placebo (Figure 3). The difference was statistically significant on days 14 and 17 after the diagnosis of severe sepsis (P<.05).”

“Figure 3. Changes in  PaO2/FIO2  (fraction of inspired oxygen) ratio from day 1 to day 28 after diagnosis of sepsis. Asterisks indicate P<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline (solid squares) vs patients receiving placebo (open squares); Student t test with Bonferroni correction. Values are mean±SEM.”

“The pressure-adjusted heart rate characterizing cardiac function was significantly different on day 6 after diagnosis (P<.05) and remained decreased compared with the placebo group (Figure 4).”

“Figure 4. Changes in pressure-adjusted heart rate (central venous pressure times the heart rate divided by the mean arterial pressure) during the 28-day study period. Asterisk indicates P<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline (solid squares) vs patients receiving placebo (open squares); Student t test with Bonferroni correction. Values are mean±SEM.”

“The 28-day mortality rate was 30% (8/27) in patients receiving pentoxifylline and 33% (8/24) in the placebo group. In-hospital mortality was 41% (11/27) in the pentoxifylline group and 54% (13/24) in the placebo group (Figure 1). There were no significant differences in the survival curves of the groups (log-rank analysis, P=.85 for 28-day survival and P=.43 for hospital survival).”

claim: In Zabel et al. (1989), healthy male volunteers underwent two endotoxin challenges separated by at least 21 days: first with 100 ng IV endotoxin plus saline infusion, and second with 100 ng IV endotoxin plus oxpentifylline (pentoxifylline) 500 mg in 500 mL saline infused over 4 hours starting 30 minutes before endotoxin. In the 9/10 subjects included in the statistical analysis (those with ≥1.0°C temperature rise), oxpentifylline prevented the endotoxin-associated rise in serum TNF at 2 hours (saline period: 38 [11] pg/mL vs oxpentifylline period: 24 [5] pg/mL; p<0.02 for between-period difference at 2 h). Oxpentifylline did not affect the clinical responses to endotoxin (symptoms such as myalgia/headache/nausea) and fever occurred to the same extent on the second challenge.
source_text:
***Summary*** Oxpentifylline (pentoxifylline), which is known to have pharmacological effects in animal models of respiratory distress syndrome, multiorgan failure, and shock, was tested in human beings after injection of endotoxin. Of ten healthy volunteers, nine met the inclusion criterion of a rise in body temperature of at least 1·0°C after 100 ng endotoxin (*Salmonella abortus equi*) as a bolus injection. ... 3 weeks later the nine volunteers were again injected with 100 ng endotoxin and oxpentifylline (500 mg over 4 h) was also infused. There was no rise in TNF levels, though IL-6 levels rose in parallel with body temperature. ...

"We studied ten male volunteers (26–38 years old) ... The subjects were admitted to the medical clinic of the Borstel research institute and studied on two occasions separated by at least 21 days. The endotoxin preparation ... was ... given as a bolus injection (100 ng) intravenously at 0800 h. ... infusion of saline (0·9%, 125 ml/h) on the first study day or oxpentifylline (500 mg in 500 ml isotonic saline; Hoechst AG Werk Albert) on the second occasion was started 30 min before endotoxin administration and continued for 4 h." ...

"In nine of the ten subjects there was a rise in body temperature of at least 1·0°C, paralleled by an increase in heart rate (fig 1). ... Since these responses were required for inclusion, the values for that individual were not included in the statistical analysis. Eight of the remaining nine subjects responded to endotoxin with symptoms such as myalgia and headache ... Two subjects also had nausea ... Systolic and diastolic blood pressure were not affected. None of the clinical responses to endotoxin were affected by oxpentifylline." ...

"The baseline serum TNF level was 21 (4) pg/ml. The level rose to 30 (6) pg/ml at 1 h and 38 (11) pg/ml at 2 h after endotoxin injection. ... In contrast, during oxpentifylline treatment there was no rise in serum TNF (baseline: 23 [7] pg/ml, 2 h after endotoxin 24 [5] pg/ml). The difference in TNF levels 2 h after endotoxin between the saline infusion and oxpentifylline infusion periods was significant (p < 0·02)." ...

"We did not include control experiments in which subjects were treated with endotoxin on the two occasions alone. ... The subjects tested in this study, however, responded to the second LPS challenge with fever to the same extent as on the first occasion."
verdict_explanation: Supported: 10 enrolled/9 analyzed with inclusion criterion; two occasions separated by at least 21 days; oxpentifylline 500 mg in 500 mL infused for 4 h starting 30 min before 100 ng IV endotoxin bolus; TNF values at 2 h (38 [11] vs 24 [5] pg/ml) and p<0.02; statement that none of the clinical responses were affected by oxpentifylline. Not supported as written: the claim adds specific physiologic outcomes (fever "~38.9 °C at 4 h", tachycardia, leukocytosis) as explicitly unmodified by oxpentifylline; the provided text reports fever/heart rate for endotoxin response (Fig 1) and states clinical responses were unaffected, but does not explicitly state oxpentifylline failed to modify heart rate or temperature values, and it describes leukocyte changes but not as an explicit 'no modification' finding. ABSTRACT
"Plasma TNF $\alpha$ , IL-1 $\beta$  and IL-6 were measured before surgery, while the patients were hypercortisolemic; on postoperative day 4 or 5, when they were hyporcortisolemic; and on postoperative day 9 or 10, when they were receiving glucocorticoid replacement." ... "During severe hyporcortisolism, on postoperative day 4 or 5, plasma IL-6 levels rose significantly, compared to the preoperative values ( $P < 0.001$ )." ... "Over the same interval, patients with severe hyporcortisolism experienced temperature elevation, fatigue, somnolence, flu-like symptoms, and anorexia" ... "Plasma IL-6 concentrations decreased significantly, albeit not to normal levels, in the hyporcortisolemic group of patients on postoperative day 9 or 10, when they were receiving glucocorticoid replacement."

Protocol
"The patients were considered to have severe hyporcortisolism if their morning plasma cortisol values were less than 2  $\mu\text{g/dL}$  on the third to fifth postoperative day." ...
"If they fulfilled this criterion, they were started on dexamethasone (500 µg, orally, daily, given around 0700 h) on the fifth postoperative day after drawing blood for cortisol and cytokine measurements." ...
"Blood was collected between 0600–0700 h for measurement of TNF $\alpha$ , IL-1 $\beta$ , and IL-6 before surgery and on postoperative days 4 or 5 and 9 or 10."

Results
"Fifteen patients had severe hypocortisolism after TSS (morning plasma cortisol, <2 µg/dL). They all experienced anorexia, fatigue, somnolence of variable degree, and nausea by postoperative day 4. These symptoms were ameliorated

after the first dose of glucocorticoid replacement." ...
"They experienced average temperature elevation of 0.6 C by days 4–5 while they were hypocortisolemic (*P* < 0.02 vs. baseline); their body temperatures returned to preoperative levels by days 9–10, after they had been placed on hydrocortisone replacement. A 5-fold increase in plasma IL-6 levels was observed by days 4–5 (*P* < 0.0001 vs. baseline), whereas glucocorticoid replacement resulted in a significant decrease in plasma IL-6 levels (*P* < 0.0001), although they remained elevated compared to the baseline levels (*P* < 0.0005)."

citation.locator: ## Diagnosis of MCAS (incl. Fig. 1; paragraphs beginning 'MCAS may be diagnosed...' through 'Thirdly, the MCAS diagnosis requires...')

claim: Gulen2024_MCAS.md states that an MCAS diagnosis is confirmed only when all three diagnostic criteria are fulfilled: (1) typical, severe, episodic mast cell activation symptoms in ≥2 organ systems; (2) laboratory evidence of an event-related, substantial transient increase in a validated mast cell activation marker during the symptomatic event compared with the patient’s baseline (with tryptase described as the gold-standard marker, and the event-related tryptase threshold given as > (sBT * 1.2 + 2) ng/mL); and (3) symptom control/response with mast cell mediator–targeting drugs. It also states that for urinary mediator metabolites (histamine, PGD2, leukotrienes), sensitivity/specificity and reliable cutoffs are not established, but it has been suggested to consider levels higher than 30% above the upper limit of normal as pathologic.
source_text:
MCAS may be diagnosed when the symptoms of MC activation are systemic (involving more than one organ system), severe, and recurrent and the MCAS criteria are fulfilled [17••, 18••]. There are three sets of criteria required for an MCAS diagnosis as illustrated in Fig. 1: (1) the presence of typical, severe, episodic MC activation symptoms in  $\geq 2$  organ systems; (2) the detection of a substantial transient increase in a validated marker of MC activation during the symptomatic event; (3) the control of symptoms with MC mediator–targeting drugs.

The clinical criterion of MCAS requires the simultaneous involvement of  $\geq 2$  organ systems [17••, 18••].

Secondly, the diagnosis of MCAS requires laboratory proof. Hence, the clinical symptoms of MCAS are associated with an acute, substantial increase in the levels of a validated mediator of systemic MC activation during an episode, either in serum or urine, compared with the patient's baseline levels.

Currently, tryptase is the most MC-specific mediator that best fulfills the laboratory criterion and is used as a gold standard to document MC activation [20–22].

To diagnose MCAS, the event-related tryptase should be greater than  $\text{sBT} * 1.2 + 2$  ng/mL to confirm the clinical suspicion of MC activation, i.e., typical clinical symptoms of anaphylaxis are also present [17••, 18••, 19•].

**Fig. 1** Diagnostic criteria for mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS). All three criteria must be fulfilled to confirm a diagnosis of MCAS: **A** clinical criterion, **B** laboratory criterion; **C** response criterion.

Mediators other than tryptase, including urinary metabolites of histamine, prostaglandin D2 (PGD2), and leukotrienes, are also available but less specific for MCs and MCAS [28, 29, 30••]. Additionally, the sensitivity and specificity of these markers have not been determined, nor have the reliable indicators of systemic MC activation, such as significant increase and cut-off levels. However, recently, it has been suggested to consider levels higher than 30% above the upper limit of normal as pathologic [18••, 30••].

Thirdly, the MCAS diagnosis requires a favorable response to agents that act as MC stabilizers or inhibitors of MC mediators, such as histamine receptor antagonists (H1- and H2-antihistamines), leukotriene blockers, MC stabilizers, and aspirin or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs) [15•, 58, 59•].

Hence, all above-mentioned three criteria should be fulfilled to confirm a diagnosis of MCAS.
verdict_explanation: The source clearly supports that all three criteria must be fulfilled (including explicit statements in Fig. 1 caption and the sentence 'Hence, all above-mentioned three criteria should be fulfilled to confirm a diagnosis of MCAS.'). It supports the tryptase diagnostic equation as written (> sBT*1.2 + 2 ng/mL) and describes tryptase as the gold standard. It also supports that urinary mediator metabolite cutoffs are not established and that it has been suggested to consider levels >30% above the upper limit of normal as pathologic (i.e., threshold is relative to ULN, not baseline). However, the candidate claim adds unsupported specifics: it asserts serum tryptase is measured '1–4 hours post-event' (the text says tryptase 'peaks in serum about 1 h after clinical onset' and discusses half-life/elevation duration but does not state a 1–4 hour sampling window), and it states urinary metabolites are 'suggested to rise substantially during flares' framed as an event-linked rise vs baseline; the quoted suggestion is specifically 'higher than 30% above the upper limit of normal' and is not framed as a flare-vs-baseline requirement in this section.
readiness_reason: The repaired claim is directly supported by exact source quotations with clear locators, and the unsupported timing detail (1–4 hours) and baseline-vs-ULN ambiguity for urinary metabolites have been removed/clarified.

citation.locator: Abstract; Making the Diagnosis; Conclusions

claim: In Chung (2014), urodynamic study—specifically an invasive pressure-flow urodynamic study—is stated to be currently the only definitive method for assessing detrusor contractile function, and the article states that urodynamics should be conducted to consolidate the diagnosis of UAB via functional demonstration of detrusor underactivity (DU). The article also states that measurement of post-void residual (PVR) may indicate detrusor failure if bladder outlet obstruction (BOO) is excluded, and that it is important to differentiate DU from BOO using urodynamic pressure/flow features (elevated detrusor pressure with low flow typifying BOO).
source_text:
**Abstract** ... "Urodynamic study is currently the only definitive method of assessing detrusor contractile function." ...

## Making the Diagnosis
"At present, many of the UAB symptoms are difficult to quantify objectively. An invasive pressure flow urodynamic study is currently the only definitive method of assessing detrusor contractile function [1••]." ... "However, it is not uncommon for some patients to exhibit concomitant urodynamic findings such as bladder outlet obstruction (BOO) or DO. It is important to differentiate between DU and BOO, with the diagnosis of BOO often typified by an elevated detrusor pressure in the presence of low-flow voiding." ...

## Conclusions
"Measurement of post-void residual may provide an indication of underlying detrusor failure if BOO is excluded, but at present, urodynamics study should be conducted to consolidate the diagnosis of UAB through demonstration of the presence of DU functionally."
verdict_explanation: Supported: the source explicitly states (in Abstract and Making the Diagnosis) that urodynamic study / an invasive pressure-flow urodynamic study is currently the only definitive method of assessing detrusor contractile function, and (in Conclusions) that urodynamics should be conducted to consolidate diagnosis via functional demonstration of DU. Part not supported as written: the source does not state that subjective LUTS and elevated PVR "do not specifically indicate" detrusor contractility failure, nor that they "cannot differentiate DU from BOO without pressure-flow measurement" in those terms. Instead, it says symptoms may not correlate strongly with underlying detrusor abnormality (Exact Definition section) and says PVR may provide an indication of detrusor failure if BOO is excluded, while emphasizing the importance of differentiating DU vs BOO using urodynamic findings.
readiness_reason: The original candidate claim contains unsupported wording about LUTS/PVR lacking specificity and an explicit statement that they cannot differentiate DU from BOO without pressure-flow measurement; the repaired claim is narrower and supported, but it is not identical to the candidate’s full assertion.

source_text:
“Furthermore, the symptoms in UAB are commonly described in other urologic conditions such as bladder outlet obstruction or benign prostatic hyperplasia.”
...
“It is important to differentiate between DU and BOO, with the diagnosis of BOO often typified by an elevated detrusor pressure in the presence of low-flow voiding.”
verdict_explanation: Supported: (1) LUTS/symptoms of UAB overlap with BOO/BPH (the source says symptoms in UAB are commonly described in BOO/BPH). Supported: (2) BOO on pressure-flow is typified by elevated detrusor pressure with low-flow voiding. Not supported: the additional, explicit paired characterization that DU is “low detrusor pressure during low-flow voiding” is not stated in the provided source text (the source mentions low detrusor pressure in cystometry and does not explicitly tie DU to low-pressure/low-flow during voiding). Evidence label corrected: this is a narrative review and contains no original human/animal studies by the author; the pressure-flow description is definitional/diagnostic framing rather than a report of a specific clinical study.

citation.locator: MATERIALS AND METHODS (program over four sessions; compliance recording; 3-point compliance grading; technique assessment and nurse specialist role); RESULTS (mean time between first and fourth visits)

claim: In Siu et al. (2003), compliance with pelvic muscle exercises was recorded from patient logs as the number of exercise sessions and contractions the patient logged each day; compliance was also rated on a 3-point scale (1=low, 2=moderate, 3=high) where high compliance was >80% of the recommended regimen, low compliance was <20%, and moderate compliance was between these ranges. Across the study’s four clinic sessions (baseline plus 2nd–4th sessions), a nurse specialist reviewed the correctness of exercise technique at each subsequent visit, and pelvic muscle strength was assessed by vaginal examination; the mean time between the first and fourth visits was 213.40 days (30.50 weeks).
source_text:
The program extended over four sessions at monthly intervals. ... To standardize the assessment, a single nurse specialist would perform vaginal assessment for the patients during each clinic visit.

Between the visits, the patient carried out a weekly charting of the frequency of incontinence. The severity of incontinence was measured as number of incontinence episodes per month. Compliance was recorded as the number of sessions and contractions the patient logged each day.

At each subsequent visit, the charts were reviewed, the strength of the patient's pelvic muscles assessed by vaginal examination, and the correctness of her exercise technique reviewed by the nurse specialist.

A three-point grading was used to rate the extent of compliance, with 1 = low compliance, 2 = moderate compliance, and 3 = high compliance. Patients who were able to comply more than 80% of the recommended exercise regimen were rated at high compliance, those who comply less than 20% were rated as low compliance, moderate compliance were for patients who had the compliance rate in between these two range. Pelvic muscle exercise technique was assessed to be either correct or incorrect.

The mean time between the first and fourth visits was 213.40 days (30.50 weeks).
verdict_explanation: Supported: four clinic sessions; compliance recorded from patient-logged number of sessions and contractions each day; 3-point compliance grading with cutoffs <20%, between, and >80%; nurse specialist reviewed correctness of technique; mean time between first and fourth visits was 213.40 days (30.50 weeks). Not supported as stated: the claim says adherence was assessed using "weekly patient self-report logs" recording daily sessions/contractions—source states compliance recorded from what the patient logged each day, while "weekly charting" is explicitly described for incontinence frequency, not explicitly as the compliance log format. Also not supported as stated: technique correctness evaluated "via digital vaginal examination"; source says technique was reviewed by the nurse specialist and strength assessed by vaginal examination, but does not specify "digital" vaginal examination for technique assessment.
readiness_reason: The candidate claim contains two material specifics not directly supported by the source text: (1) that compliance used weekly self-report logs (weekly is stated for incontinence charting, not explicitly for compliance), and (2) that technique correctness was evaluated via "digital" vaginal examination (not specified). A repaired claim is possible only by removing or qualifying those specifics.
original_claim: Siu et al. (2003) assessed pelvic floor exercise adherence using weekly patient self-report logs recording daily number of exercise sessions and contractions across four clinic visits over a mean 213.40 days (30.50 weeks), and graded compliance on a 3-point ordinal scale: Grade 1 (<20% of recommended regimen), Grade 2 (20% to 80%), Grade 3 (>80%); exercise technique correctness was evaluated by a nurse specialist via digital vaginal examination.

claim: Alewijnse et al. (2003) reported sequential longitudinal multiple linear regression analyses predicting adherence behavior at 12-month follow-up (n = 75). In the final model, R² = 0.50 and adjusted R² = 0.42; adherence behavior at post-test was a significant predictor (standardized β = 0.428, P = 0.000), weekly wet episodes at pre-test was a significant predictor (β = 0.276, P = 0.010), and intention was not significant (β = −0.095, P = 0.368). In the Results text, they reported that the final step showed an R² change = 0.133 with P < 0.001 for the contribution of post-test adherence behavior to variability in long-term adherence over and above proximal variables and the self-help guide, and a significant contribution of the distal variables weekly wet episodes and sex education at school.
source_text:
**Table III.** *Sequential longitudinal multiple linear regression analyses with adherence behavior at 12-month follow-up (n = 75) as dependent variable and the independent variables from pre-test that significantly predicted adherence behavior; standardized coefficient, P values and explained variance for the final equation* | Independent variables | $R^2 = 0.05,$
$R^2_{adj} = 0.04$ | | $R^2 = 0.29,$
$R^2_{adj} = 0.24$ | | $R^2 = 0.36,$
$R^2_{adj} = 0.28$ | | $R^2 = 0.36,$
$R^2_{adj} = 0.28$ | | $R^2 = 0.50,$
$R^2_{adj} = 0.42$ | | ... | weekly wet episodes | | | 0.325 | 0.005 | 0.361 | 0.002 | 0.362 | 0.002 | 0.276 | 0.010 | ... | intention | | | | | | | −0.047 | 0.686 | −0.095 | 0.368 | ... | adherence behavior at post-test | | | | | | | | | 0.428 | 0.000 | ### Predictors of adherence behavior "Results are presented in Table III. One year after therapy, the final step of the analyses showed a significant contribution of post-test adherence behavior to variability in long-term adherence over and above proximal variables and the self-help guide, and a significant contribution of the distal variables of weekly frequency of wet episodes and sex education at school, $R^2$ change = 0.133, $P < 0.001$ ." "This final model predicted 50% (adjusted 42%) of the variance in adherence behavior 1 year after therapy." ## Discussion "This study is the first to assess predictors of long-term adherence to PFME therapy among women with UI. Total explained variance of long-term adherence behavior 1 year after PFME therapy was fairly high. The prediction of long-term adherence with pre-test data yielded an $R^2 = 0.50$ (adjusted $R^2 = 0.42$ )." "An important finding was that, in contrast to the theoretical assumption of the ASE model (De Vries *et al.*, 1988), the longitudinal analysis revealed that intention at pre-test did not significantly predict long-term adherence behavior."
verdict_explanation: Supported from Table III: n=75; final model R²=0.50 and adjusted R²=0.42; β and P values for post-test adherence (β=0.428, P=0.000), weekly wet episodes (β=0.276, P=0.010), and intention (β=−0.095, P=0.368). Supported from Results text: R² change=0.133, P<0.001, but the text attributes this change to the final step contribution of post-test adherence plus distal variables (weekly wet episodes and sex education), not solely to post-test adherence as the candidate claim states. Not supported in the provided source text: an overall model P value reported as 'P<0.001' for the entire model (the only P<0.001 statement given is for R² change), and the characterization of post-test adherence as 'the strongest independent predictor' is not explicitly stated in the source (though it is significant and larger than weekly wet episodes in the final model). Evidence label CLINICAL is appropriate because this is a longitudinal prospective human study regression analysis.
readiness_reason: mechanical check: the validator's source_text was not found in the named source file (none); After repair, the claim is fully supported by direct quotations from Table III and the adjacent Results/Discussion text, with correct attributions and without adding unsupported statements (e.g., overall model P value or sole attribution of R² change to post-test adherence).
original_claim: Alewijnse et al. (2003) reported a sequential longitudinal regression model predicting 12-month adherence (n=75; overall R2=0.50, adjusted R2=0.42, P<0.001) in which post-test (end-of-therapy) adherence was the strongest independent predictor (standardized β=0.428, P<0.001; final block R2 change=0.133, P<0.001) and baseline symptom severity measured as weekly wet episodes also predicted higher 12-month adherence (standardized β=0.276, P=0.010), while baseline intention was not significant (β=−0.095, P=0.368).
