claim: Brown et al. (2020) retrospectively reviewed 958 new urogynecology consultations; 35% (335/958) were referred to pelvic floor physical therapy (PFPT). Among those referred (N=335), 224/335 (67%) attended PFPT (defined as at least one PFPT visit not including the same-day PFPT visit), and 141/335 (42%) completed PFPT (defined as having a PFPT discharge summary or attending ≥3 PFPT visits). Patients who saw PFPT the same day as their initial urogynecology visit were more likely to attend PFPT than those who did not (67/74, 91% vs 157/259, 61%; p<0.001); completion did not differ significantly (36/74, 49% vs 105/259, 41%; p=0.15). In logistic regression (Table 2), same-day PFPT was associated with PFPT attendance (OR 6.22 [2.75, 14.08]; adjusted OR 6.03 [2.66, 13.69]) and was not statistically significant for PFPT completion (OR 1.36 [0.81, 2.29]; adjusted OR not reported).
source_text:
**Abstract – Results**—"PFPT referral was made for 35% (335/958), of whom 67% attended and 42% completed PFPT. Patients who saw PFPT the same day as their first urogynecology visit were significantly more likely to attend PFPT than those who did not (91% vs. 61%,  $p < 0.001$ ), but completion rates did not differ (49% vs. 41%,  $p = 0.15$ )." ...

**Materials and methods** "Patients were identified as having been referred to PFPT if an order was placed for PFPT consultation on the day of initial urogynecology consultation. Those patients who attended at least one PFPT visit (not including their same-day PFPT visit) were categorized as having attended PFPT. Those patients who had a discharge summary from PFPT or who attended at least three PFPT visits were categorized as having completed PFPT." ...

**Results** "Among the 981 patients identified in the initial medical records query, 98% (958/981) met criteria for inclusion, and 35% (335/958) of included patients were referred to PFPT (Fig. 1)." ... "Among the 335 patients referred to PFPT, 224 (67%) attended PFPT and 141 (42%) completed PFPT." ... "Patients who saw PFPT the same day as their initial urogynecology visit were statistically significantly more likely to attend PFPT than those who did not (91% vs. 61%,  $p < 0.001$ ), but completion rates did not differ significantly between the two groups (49% vs. 41%,  $p = 0.15$ )." ...

claim: Support is partially established. Staubach et al. (1998) describe a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in surgical ICU patients with severe sepsis (n=51; pentoxifylline 27 vs placebo 24). Pentoxifylline was given as a continuous intravenous infusion at 1 mg/kg body weight per hour (maximum 1800 mg/day) for 28 days or until ICU discharge or death. They report median serum pentoxifylline concentrations of 3628 ng/mL on day 1 and 1620 ng/mL on day 2, reaching a steady state from day 3 to the end of the 28-day study; the first metabolite (BL 194) showed 1.3- to 2.5-fold higher serum concentrations than the parent drug. They report between-group differences favoring pentoxifylline for MOD score (significant on day 14; Student t test with Bonferroni correction, P<.05), PaO2/FiO2 ratio (significant on days 14 and 17; P<.05), and pressure-adjusted heart rate (significant on day 6; P<.05). They report no significant differences in survival (log-rank P=.85 for 28-day survival; P=.43 for hospital survival) and state that no adverse effects were observed/reported. The candidate’s additional claim that PAHR was lower “from day 6 through day 28” and that dosing was “for up to 28 days” (vs explicitly “during 28 days or until...”) is not supported exactly as written here.
source_text:
**Design:** Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. ... **Patients:** Fifty-one surgical patients with severe sepsis were randomized to receive pentoxifylline continuously (27 patients) or saline infusion as placebo (24 patients). ... **Interventions:** Patients received pentoxifylline (1 mg/kg of body weight per hour; maximum, 1800 mg/d) during 28 days or until they were discharged from the intensive care unit or died. ... No adverse effects of pentoxifylline treatment were observed. The 28-day mortality rate was 30% (8/27) in pentoxifylline-treated patients and 33% (8/24) in the placebo group. Hospital mortality was 41% (11/27) in the pentoxifylline group and 54% (13/24) in the placebo group. ... The multiple organ dysfunction score decreased in patients receiving pentoxifylline 4 days after diagnosis of sepsis compared with placebo-treated patients; a significant difference was reached on day 14 ( $P < .05$ ; Student  $t$  test, Bonferoni correction). The  $\text{PaO}_2/\text{FIO}_2$  (fraction of inspired oxygen) ratio was significantly improved in pentoxifylline-treated patients on days 14 and 17 ( $P < .05$ ), and the pressure-adjusted heart rate was significantly improved on day 6 ( $P < .05$ ) compared with the placebo group.

Fifty-one surgical patients were randomly assigned within 12 hours after diagnosis of sepsis to receive a continuous intravenous infusion of pentoxifylline (Rentyllin, Rentschler, Germany) 1 mg/kg of body weight per hour, to a maximum of 1800 mg/d or normal saline solution as placebo during 28 days or until patients were discharged from the ICU or died.

The 28-day mortality rate was 30% (8/27) in patients receiving pentoxifylline and 33% (8/24) in the placebo group. In-hospital mortality was 41% (11/27) in the pentoxifylline group and 54% (13/24) in the placebo group (**Figure 1**). There were no significant differences in the survival curves of the groups (log-rank analysis,  $P=.85$  for 28-day survival and  $P=.43$  for hospital survival). Adverse effects were not reported in any patient.

From day 4 after the diagnosis of sepsis, the score decreased in patients receiving pentoxifylline compared with placebo-infused patients (**Figure 2**). This difference reached significance on day 14 after the diagnosis of sepsis ( $P<.05$ ). The  $\text{PaO}_2/\text{FiO}_2$  ratio as a parameter for pulmonary dysfunction increased from day 7 in patients receiving pentoxifylline compared with patients receiving placebo (**Figure 3**). The difference was statistically significant on days 14 and 17 after the diagnosis of severe sepsis ( $P<.05$ ).

The pressure-adjusted heart rate characterizing cardiac function was significantly different on day 6 after diagnosis (*P*<.05) and remained decreased compared with the placebo group (**Figure 4**). ... The median serum concentration of pentoxifylline was 3628 ng/mL on the first day after starting infusion and 1620 ng/mL on day 2; it reached a steady state from day 3 until the end of the 28-day study. A similar pattern was demonstrated for the first metabolite of pentoxifylline (BL 194) with a 1.3- to 2.5-fold higher serum concentration than the parent drug (**Figure 5**).

**Figure 2.** *Serial multiple organ dysfunction (MOD) score ... Asterisk indicates* P*<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline ... vs patients receiving placebo ...; Student* t *test with Bonferroni correction.*

**Figure 3.** *Changes in  $\mathrm{PaO_2/FIO_2}$  ... Asterisks indicate* P*<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline ... vs patients receiving placebo ...; Student* t *test with Bonferroni correction.*

**Figure 4.** *Changes in pressure-adjusted heart rate ... Asterisk indicates* P*<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline ... vs patients receiving placebo ...; Student* t *test with Bonferroni correction.*

**Figure 1.** *Kaplan-Meier 28-day survival ... Survival did not differ significantly between patient groups (*P *= .85 for 28-day survival and* P *= .43 for hospital survival).*
verdict_explanation: Trial design/population (randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled; surgical ICU severe sepsis; n=51 with 27 vs 24), dosing (continuous IV 1 mg/kg/h; max 1800 mg/d; during 28 days or until ICU discharge/death), serum concentrations/steady state (median 3628 ng/mL day 1; 1620 ng/mL day 2; steady state from day 3 to end of 28-day study), metabolite ratio (BL 194 1.3- to 2.5-fold higher), MOD and PaO2/FiO2 timepoints with P<.05 and Bonferroni correction, PAHR significant on day 6, and survival P-values (log-rank P=.85 and P=.43) plus “no adverse effects” are supported. However, the candidate overstates/over-specifies PAHR as being lower 'from day 6 through day 28' (the text says significant on day 6 and 'remained decreased' without specifying significance across all later timepoints) and paraphrases the intervention duration as 'for up to 28 days' rather than the stated 'during 28 days or until ... discharged ... or died.'
readiness_reason: The candidate claim contains at least one unsupported specificity (PAHR lower from day 6 through day 28) and imprecise duration phrasing; it should be split/repaired into strictly supported sub-claims before witness construction.
original_claim: Staubach et al. (1998) report a prospective randomized double-blind placebo-controlled ICU trial in surgical severe sepsis (n=51; PTX 27 vs placebo 24) where pentoxifylline was given as continuous IV infusion 1 mg/kg/hour (max 1,800 mg/day) for up to 28 days; steady-state serum PTX concentrations were reported (median 3,628 ng/mL Day 1; 1,620 ng/mL Day 2; stable from Day 3–28) and metabolite BL 194 was 1.3–2.5× higher than parent; organ dysfunction measures improved at some timepoints (e.g., MOD score reduction on Day 14, PaO2/FiO2 improved Days 14 and 17, PAHR lower from Day 6 through Day 28; P<0.05 as stated), but 28-day mortality (30% vs 33%, P=0.85) and in-hospital mortality (41% vs 54%, P=0.43) did not differ, and the study reports zero adverse drug reactions/toxicities.

claim: Bahaa et al. (2024) report a randomized, double-blinded clinical trial in mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis in which 52 patients were analyzed (n=26/group) after 24 weeks: mesalamine 1 g t.i.d. plus placebo vs mesalamine 1 g t.i.d. plus pentoxifylline (PTX) 400 mg twice daily. Between-group comparisons after treatment favored the PTX group for NRS pain (median 1 (0–1.25) vs 2 (0.25–3), Mann-Whitney p=0.007, Z=-2.684), diarrhea (6/26 vs 16/26, chi-square p=0.01), rectal bleeding (7/26 vs 11/26, chi-square p=0.04), ESR (after-treatment p=0.002), DAI (PTX 87.65 ± 25.84 vs mesalamine 129.9 ± 40.1; after-treatment p=0.0001), and SF-36 (PTX 65.31 ± 12.88 vs mesalamine 55.27 ± 9.689; after-treatment p=0.0026). The study also reports between-group differences after treatment in inflammatory biomarkers (IL-6, TNF-α, S1P, fecal MPO; Table 3) and colonic gene expression (STAT-3 and ZO-1; Table 5), each with a between-group p-value. Adverse event frequencies did not significantly differ between groups for vomiting, headache, itching, or hypotension (Table 6).

source_text:
Abstract: "Injection of lipopolysaccharide (10 mg/kg, i.v.) resulted in a significant fall in mean arterial pressure and an increase of heart rate. In contrast, animals pretreated with pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, i.v., at 30 min prior to lipopolysaccharide) maintained a significantly higher mean arterial pressure..." ... "The pressor effect of noradrenaline (1  $\mu$ g/kg, i.v.) was also significantly reduced after the treatment of rats with lipopolysaccharide." ... "Pretreatment of lipopolysaccharide-rats with pentoxifylline partially, but significantly, prevented this lipopolysaccharide-induced hyporeactivity to noradrenaline in vivo and ex vivo." ... "Treatment of conscious mice with a high dose of endotoxin (60 mg/kg, i.p.) resulted in a survival rate of only 10% at 36 h ( $n = 20$ ). However, therapeutic application of pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, i.p. at 0, 6, 15 and 24 h after lipopolysaccharide) increased the 36-h survival to 35% ( $n = 20$ )." 

Methods 2.1: "After recording of the baseline haemodynamic parameters, the animals were given saline or pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, *i.v.*). At 30 min after injection of vehicle (saline) or pentoxifylline, the animals received saline or *E. coli* lipopolysaccharide (10 mg/kg, *i.v.*) and were monitored for 240 min. The pressor responses to noradrenaline (1  $\mu$ g/kg, *i.v.*) were reassessed... at every hour after vehicle or lipopolysaccharide injection."

Results 3.1: "Pretreatment of lipopolysaccharide-rats with pentoxifylline attenuated the delayed hypotension (i.e., after 120 min). Thus, the mean arterial pressure of lipopolysaccharide-rats pretreated with pentoxifylline was significantly higher than that of the respective lipopolysaccharide control group at 120–240 min (Fig. 1a)."

Fig. 1 caption: "Different LPS-treated groups of animals were pretreated with vehicle (saline, LPS;  $n=16$ ) or PTF (3 mg/kg, i.v. at 30 min prior to LPS, PTF/LPS;  $n=16$ )." ... "\* $P < 0.05$  represents significant differences when compared to SOP at the same time point.  $\dagger P < 0.05$  represents significant differences between treated and untreated LPS-rats."

Results 3.2: "Pretreatment of lipopolysaccharide-rats with pentoxifylline enhanced the pressor responses to noradrenaline (Fig. 2a). Thus, the pressor responses to noradrenaline at 1–4 h in lipopolysaccharide-rats pretreated with pentoxifylline were significantly greater than those in animals treated with lipopolysaccharide alone ( $P < 0.05$ ; Fig. 2a)."

Fig. 2 caption: "The changes in (a) pressor responses to NA (1 µg/kg, i.v.)..." ... "†*P* < 0.05 represents significant differences between treated and untreated LPS-rats."

Methods 2.5: "Different groups of animals received vehicle (saline) together with lipopolysaccharide ( $n = 20$ ) or lipopolysaccharide plus pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, i.p. at 0, 6, 15 and 24 h after lipopolysaccharide,  $n = 20$ )."

Results 3.5: "The administration of a high dose (60 mg/kg, i.p.) of lipopolysaccharide to mice was associated with a 36-h survival rate of only 10% of the animals. In contrast, lipopolysaccharide-mice treated with pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, i.p. at 0, 6, 15 and 24 h after lipopolysaccharide,  $n = 20$ ) had a higher survival rate, 35%, at 36 h (Fig. 5)."

source_text:
## Abstract

"Using a porcine model of abdominal trauma resulting from the combined insults of haemorrhage and infection, a randomised placebo-controlled trial was conducted of pentoxifylline (20 mg/kg bolus followed by 20 mg/kg infusion over 1 h) administered in addition to a colloid resuscitation regimen. Female Large White pigs (45–60 kg) were bled 40% of their blood volume and peritonitis was induced using *E. coli* (O18: K1: H7) in an autoclaved faecal suspension. Animals were resuscitated with either colloid alone ( $n = 5$ ) or colloid plus pentoxifylline ( $n = 5$ )." ...

### 2.3. Experimental procedure

"All animals underwent a rapid fixed-volume haemorrhage (26 ml/kg = 40% blood volume). On completion of the haemorrhage, peritonitis was induced using the faecal inoculum. All animals were resuscitated at 1 h with 3.5% polygeline (Haemacel® , Hoechst Roussel Ltd., Uxbridge, UK) with a volume identical to that of the blood removed." ... "Animals were randomised to a pentoxifylline-treated or control group. Simultaneously with the commencement of resuscitation the pentoxifylline-treated group were given a 20 mg/kg bolus of pentoxifylline in 30 ml water followed by a further 20 mg/kg of pentoxifylline in 30 ml infused over 60 min. Control animals received 30 ml 0.9% saline as both the bolus and infusion." ...

## 3. Results

"In the control group the median time to death was 11 h with only one animal surviving 24 h. In the pentoxifylline-treated group the median time to death was 16 h with two animals surviving 24 h. There was no difference in survival between the two groups." ...

### 2.4. Statistical analyses

"Survival analysis was by the Peto and Peto log rank test." ...

Table 1

"| MAP (mmHg) | Control | 68 (11) | 51 (8) | 92 (10)* | 83 (6)* | 68 (13) |
|  | PTX | 75 (4) | 45 (10) | 62 (10) | 57 (15) | 55 (23) |" ...

"| Urine output (ml/kg per h) | Control | – | 0.56 (0.28) | 1.11 (0.55) | 1.28 (0.18)* | 1.00 (1.35) |
|  | PTX | – | 0.20 (0.32) | 0.32 (0.71) | 0.63 (0.74) | 0.31 (0.55) |" ...

"| Systemic vascular resistance index (dyne s/cm5 per m2) | Control | 680 (60) | 960 (330) | 580 (70)* | 790 (280)** | 820 (180) |
|  | PTX | 730 (80) | 1010 (230) | 420 (70) | 520 (190) | 760 (270) |" ...

"a Data presented as median (interquartile range)."

"*  $P < 0.01$ ,

claim: In anesthetized pigs with fecal peritonitis, pentoxifylline (PTF) pretreatment as a continuous infusion (60 mg/h) started 120 minutes before peritonitis induction was associated with smaller increases in systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) at 300 minutes: SVR increased to 133% above baseline in untreated test pigs vs 36% above baseline in PTF-pretreated pigs at 300 min; PVR increased to 462% above baseline in untreated test pigs vs 140% above baseline in PTF-pretreated pigs at 300 min. The source reports significant between-group differences in SVR at all points from baseline to 300 min except at 30 min, and in PVR at 270 and 300 min.
source_text:
Anesthesia was induced in 12 pigs (25 to 35 kg) with azaperone (2.0 mg/kg im) and metomidate (10 mg/kg ip). ... A laparotomy was performed and 35 ml of aspirated cecal content was spread in the peritoneum to induce peritonitis (PI). In six animals an infusion of PTF (60 mg/h) was started 120 min before PI and maintained for the study duration. ...

### *Hemodynamics*

In the test group there was a progressive increase in SVR to 133% above baseline at 300 min. In marked contrast, SVR increased only to 36% above baseline in the PTF group at 300 min. There were significant differences between the two groups at all points from baseline to 300 min other than at 30 min.

In both groups, PVR increased progressively, reaching a maximum 462% above baseline in the test group and 140% above baseline in the PTF group at 300 min. There were significant differences between the two groups at 270 and 300 min.

claim: Support is PARTLY established. Roberts et al. state that with oral preparations of pentoxifylline (PTX) peak plasma levels are less than 5 μmol/l, and that PTX is converted to active metabolites but the combined level of all active forms is unlikely to exceed 10 μmol/l; they also refer to 5–10 μmol/l as a “clinically achievable concentration” in the Abstract and note that many in vitro studies used millimolar PTX, which they discuss as complicating interpretation. The source does not state that the <5 μmol/l and ≤10 μmol/l figures were measured by (capillary) gas chromatography in their human subjects; the gas chromatography method described pertains to PTX measurements in monkey plasma in their primate experiments.
source_text:
Abstract: “The study confirmed that PTX at clinically achievable concentration (5–10 μmol/l) attenuated the responses of human neutrophils to chemotactic peptide, whereas it did not inhibit the effect of GM-CSF on neutrophil function even at high concentrations.”

Introduction: “The interpretation of the effects of PTX on phagocyte function are confused in many cases by the use of PTX in in vitro experiments at much higher concentrations than are obtained clinically. With oral preparations of PTX peak plasma levels are less than 5 μmol/l (6, 21). PTX is converted to active metabolites but the combined level of all active forms of the drug are unlikely to exceed 10 μmol/l. In many previous studies, levels in the millimolar range have been used. At these levels PTX is a potent inhibitor of phagocyte phosphodiesterase activity (18, 22, 23) which undoubtedly blocks receptor-mediated activation of the respiratory burst (18, 22, 24). It is not clear whether PTX can elevate cyclic AMP levels in the low micromolar range.”

Materials and methods – Experiments in primates: “Plasma was separated from these blood samples, stored at −20°C, and the concentration of PTX determined by capillary gas chromatography (31), following a 200-fold dilution with blank human plasma to bring the concentrations within the normal range of the assay.”
verdict_explanation: Correct that the paper states: (a) “With oral preparations of PTX peak plasma levels are less than 5 μmol/l”, and (b) “the combined level of all active forms of the drug are unlikely to exceed 10 μmol/l.” Correct that the Abstract uses “clinically achievable concentration (5–10 μmol/l)” and that the Introduction criticizes/confounds interpretation due to prior millimolar in vitro concentrations. readiness_reason: The candidate claim contains unsupported specifics (controlled-release; measured by blood gas chromatography; “therapeutic range” framing; “artifact-prone” wording). claim: Support is partially established: Roberts et al. report that (i) PTX at 0.5–50 µmol/L did not alter FMLP-stimulated cAMP responses, whereas 100 or 500 µmol/L PTX enhanced the magnitude and duration of the FMLP-induced cAMP transient; and (ii) PTX at up to 50 µmol/L did not change resting or FMLP-stimulated intracellular Ca2+, while 500 µmol/L reduced both resting and stimulated [Ca2+]i with p<0.05; and in Discussion they state it is therefore unlikely that effects of PTX at ≤50 µmol/L are due to phosphodiesterase inhibition. However, the candidate claim's specific numeric cAMP values 'from ~18 to ~45 pmol/10^6 cells' and its statement that 100 and 500 µmol/L 'approximately doubled' to ~45 pmol/10^6 cells are not supported as written because the Results text reports cAMP in pmol/10^7 cells and does not provide a ~45 pmol/10^6 value.
source_text: b) *Effect on cAMP:* The resting level of cAMP in purified neutrophils was  $7.0 \pm 4.2$  pmol/ $10^7$  cells (mean  \pm 1  SD,  $n = 11$ ) and there was no significant change when cells were incubated for 15 to 30 min with a range of PTX concentrations up to 500  $\mu$ mol/l. The resting level of cAMP for these experiments (mean  \pm 1  SD) was  $7.0 \pm 4.2$ ,  $10.1 \pm 2.7$ ,  $12.0 \pm 2.9$ ,  $5.1 \pm 2.0$ ,  $5.1 \pm 5.4$ ,  $8.7 \pm 6.2$  and  $13.0 \pm 11.2$  pmoles/ $10^7$  cells for 0, 0.5, 1, 10, 50, 100 and 500  $\mu$ mol/l PTX, respectively. In 8 experiments FMLP stimulated a rapid increment in cAMP from resting levels to  $18.1 \pm 5.4$  pmol/ $10^7$  cells within 10 to 20 s of stimulation. Pre-incubation with 100 or 500  $\mu$ mol/l PTX 15 min before FMLP stimulation enhanced both the magnitude and duration of the cAMP responses (Fig. 5a) ( $p < 0.001$ ,  $n = 5$ , Students t-test). Lower concentrations of PTX between 0.5 to 50  $\mu$ mol/l did not induce these effects (Fig. 5b). ... a) *Effect on FMLP-stimulated calcium transients:* ... The mean resting level of  $[Ca^{2+}]_i$  in purified neutrophils was  $88 \pm 10$  nmol/l ( $\pm 1$  SE,  $n = 6$ ) and increased to  $799 \pm 197$  nmol/l after stimulation with 1  $\mu$ mol/l FMLP. Preincubation of cells with up to 50  $\mu$ mol/l PTX did not change either the resting or stimulated  $[Ca^{2+}]_i$ , whereas 500  $\mu$ mol/l PTX reduced the resting level to  $73 \pm 12$  nmol/l and the stimulated level to  $571 \pm 144$  nmol/l, values which were significantly different from control by paired Student's t-test ( $p < 0.05$ ). ... claim: In ICR mice given *E. coli* lipopolysaccharide (LPS) 60 mg/kg intraperitoneally, 36-hour survival was 10% (n=20). Therapeutic pentoxifylline (PTF) 3 mg/kg intraperitoneally, administered at 0, 6, 15, and 24 hours after LPS, increased 36-hour survival to 35% (n=20). The paper states that survival-rate differences were analyzed using a chi-square test with statistical significance at P<0.05, but it does not report a specific P value for this survival comparison.
source_text:
### 2.5. Survival studies

Survival studies were performed with mice (28–35 g), whose stock originated from the Institute of Cancer Research of National Institute of Health, USA, were purchased from the National Animal Centre (Taipei, Taiwan, R.O.C.). Lipopolysaccharide (60 mg/kg, i.p.) was injected in the presence of vehicle or drugs and survival was monitored every 6 up to 36 h. Different groups of animals received vehicle (saline) together with lipopolysaccharide ( $n = 20$ ) or lipopolysaccharide plus pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, i.p. at 0, 6, 15 and 24 h after lipopolysaccharide,  $n = 20$ ).
...
### 2.7. Statistical analysis

All values in the figures and text are expressed as means  $\pm$  S.E.M. of  $n$  observations, where  $n$  represents the number of animals studied. Statistical evaluation was performed with an analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by a multiple comparison test (Scheffe's test), except for the inducible NO synthase expression which was analysed by unpaired Student's *t*-test. The chi-square test was used for determining the significance of differences in survival rate between control and drug-treated groups. A *P* value less than 0.05 was considered to be statistically significant.
...
### 3.5. Effects of pentoxifylline on the survival rate of mice treated with lipopolysaccharide

The administration of a high dose (60 mg/kg, i.p.) of lipopolysaccharide to mice was associated with a 36-h survival rate of only 10% of the animals. In contrast, lipopolysaccharide-mice treated with pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, i.p. at 0, 6, 15 and 24 h after lipopolysaccharide,  $n = 20$ ) had a higher survival rate, 35%, at 36 h (Fig. 5).
verdict_explanation: Supported: ICR mice; LPS dose/route (60 mg/kg, i.p.); monitoring to 36 h; survival rates at 36 h (10% vs 35%); PTF dose/route and dosing times (3 mg/kg, i.p. at 0, 6, 15, 24 h after LPS); group sizes reported as n=20 for each group. Not supported as stated: the claim gives numerators (2/20 and 7/20) which are not stated in the source text (only percentages and n=20 are stated), and it asserts a specific result P value ('P < 0.05 by Chi-square test') for this comparison, but the paper provides only the general statement that chi-square was used and that P<0.05 was considered significant; it does not report an explicit P value for Fig. 5 / §3.5.
readiness_reason: After removing unsupported numerators and the unreported specific P value, the remaining claim is directly supported by the cited sections and can be faithfully quoted/condensed.

Injection of lipopolysaccharide (10 mg/kg, i.v.) resulted in a significant fall in mean arterial pressure and an increase of heart rate. In contrast, animals pretreated with pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, i.v., at 30 min prior to lipopolysaccharide) maintained a significantly higher mean arterial pressure but showed no effect on the tachycardia when compared to rats given only lipopolysaccharide (lipopolysaccharide-rats). ... After recording of the baseline haemodynamic parameters, the animals were given saline or pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, i.v.). At 30 min after injection of vehicle (saline) or pentoxifylline, the animals received saline or E. coli lipopolysaccharide (10 mg/kg, i.v.) and were monitored for 240 min. ...

Pretreatment of lipopolysaccharide-rats with pentoxifylline attenuated the delayed hypotension (i.e., after 120 min). source_text:
**Interventions:** Six groups of ventilated swine were studied for 5 hours. Group 1 swine (control, n=8) received saline solution only. Group 2 swine (sepsis, n=8) received a 1-hour infusion of *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. Groups 3, 4, and 5 swine received the *P aeruginosa* infusion and a 20 mg/kg bolus followed by a 6 mg/kg per hour infusion of pentoxifylline. Group 3 swine (n=6) received pentoxifylline prior to the onset of sepsis; group 4 swine (n=6) received pentoxifylline at 1 hour and group 5 swine (n=4) at 2 hours after the onset of the *P aeruginosa* infusion. ...

**Results:** ... Administration of pentoxifylline to group 5 animals in established septic shock caused uncontrolled, fatal systemic hypotension in two of the four animals. ...

... Group 2 swine (sepsis, n=8) received a 1-hour intravenous infusion of live *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, PAO strain (5×10^8 colony forming units per milliliter at 0.3 mL/20 kg per minute). Three further groups of animals with sepsis were studied, each receiving a 20-mg/kg bolus of pentoxifylline (Hoechst-Roussel, Somerville, NJ) followed by an infusion (6 mg/kg per hour) until the end of the experiment. Group 3 swine (pretreatment pentoxifylline, n=6) commenced the pentoxifylline regimen 15 minutes prior to the bacterial infusion. Group 4 swine (posttreatment pentoxifylline, n=6) received the bolus of pentoxifylline immediately following the termination of the bacterial infusion at 1 hour into the experiment. Group 5 swine (delayed treatment pentoxifylline, n=4) commenced pentoxifylline treatment 1 hour after the bacterial infusion for 2 hours. ...

In the delayed treatment group (group 5), we observed a 50% mortality rate, and therefore, the study in this group was terminated at four animals. Profound hypotension developed on initiation of pentoxifylline infusion in the two animals that died, with neither animal surviving beyond 3 hours. ... Because of the small numbers in the delayed treatment group, no statistical conclusions could be obtained and the data have not been included in this article.

Significant pulmonary arterial hypertension developed within 30 minutes in all groups compared with con-

trols, although pretreatment with pentoxifylline significantly attenuated the rise in pulmonary arterial pressure (**Figure 1**). Pulmonary arterial hypertension persisted in untreated and posttreated animals but returned to control levels in pretreated animals at 2 hours.

## ABSTRACT

**Background:** This study investigated the effects of pentoxifylline (PTX) combined with resuscitation fluids on microcirculatory dysfunctions in a two-hit model of shock and sepsis. **Materials and methods:** Male Wistar rats (250 g) were submitted to hemorrhagic shock and reperfusion followed by sepsis induced by cecal ligation and puncture. For the initial treatment of shock, rats were randomly divided into: sham, no injury, no treatment; hypertonic saline solution (HS) (7.5%, 4 mL/kg); lactated Ringer's solution (LR, 3 × shed blood volume); HS + PTX (4 mL/kg + 25 mg/kg PTX); and LR + PTX (3 × shed blood volume + 25 mg/kg PTX). ... **Results:** Lactated Ringer's solution induced marked increases ( $P < 0.001$ ) in the number of rolling leukocytes per 10 min (two-fold), adherent leukocytes per 100  $\mu\text{m}$  venule length (six-fold), migrated leukocytes per 5000  $\mu\text{m}^2$  (eight-fold), P-selectin and ICAM-1 expression (four-fold), and lung neutrophil infiltration (three-fold) compared with sham. In contrast, PTX attenuated leukocyte–endothelial interactions, P-selectin and ICAM-1 expression at the mesentery when associated with either LR ( $P < 0.001$ ) or HS ( $P < 0.05$ ). Neutrophil migration into the lungs was similarly reduced by PTX ( $P < 0.05$ ).

...

### 2.2. Hemorrhagic shock/reperfusion and CLP

The animals were randomized into five groups: (1) sham group (only anesthesia, intubation, and catheterization), (2) HS group: HSR with HS 7.5% (4 mL/kg), (3) LR group: HSR with LR (3 × shed blood volume), (4) HSPTX group: HSR with HS and PTX (25 mg/kg), and (5) LRPTX group: HSR with LR and PTX (25 mg/kg). source_text:
ABSTRACT: "Studies were performed in sham-PUO rats and rats with 14-day PUO or 30-day PUO receiving vehicle in drinking water or PTF (400 mg/liter in drinking water). At day-14 PUO, glomerular filtration rate (GFR) was markedly and similarly depressed in rats receiving vehicle or PTF as compared with sham-operated rats. However, at day-30 PUO, GFR in rats receiving PTF was significantly higher than that in rats receiving vehicle, approaching the level seen in the sham-operated rats. At day-30 PUO, histologic studies also revealed a marked reduction of TIF in rats treated with PTF as compared with the rats receiving vehicle in drinking water." ...

3. Results: "At day 30 following PUO, GFR in the rats without PTF treatment (Group 5) decreased further. In contrast, in rats treated with PTF (Group 6), GFR was significantly higher as compared with that in Group 5 and similar to the sham-operated rats (Group 1 and Group 4). Thus, PTF treatment for a shorter duration failed to preserve filtration function, whereas prolonged treatment with PTF afforded preservation of GFR." ... "The fibrosis score in 14-day PUO treated with PTF was 1.00 (95% CI 0.89–2.00), slightly lower but did not reach statistical significant when compared with that in 14-day PUO." ... "At day-30 PUO, the median fibrosis score in rats treated with PTF was 1.00 (95% CI 0.14–1.42), significantly less than the score in rats without PTF treatment (median score 3.0; 95% CI 2.44–3.12) ( $P < 0.01$ ). Thus, at PUO day-14 treatment with PTF did not significantly attenuate renal fibrosis; however, PTF treatment led to a significant reduction in tubulointerstitial fibrosis on day 30." ... "The treatment with PTF decreased the expression of  $\alpha$ -SMA slightly but not significantly." ... "In contrast to findings at day 14, expression of  $\alpha$ -SMA at day 30 was significantly reduced in PUO rats treated with PTF as compared with that in PUO rats without PTF treatment."

4. Discussion: "At day 14 after PUO, GFR was markedly reduced, accompanied by tubulointerstitial fibrosis. However, at this time the benefit of treatment with PTF was not yet apparent as GFR remained significantly suppressed as in the sham-operated rats. Expression of  $\alpha$ -SMA in the PUO kidney was insignificantly reduced. However, at day 30 after PUO, GFR was substantially higher in PUO rats treated with PTF than those without. The benefits of renal protection by PTF were also supported by histological examination as well as expression of  $\alpha$ -SMA." ... "Our data also support the notion that the renal protection exerted by PTF requires sufficient time span of the treatment to manifest this protection."

*Administration of PTX.* One hour after CLP, animals were re-anesthetized with methoxyflurane inhalation and the femoral vein was cannulated using PE-50 tubing. PTX (50 mg/kg body wt in 1 mL normal saline solution; Sigma, St. Louis, MO) was infused through the venous catheter at a constant infusion rate over a period of 90 min. ... 

Twenty hours after CLP (i.e., the late, hypodynamic stage of sepsis), the thoracic aorta and small intestine were isolated and precontracted by norepinephrine. Rat ADM ( $10^{-7}$  M) was applied, and the percentage of ADM-induced relaxation in the aortic rings and resistance vessels in the small intestine was determined.

**Effects of PTX on ADM-induced relaxation.** Application of ADM to vessels from sham-operated animals induced  $76.4 \pm 2.6\%$  relaxation in NE-preconstricted aortic rings (Fig. 1A) and  $94.5 \pm 2.4\%$  relaxation in intestinal vessels (Fig. 1B). Vascular responsiveness to ADM 20 h after CLP was significantly reduced in both the aortic rings ( $56.8 \pm 4.2\%$ ) and intestinal vessels ( $78.4 \pm 2.9\%$ ). However, vessels isolated from septic animals that received PTX treatment displayed no significant reduction in ADM responsiveness 20 h after CLP (aortic rings,  $73.2 \pm 5.3\%$ ; intestinal vessels,  $87.8 \pm 1.9\%$ ) as compared with vessels from sham-operated animals (Fig. 1).

Values are expressed as percentages (%) of vascular relaxation following initial norepinephrine-induced vascular tension. All measurements were performed 20 h after CLP or sham operation. The data are presented as means  $\pm$  SEM and compared by ANOVA and Tukey's test.  $n = 6-8$  animals/group. \* $P < 0.05$  versus Sham group; # $P < 0.05$  versus CLP group.

Although the plasma cytokine levels in PTX-treated animals were slightly elevated when compared with those of sham-operated animals, there were no statistically significant differences between these two groups (Fig. 3).

### EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN

Six groups of animals were studied. Group 1 swine (control, n=8) received a 1-hour intravenous infusion of sterile saline solution. Group 2 swine (sepsis, n=8) received a 1-hour intravenous infusion of live *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, PAO strain (5×10^8 colony forming units per milliliter at 0.3 mL/20 kg per minute). Three further groups of animals with sepsis were studied, each receiving a 20-mg/kg bolus of pentoxifylline (Hoechst-Roussel, Somerville, NJ) followed by an infusion (6 mg/kg per hour) until the end of the experiment. Group 3 swine (pretreatment pentoxifylline, n=6) commenced the pentoxifylline regimen 15 minutes prior to the bacterial infusion. Group 4 swine (posttreatment pentoxifylline, n=6) received the bolus of pentoxifylline immediately following the termination of the bacterial infusion at 1 hour into the experiment. Group 5 swine (delayed treatment pentoxifylline, n=4) commenced pentoxifylline treatment 1 hour after the bacterial infusion for 2 hours. Group 6 swine (control pentoxifylline, n=3) received the pentoxifylline regimen only. All groups were studied for a total of 5 hours.

... 

## RESULTS

In the delayed treatment group (group 5), we observed a 50% mortality rate, and therefore, the study in this group was terminated at four animals. Profound hypotension developed on initiation of pentoxifylline infusion in the two animals that died, with neither animal surviving beyond 3 hours. However, in the two animals that survived to 5 hours, we noted similar hemodynamic and pulmonary function measurements to those of the posttreatment group. Because of the small numbers in the delayed treatment group, no statistical conclusions could be obtained and the data have not been included in this article.

claim: In 58 male Sprague-Dawley rats with prior right nephrectomy, the solitary left renal pedicle was clamped for 45 minutes; pentoxifylline (PTX) 100 mg/kg (subcutaneous) or 0.9% NaCl 1 mL was administered either 60 minutes before ischemia, 1 minute into ischemia, or 60 minutes after clamp release. For PTX given 1 minute into ischemia or 60 minutes after clamp release, the analyzed parameters did not differ versus respective controls (no P-value reported; Table 1 shows no significance marker). Methods. In 58 male 10-week-old Sprague-Dawley rats, 14 days after right nephrectomy, a 45-minute clamping of solitary renal pedicle was conducted. PTX 100 mg/kg body weight or 0.9% NaCl 1 mL were given subcutaneously either 60 minutes before renal ischemia, 1 minute into ischemia, or 60 minutes after clamp release. Creatinine clearance ( $Cl_{Cr}$ ; mL/min/kg body weight), fractional excretions of sodium ( $FE_{Na}$ [%]) and potassium ( $FE_K$ [%]), and urine protein/ $Cl_{Cr}$ ratio ( $U_{prot}/Cl_{Cr}$ [mg/1 mL $Cl_{Cr}$ ]) at 48 hours after IRI were compared between PTX-treated animals and respective controls (Mann-Whitney *U* test). ... Results. Kidney function was improved in rats given PTX before IRI compared with controls: $Cl_{Cr}$ $2.10 \pm 0.44$ versus $1.03 \pm 0.18$ ; $FE_{Na}$ $0.16 \pm 0.12$ versus $0.84 \pm 0.55$ ; $FE_K$ $40.3 \pm 13.0$ versus $75.5 \pm 17.9$ , respectively (all $P < .001$ ). There was no difference in proteinuria: $U_{prot}/Cl_{Cr}$ $0.004 \pm 0.002$ versus $0.004 \pm 0.002$ . Conversely, the analyzed parameters did not differ between animals administered PTX during IRI and controls: $Cl_{Cr}$ $0.42 \pm 0.34$ versus $0.73 \pm 0.43$ ; $FE_{Na}$ $2.98 \pm 2.71$ versus $3.16 \pm 3.05$ ; $FE_K$ $280.1 \pm 155.7$ versus $206.2 \pm 154.1$ ; and $U_{prot}/Cl_{Cr}$ $0.031 \pm 0.029$ versus $0.029 \pm 0.031$ , respectively, nor between rats given PTX after IRI and controls: $Cl_{Cr}$ $0.29 \pm 0.38$ versus $0.40 \pm 0.47$ ; $FE_{Na}$ $4.25 \pm 3.55$ versus $3.80 \pm 3.94$ ; $FE_K$ $284.9 \pm 117.5$ versus $243.0 \pm 150.6$ ; and $U_{prot}/Cl_{Cr}$ $0.044 \pm 0.018$ versus $0.055 \pm 0.061$ , respectively. ... We obtained 58 male Sprague-Dawley rats (10 weeks old, weighing 250–300 g) ... Two weeks after right nephrectomy the left kidney pedicle was clamped for 45 minutes. PTX 100 mg/kg body weight ... or 0.9% NaCl 1 mL were given subcutaneously either 60 minutes before renal ischemia (groups 1 and 2, respectively), 1 minute into ischemia (groups 3 and 4), or 60 minutes after clamp release (groups 5 and 6). ... As shown in Table 1, PTX attenuated the ischemia-induced impairment of renal function (except for proteinuria) in a 48-hour observation only when administered before renal ischemia was initiated. ABSTRACT—... Fourteen anesthetized, ventilated, and paralyzed dogs, received intravenous 2 mg/kg of Escherichia coli endotoxin followed by a continuous infusion of 20 ml/kg·h of saline. ... Seven dogs were pretreated with PTX as an intravenous bolus of 20 mg/kg, followed by a continuous infusion at 20 mg/kg·h, and the other seven dogs served as a control group. ... In addition, the critical Do2 (Do2crit) was lower and the critical oxygen extraction ratio was higher in the PTX treated than in the control group (9.1 ± 1.8 vs. 11.6 ± 2.4 ml/kg·min, and 70.6 ± 14.0 vs. 49.3 ± 14.6%, both p < .05 ). The VO2/Do2 dependency slope was also steeper in the PTX-treated than in the control group (.80 ± .28 vs. .43 ± .19, p < .05 ). ... The peak tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF) release was significantly attenuated by PTX (185 ± 70 vs. 260 ± 80 pg/ml, p < .05 ). ...

### Experimental protocol

claim: In male Sprague–Dawley rats, endotoxin (Salmonella typhimurium, 20 mg/kg ip) impaired pulmonary artery ring relaxation measured 6 hr later; concurrent pentoxifylline (50 mg/kg ip) attenuated (but did not eliminate) this impairment for ACh, A23187, and SNP. At the highest tested concentration (10^-6 M) in isolated rings precontracted with phenylephrine (PE), remaining ring tension (mg of PE-induced tension) was: ACh—control 11 ± 4 mg vs endotoxin 216 ± 16 mg (P < 0.05 vs control) vs PTX+endotoxin 86 ± 21 mg (impaired vs control, P < 0.05; less impaired than endotoxin alone, P < 0.05); A23187—control 11 ± 6 mg vs endotoxin 185 ± 26 mg (P < 0.05 vs control) vs PTX+endotoxin 93 ± 11 mg (impaired vs control, P < 0.05; less impaired than endotoxin alone, P < 0.05); SNP—control 0 mg vs endotoxin 54 ± 10 mg (P < 0.05 vs control) vs PTX+endotoxin 7 ± 4 mg (similar to control; less impaired than endotoxin alone, P < 0.05). Concentration–response curves were generated over 10^-9 to 10^-6 M for ACh, A23187, and SNP.
source_text:
*Experimental protocol.* Awake, fed rats were administered endotoxin (*Salmonella typhimurium*, 20 mg/kg ip) that was freshly prepared in 0.9% saline (1 cc). Control rats received an equal volume of saline. A third group received concurrent injections of pentoxifylline (50 mg/kg ip) and endotoxin. Pulmonary vasomotor control mechanisms were studied in isolated pulmonary arterial rings 6 hr after treatment. ...

*Pulmonary vasorelaxation by endothelium-dependent and -independent mechanisms.* ... Cumulative concentration–response curves were then generated over the concentration range of 10^-9 to 10^-6 *M* (ACh, A23187, and SNP). ... The ring tension remaining in the rings in response to each dose of vasorelaxing agent was expressed in milligrams of PE-induced tension. ...

Pulmonary artery rings from saline-injected rats were precontracted to  $277 \pm 15$  mg of PE-induced tension and relaxed to  $11 \pm 4$  mg tension with ACh  $10^{-6}\ M$ . Rings from endotoxin-treated rats were precontracted to  $274 \pm 15$  mg tension, and  $216 \pm 16$  mg of PE-induced tension remained in response to ACh  $10^{-6}\ M$  ( $P < 0.05$  versus control). Rings from PTX plus endotoxin-treated rats were precontracted with PE to  $290 \pm 18$  mg tension with  $86 \pm 21$  mg of tension remaining in response to ACh  $10^{-6}\ M$ . ... One month following surgery, median (interquartile range) C-reactive protein was  $0.48 \text{ mg dL}^{-1}$  (0.14–0.90) vs  $0.10 \text{ mg dL}^{-1}$  (0.06–0.39) during active CS ( $P \leq .001$ ). Similarly, interleukin-6 1 month after surgery was  $7.2 \text{ pg mL}^{-1}$  (3.3–11.7) vs  $1.7 \text{ pg mL}^{-1}$  (1.5–2.5) during active CS ( $P \leq .001$ ). ... This proinflammatory state lasted until 1 year following surgery.

In the cohort of 80 patients, early remission 1 month after surgery was characterized by a 4.8-fold increase in CRP concentrations compared with the time of active CS [median CRP 0.48 mg dL<sup>-1</sup> (0.14–0.90) vs 0.10 mg dL<sup>-1</sup> (0.06–0.39),  $P \leq .001$ ]. C-reactive protein levels remained significantly elevated compared with baseline including the 12 months follow-up (Figure 1).

The CS subgroup of 25 patients was similar in clinical and biochemical characteristics to the main cohort (data not shown). Interleukin-6 levels showed a 4.2-fold increase 1 month after surgery compared with the time point of active CS [median IL-6 7.2 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (3.3–11.7) vs 1.7 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (1.5–2.5),  $P \leq .001$ ], and an elevation of more than 3-fold compared with the 25 matched control subjects [median IL-6 7.2 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (3.3–11.7) vs 2.0 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (1.5–3.6),  $P \leq .001$ ]. Interleukin-6 levels remained significantly increased at 3- and 6-month follow-up visits compared with baseline and matched controls (Figure 2A).

**Figure 4.** (A) Relationship between C-reactive protein concentrations (mg dL<sup>-1</sup>) 3 months after successful surgery for Cushing's syndrome and age- and gender-corrected grip strength (normalized grip strength, % of normal controls) 12 months after surgery. Line indicates estimated linear regression line.  $N$  = 50, Spearman's coefficient  $-0.371$ ,  $R^2$  = 0.155,  $P$  = .008. (B) Relationship between C-reactive protein concentrations (mg dL<sup>-1</sup>) 3 months after successful surgery for Cushing's syndrome and Short Form 36 health survey (SF-36) Physical Component Summary 12 months after surgery. Line indicates estimated linear regression line.  $N$  = 38, Spearman's coefficient  $-0.356$ ,  $R^2$  = 0.127,  $P$  = .028.

After adjustment for age and BMI, the influence of CRP levels 3 months after surgery on muscle

function 1 year in remission remained significant in the multi-variable linear regression analysis (Table S6).

claim: Support is PARTLY established. Ueland et al. (2023) report that, when ACS and CS patients are combined, 49 of 92 OLINK (PEA) inflammatory/cardiovascular biomarkers differed significantly vs healthy controls after correction for possible FDR and smoking habits, with 46 upregulated and 3 downregulated (TRANCE, TNFβ, ST1A1). Figure 2 reports mean differences (NPX) with 95% CIs including FGF21 2.0 (1.8–2.2) and IL6 0.8 (0.6–1.0). For postoperative follow-up, the paper reports postoperative samples for 17 patients a median 24 months after surgery/biochemical cure in the Abstract (range 6–40 months), but in the Results text the postoperative specimens are described as median 24 months with range 11–61 months. The paper states there was no significant normalization postoperatively; Figure 3 shows summed NPX groups (CXCL9/CXCL10/HGF; FGF-21/MCP-1; IL8/IL18/OPG/CSF-1) remained higher vs healthy controls (P<0.01) and did not significantly change from pre- to postoperative (P=0.33, 0.91, 0.66 respectively). The phrase “zero normalization” is not used in the supplied source text.
source_text:
Abstract – Results: "Combined, the ACS and CS patients displayed significant differences in levels of 49/92 inflammatory biomarkers (46 increased/3 decreased) compared with healthy controls." ... "Postoperative samples were available for 17 patients, median 24 months (range 6–40) after surgery and biochemical cure." ... "There was no significant normalization of the biomarkers postoperatively."

Results – Inflammatory biomarkers: "Forty-nine of the 92 inflammatory and cardiovascular biomarkers differed significantly between patients with ACS/CS and healthy controls, after correction for possible FDR and smoking habits (for complete list, see Table S2). Forty-six biomarkers were upregulated in patients, and three were downregulated (Figures 1 and 2)."

Figure 2 table (mean differences): "| Biomarker     | Mean Difference (NPX) | 95% CI      |
|---------------|-----------------------|-------------|
| FGF21         | 2.0                   | 1.8 - 2.2   |
| IL6           | 0.8                   | 0.6 - 1.0   |" ...

Text below Figure 2: "The three biomarkers that showed significantly lower levels in the ACS/CS group compared with healthy controls were TNF-related activation-induced cytokine (TRANCE), tumour necrosis factor- \$\beta\$  (TNF \$\beta\$ ), and sulfotransferase 1A1 (ST1A1)."

Results – Subject characteristics: "Pre- and postoperative samples were obtained from 13 patients, and 4 patients provided only postoperative samples. The postoperative specimens were collected a median of 24 (range 11–61) months after surgery. All surgically treated patients were biochemically cured at the time of sample collection and had been without corticosteroid supplements for at least 6 months."

Figure 3 panels: "A

Sum of NPX levels for biomarkers related to heart failure (CXCL9, CXCL10, and HGF)

Healthy controls Patients preoperatively Patients postoperatively

\$P < 0.01\$   \$P = 0.33\$" ... "B

Sum of NPX levels for biomarkers related to glucose metabolism (FGF-21 and MCP-1)

Healthy controls Patients preoperatively Patients postoperatively

\$P < 0.01\$   \$P = 0.91\$" ... "C

Sum of NPX levels for biomarkers related to bone metabolism (IL8, IL18, OPG, CSF-1)

Healthy controls Patients preoperatively Patients postoperatively

\$P < 0.01\$   \$P = 0.66\$"

Figure 3 caption: "**Figure 3.** Boxplot showing the distribution of biomarker levels related to heart failure (A), glucose metabolism (B), and bone metabolism (C), in healthy controls, compared with patients preoperatively and postoperatively, respectively. All panels show significantly higher levels in ACS/CS patients compared with healthy controls and a lack of normalization postoperatively."
verdict_explanation: Correctly attributes: (a) 49/92 differing (46 increased/3 decreased) vs controls for the combined ACS+CS group; (b) the downregulated biomarkers are TRANCE, TNFβ, ST1A1; (c) Figure 2 reports FGF21 mean difference 2.0 NPX (95% CI 1.8–2.2) and IL6 0.8 NPX (0.6–1.0); (d) postoperative follow-up includes 17 patients and Figure 3 reports no significant pre- vs post-op changes with P=0.33, 0.91, 0.66 while still differing vs healthy controls at P<0.01. Defects: the claim says baseline and "patients with autonomous cortisol secretion/Cushing’s syndrome" (implying separate groups), but the source specifies the 49/92 finding for patients with ACS/CS combined vs controls. The postoperative timing range is inconsistent within the paper: Abstract says range 6–40, Results says 11–61; the candidate’s "range 6–40" matches the Abstract but not the Results. The wording "zero normalization" is not present in the source; the source wording is "no significant normalization" / "not normalized" / "lack of normalization".
readiness_reason: The candidate claim contains material wording/attribution issues (baseline framing; “zero normalization” not source language) and a key internal range discrepancy in the source (6–40 vs 11–61 months) that must be resolved or explicitly represented before witness construction.

(2019) report lower aerobic exercise capacity in patients in long-term remission from Cushing’s syndrome versus individually matched controls, including lower VO2peak, maximal workload, and oxygen pulse; in biopsy subgroups they report no statistically significant differences in measured muscle fiber cross-sectional area, capillarization measures, mitochondrial content (COXIV fluorescence), or microvascular/endothelial eNOS and NAD(P)H oxidase subunit proteins, and they hypothesize that persistent cardiac dysfunction may limit blood supply to muscles. The source also reports biopsy consent (13 pairs) but usable analytic sample sizes vary by assay (e.g., 7–8 pairs for Table 4 outcomes; 7–8 pairs for Table 5 outcomes), so '8 matched pairs for vastus lateralis biopsies' is not fully accurate as a blanket biopsy sample size.
source_text:
Abstract (Findings): "Patients showed a lower mean  $VO_{2peak}$  (SD) (28.0 (7.0) vs. 34.8 (7.9) ml  $O_2$ /kg bw/min,  $P<0.01$ ), -maximal workload (SD) (176 (49) vs. 212 (67) watt,  $P=0.01$ ) and -oxygen pulse (SD) (12.0 (3.7) vs. 14.8 (4.2) ml/beat,  $P<0.01$ ) at  $VO_{2peak}$ . No differences were seen in muscle fiber type specific cross-sectional area, -capillarization measures, -mitochondrial content and -protein content of eNOS, eNOS-P-ser1177, NOX2, p47phox and p67phox." 

Abstract (Interpretation): "As differences in muscle fiber and microvascular outcome measures are not statistically significant, we hypothesize that cardiac dysfunction, seen in active CS, persists during remission and limits blood supply to muscles." 

Table 2: "VO2peak : (ml O2 /kg/min) | 28.0 ± 7.0 | 34.8 ± 7.9 | 0.80 | <0.01**" ... "Work load: (watt) | 176 ± 49 | 212 ± 67 | 0.83 | 0.01*" ... "VO2/HR: (ml/beat) | 12.0 ± 3.7 | 14.8 ± 4.2 | 0.83 | 0.01*" 

Results (Aerobic exercise capacity): "Mean VO2peak of patients in long-term remission of CS was significantly lower compared to matched controls (P<0.01) (Figure 1). A significantly lower maximal workload (P=0.01) and shorter test duration (P=0.02) was observed in patients in long term remission of CS compared to the control group." ... "Furthermore, oxygen pulse was lower in the patients compared to their controls (P=0.01)." 

Results (Skeletal muscle capillarization and mitochondrial content): "Thirteen paired couples provided informed consent to undergo skeletal muscle biopsy. Due to technical problems (frost damage) and/or a small biopsy sample size in one of the 2 members of a paired couple, mitochondrial content and skeletal muscle capillarization could not be determined in five paired couples. No differences were found between the patients and their matched controls with regard to muscle total fiber cross sectional area, capillary contacts, capillary density and capillary-fiber perimeter exchange index. In addition, no differences were found between patients and controls in mitochondrial content (Table 4)." 

Table 4 (selected rows): "Average total fiber cross-sectional area (mm2 ) | N 8 | 4527 ± 897 | 4846 ± 2364 | 0.93 | 0.71" ... "Capillary density (capillaries/mm2 ) | N 8 | 569 ± 91 | 596 ± 93 | 0.95 | 0.58" ... "Mitochondrial content type 1 fibers | N 7 | 18.9 ± 4.3 | 19.4 ± 5.3 | 0.97 | 0.89" 

Results (Skeletal muscle eNOS, eNOS-P-ser1177, NOX2, p47phox and p67phox protein content): "In 8 paired couples skeletal muscle eNOS and eNOS-P-ser1177 protein content and eNOS ser1177 phosphorylation (Figure 2), and in 7 paired couples NOX2, p47phox and p67phox protein content were determined specifically in the endothelial layer of muscle capillaries and terminal arterioles (Figure 3)." ... "No statistically significant differences were detected in the mean protein content of eNOS, eNOS-P-ser1177 and the NAD(P)H-oxidase subunits between the patients and controls (Table 5)." 

Table 5 (selected rows): "eNOS protein content | N 8 | 86.0 ± 29.5 | 75.5 ± 21.7 | 1.14 | 0.13" ... "NOX2 protein content (endothelial specific) | N 7 | 86.3 ± 28.5 | 88.0 ± 36.7 | 0.98 | 0.72" ... "p47phox | N 7 | 118.9 ± 38.3 | 120.7 ± 45.6 | 0.99 | 0.95" 

Discussion: "As the patient/matched control ratio for each of the measured variables was close to 1.0 (Table 4 and Table 5) this leads to the conclusion that the reduction in VO2peak in the patients must be the result of impairments in the blood supply to the exercising muscle or of a reduction in the efficiency of mitochondrial respiration (lower ATP/O ratio) in the exercising muscle." ... "A lower oxygen pulse was detected in the patients in long term remission. This finding might be caused by a limitation in exercise cardiac output"
verdict_explanation: Exercise outcomes (VO2peak, workload, oxygen pulse) and their units/P-values are supported by the Abstract and Table 2, except that the Abstract reports oxygen pulse P<0.01 while Table 2 reports P=0.01; the candidate’s oxygen pulse P=0.01 is consistent with Table 2 but not the Abstract’s threshold statement. The 'no significant differences' language for the biopsy-derived measures is supported, and the cardiac-limitation hypothesis is supported (authors hypothesize persistent cardiac dysfunction limiting blood supply; they also link low oxygen pulse to limited exercise cardiac output). However, the source does not provide or describe a '19.5% reduction' in VO2peak; it reports a patient/control ratio of 0.80 (~20% lower). Also, biopsy participation was 13 matched pairs with varying usable N by assay (Table 4 N=7–8; Table 5 N=7–8), so stating a single biopsy subset size of '8 matched pairs' as a blanket description is inaccurate without qualification. The candidate’s specific list 'microvascular eNOS/NOX2-related proteins' is generally supported, but Table 5 includes additional measurements (e.g., membrane-specific NOX2) and reports ratios not always ≈1.0 (e.g., eNOS protein content P/C ratio 1.14).

claim: In a randomized, double-blind clinical trial at a single center (2022), 60 men with BPH/LUTS were randomized to pentoxifylline 400 mg every 8 hours plus tamsulosin 0.4 mg/day (n=30) versus placebo plus tamsulosin 0.4 mg/day (n=30) for 12 weeks. source_text:
This randomized, double-blind clinical trial recruited 60 patients with BPH from a single center in 2022. ... they were randomly allocated to intervention (Pentoxifylline + tamsulosin) and control (placebo + tamsulosin) groups. ... after the 12th week.

### 2.3 | Study design
... 60 out of 75 patients were qualified and randomized with a random sequence generator into two groups: Pentoxifylline (Farabi company, Iran) and tamsulosin (Astellas international company). An equal number of patients received either fixed doses of Pentoxifylline 400 mg/Q8h plus tamsulosin 0.4 mg/day (Intervention Group)17 or tamsulosin 0.4 mg/day with placebo (Control Group) for 12 weeks.

Out of 75 patients who were recruited into the study, 60 subjects were randomly allocated to the study groups. The intervention group was composed of 30 men treated with PTX + tamsulosin, while the control group was composed of 30 men treated with placebo + tamsulosin for 12 weeks.

**TABLE 4** Subjective and objective parameter changes from baseline (visit 1) to endpoint measures between two groups.

| Variable               | Changes (intervention group) | Changes (control group) | p value |
|------------------------|------------------------------|-------------------------|---------|
| IPSS-T (mean)          | –8.73 ± 4.13                 | –5.13 ± 1.36            | <.001   |
| Qmax (mL/s) (mean)     | +4.48 ± 1.03                 | +2.67 ± 0.57            | <.001   |
| PVR (mL) (mean)        | –32.93 ± 16.33               | –13.17 ± 9.23           | <.001   |

### 3.4 | Safety
From the included patients, mild adverse events were observed in 11 patients of the intervention group and 13 patients of the control group, as shown in Table 5. The adverse effect of most patients was mild dyspepsia, which required no treatment.

During the study, none of the patients reported any evidence of a severe adverse effect, neither threatening hypotension nor syncope. Vital signs remained almost stable in the participants. Also, none of the subjects experienced any urinary retention episodes. Overall, all the patients continued receiving their allocated medicines, and therapy did not stop for TEAEs (treatment-emergent adverse events).

**TABLE 5** Adverse events.

| Adverse events       | Intervention Group | Control Group |
|----------------------|--------------------|---------------|
| Headache             | 2                  | 1             |
| Hypotension          | 2                  | 1             |
| Dyspepsia            | 4                  | 2             |
| Ejaculation disorder | 1                  | 3             |
| Dizziness            | 2                  | 1             |
| Altered vision       | 0                  | 1             |
| Diarrhea             | 0                  | 1             |
| Erectile dysfunction | 0                  | 2             |
| Loss of libido       | 0                  | 1             |

source_text:
**Animals**—6 healthy adult mixed-breed dogs.

**Procedures**—Intradermal injections (0.1 mL each) of PBS solution, histamine phosphate, and cross-linking rabbit-origin anti-canine IgE antibodies (3 injections/dog) were administered at 0 hours on day 0; wheal sizes were evaluated at 20 minutes, 6 hours, and 24 hours. ... On day 2, treatment with pentoxifylline (20 mg/kg, PO, q 8 h) was initiated and continued until day 30. For each dog, injection, measurement, and biopsy procedures were repeated on days 30 to 31 and on days 37 to 38 (ie, after discontinuation of pentoxifylline administration).

On day 2, oral treatment with pentoxifylline was initiated at a dosage of 20 mg/kg (compounded into a liquid to allow precise dosing) 3 times daily. Treatment continued for 29 days (until day 30). Two hours after discontinuation of drug treatment on day 30, each dog was sedated with dexmedetomidine and again admin-

istered the intradermal injections, as performed on day 0, this time on the right side of the thorax. Macroscopic changes were evaluated at 20 minutes and 6 hours after administration of the injections. ... At 24 hours after these repeated injections (day 31), each dog was again sedated with dexmedetomidine; macroscopic changes at the injection sites were evaluated, and biopsy specimens of noninjected skin and skin at the site of injection of anti-canine IgE antibodies were collected for histologic examination. ...

On day 37, the sedation and intradermal injection procedures were repeated for each dog on the left side of the thorax, ventral to the day 0 injection sites. Macroscopic changes were evaluated at 20 minutes and 6 hours after administration of the injections. ... At 24 hours after these repeated injections (day 38), each dog was again sedated with dexmedetomidine; macroscopic changes at the injection sites were evaluated, but biopsy specimens of skin were not collected. ...

**Grading of macroscopic reactions**—At 20 minutes, 6 hours, and 24 hours after intradermal injections were administered on days 0, 30, and 37, the injection sites were evaluated ...

**Treatment with pentoxifylline**—Treatment with pentoxifylline (20 mg/kg, PO, q 8 h) was initiated on day 2 and continued until 2 hours before the dogs were sedated on day 30.

source_text:
Results (Abstract)—“Pentoxifylline administration was associated with a significant decrease in wheal size at 6 and 24 hours (but not at 20 minutes) after injection of anti-canine IgE. Repeated injections performed 1 week after drug discontinuation revealed partial recovery of the 6-hour cutaneous reaction and complete recovery of the 24-hour cutaneous reaction.”

Results—“Treatment with pentoxifylline from day 2 through day 30 had no effects on the subjective features of the macroscopic immediate reaction (erythema and induration), and there was no significant ( $P > 0.05$ ) effect on wheal area, compared with findings prior to the administration of pentoxifylline (Figures 1 and 2). In contrast, the 6-hour late-phase wheal reaction induced by anti-canine IgE antibodies was significantly ( $P < 0.05$ ) reduced on day 30, relative to wheal area prior to administration of pentoxifylline. This inhibition was even more marked at the 24-hour time point (day 31).”

Results—“To determine the duration of pentoxifylline-mediated inhibition of the macroscopic cutaneous late-phase reaction, the injection and measurement procedure was repeated on day 37 (1 week after cessation of pentoxifylline administration) with further measurement of wheal area at 24 hours after injection (day 38). On day 38, the 6-hour late-phase reaction was not significantly ( $P < 0.05$ ) different from the pretreatment wheal area (Figure 2), whereas the 24-hour reaction was somewhat larger than the pretreatment wheal area.”

Figure 2 legend—“†Values within a bracket are significantly ( $P = 0.01$ ) different.”

Discussion—“We determined that treatment with pentoxifylline for 29 days did not result in significant inhibition of immediate reactivity to anti-IgE antibodies. However, the macroscopic late-phase response was significantly inhibited at both 6 and 24 hours after injection of anti-IgE antibodies. This inhibitory effect was no longer evident 1 week after cessation of pentoxifylline administration.”

Discussion (end)—“This inhibitory effect was essentially resolved 7 days after discontinuation of drug administration.”
verdict_explanation: Directionality and qualitative statistical conclusions are supported (no significant effect at 20 minutes; significant reduction at 6 and 24 hours with pentoxifylline; partial recovery at 6 hours and complete recovery at 24 hours after stopping, as stated in the Abstract). However, the candidate’s specific numeric wheal-area values are only approximations from the embedded figure image, not explicitly reported in the text, and the candidate’s exact statistical phrasings/thresholds do not match the paper: the paper states “no significant (P > 0.05)” for immediate/wheal area generally and “significantly (P < 0.05) reduced” for day 30 vs pretreatment, while Figure 2 specifies “P = 0.01” for bracketed comparisons. Also, the Results sentence “not significantly (P < 0.05) different” is internally inconsistent; it does not provide a clear supported statement for recovery equivalence beyond the described “partial”/“complete” recovery in the Abstract and Discussion. The terms “fully recovered” and “fades within 7 days” are not the authors’ exact wording; the paper uses “complete recovery” and “essentially resolved 7 days after discontinuation.”
readiness_reason: The candidate mixes unverified approximate numeric wheal areas with statistical claims not stated exactly in the source; recovery-time statistical statements are unclear/inconsistent in Results, and the author-exact wording differs (“complete recovery”/“essentially resolved” vs “fully recovered”/“fades within 7 days”). A witness-ready FRD would need to drop or qualify the numeric values and align statistical language to what is explicitly stated.

claim: Pentoxifylline administration was associated with a significant decrease in wheal size at 6 and 24 hours (but not at 20 minutes) after injection of anti-canine IgE.
source_text:
Results (Abstract)—“Pentoxifylline administration was associated with a significant decrease in wheal size at 6 and 24 hours (but not at 20 minutes) after injection of anti-canine IgE.”

Results—“Treatment with pentoxifylline from day 2 through day 30 had no effects on the subjective features of the macroscopic immediate reaction (erythema and induration), and there was no significant ( $P > 0.05$ ) effect on wheal area, compared with findings prior to the administration of pentoxifylline (Figures 1 and 2). In contrast, the 6-hour late-phase wheal reaction induced by anti-canine IgE antibodies was significantly ( $P < 0.05$ ) reduced on day 30, relative to wheal area prior to administration of pentoxifylline. This inhibition was even more marked at the 24-hour time point (day 31).”
verdict_explanation: Directionality and qualitative statistical conclusions are supported (no significant effect at 20 minutes; significant reduction at 6 and 24 hours with pentoxifylline; partial recovery at 6 hours and complete recovery at 24 hours after stopping, as stated in the Abstract). However, the candidate’s specific numeric wheal-area values are only approximations from the embedded figure image, not explicitly reported in the text, and the candidate’s exact statistical phrasings/thresholds do not match the paper: the paper states “no significant (P > 0.05)” for immediate/wheal area generally and “significantly (P < 0.05) reduced” for day 30 vs pretreatment, while Figure 2 specifies “P = 0.01” for bracketed comparisons. Also, the Results sentence “not significantly (P < 0.05) different” is internally inconsistent; it does not provide a clear supported statement for recovery equivalence beyond the described “partial”/“complete” recovery in the Abstract and Discussion. The terms “fully recovered” and “fades within 7 days” are not the authors’ exact wording; the paper uses “complete recovery” and “essentially resolved 7 days after discontinuation.”

claim: Support is partially established: In cured postoperative Cushing’s syndrome patients who became severely hypocortisolemic (defined as morning plasma cortisol <2 µg/dL on postop day 3–5), mean body temperature increased on postop days 4–5 (37.35±0.15°C vs 36.74±0.12°C pre-op; P<0.02) and plasma IL-6 increased (9.38±0.58 pg/mL vs 1.98±0.44 pg/mL; P<0.0001), with IL-6 decreasing on postop days 9–10 while on glucocorticoid replacement (5.24±0.52 pg/mL; P<0.0001 vs postop days 4–5; still elevated vs pre-op P<0.0005). TNF-α also increased on postop days 4–5 (5.93±2.12 pg/mL vs 3.53±1.20 pg/mL; P<0.02). Symptoms in the severe hypocortisolism group included anorexia, fatigue, somnolence, nausea, flu-like symptoms, and temperature elevation/mild pyrexia; symptoms were reported as ameliorated after the first dose of glucocorticoid replacement. Patients without postoperative hypocortisolism (n=3) had no significant elevation of IL-6 and lacked the corresponding symptomatology, including temperature elevation. The denominator '15/17 Cushing’s disease patients' is NOT supported by the source as written: the paper reports 17 Cushing’s disease patients total and states 'Fifteen patients had severe hypocortisolism after TSS' (i.e., 15 after pituitary surgery), but does not state '15/17 CD patients after withholding glucocorticoids' in the way claimed; Table 2 reports n=15 for postop D4–5 and n=17 pre-op and postop D9–10 for the cured group.
source_text:
ABSTRACT "To test the hypothesis that endogenous glucocorticoids exert a negative tonic effect on the secretion of these cytokines, we studied 17 patients with Cushing's disease and 2 patients with primary adrenal Cushing's syndrome before and after surgery. Plasma TNF $\alpha$ , IL-1 $\beta$ and IL-6 were measured before surgery, while the patients were hypercortisolemic; on postoperative day 4 or 5, when they were hyporcortisolemic; and on postoperative day 9 or 10, when they were receiving glucocorticoid replacement. During severe hyporcortisolism, on postoperative day 4 or 5, plasma IL-6 levels rose significantly, compared to the preoperative values ( $P < 0.001$ ). During the same interval, TNF $\alpha$ and IL-1 $\beta$ also rose, albeit to a lesser extent. Over the same interval, patients with severe hyporcortisolism experienced temperature elevation, fatigue, somnolence, flu-like symptoms, and anorexia, symptoms that have been traditionally attributed to glucocorticoid deficiency; these were also experienced by subjects that received recombinant human IL-6. There was no postoperative increase in any of the cytokines studied in the patients who were not hyporcortisolemic after surgery and who also lacked the corresponding symptomatology. Plasma IL-6 concentrations decreased significantly, albeit not to normal levels, in the hyporcortisolemic group of patients on postoperative day 9 or 10, when they were receiving glucocorticoid replacement." Subjects and Methods > Protocol "Patients with Cushing's disease underwent selective transsphenoidal adenomectomy (TSS). None had total hypophysectomy. Postoperatively, they received treatment with dexamethasone (500 $\mu\text{g}$ , iv, every 6 h for a total of six doses) to provide glucocorticoid coverage for the stress of surgery. After the sixth dose of dexamethasone, the patients were not placed on glucocorticoid replacement so as to assess the activity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. The patients were considered to have severe hyporcortisolism if their morning plasma cortisol values were less than 2 $\mu\text{g/dL}$ on the third to fifth postoperative day. ... If they fulfilled this criterion, they were started on dexamethasone (500 µg, orally, daily, given around 0700 h) on the fifth postoperative day after drawing blood for cortisol and cytokine measurements." Results "Fifteen patients had severe hypocortisolism after TSS (morning plasma cortisol, <2 µg/dL). They all experienced anorexia, fatigue, somnolence of variable degree, and nausea by postoperative day 4. These symptoms were ameliorated after the first dose of glucocorticoid replacement." "The body temperature and the plasma inflammatory cytokine values of all patients with severe postoperative hypocortisolism are shown in Table 2. They experienced average temperature elevation of 0.6 C by days 4–5 while they were hypocortisolemic (*P* < 0.02 vs. baseline); their body temperatures returned to preoperative levels by days 9–10, after they had been placed on hydrocortisone replacement. A 5-fold increase in plasma IL-6 levels was observed by days 4–5 (*P* < 0.0001 vs. baseline), whereas glucocorticoid replacement resulted in a significant decrease in plasma IL-6 levels (*P* < 0.0001), although they remained elevated compared to the baseline levels (*P* < 0.0005). A less dramatic increase in plasma TNF $\alpha$ levels occurred while the patients were hypocortisolemic (*P* < 0.02 vs. baseline) ..." TABLE 2. source_text:
Subjects and Methods > Protocol
"Postoperatively, they received treatment with dexamethasone (500  $\mu\text{g}$ , iv, every 6 h for a total of six doses) to provide glucocorticoid coverage for the stress of surgery. After the sixth dose of dexamethasone, the patients were not placed on glucocorticoid replacement so as to assess the activity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. The patients were considered to have severe hyporcortisolism if their morning plasma cortisol values were less than 2  $\mu\text{g/dL}$  on the third to fifth postoperative day.

... If they fulfilled this criterion, they were started on dexamethasone (500 µg, orally, daily, given around 0700 h) on the fifth postoperative day after drawing blood for cortisol and cytokine measurements."

claim: In adult male Sprague–Dawley rats subjected to polymicrobial sepsis by CLP, pentoxifylline (PTX) 50 mg/kg (in 1 mL normal saline) infused intravenously via femoral vein starting 1 h after CLP over 90 min prevented the CLP-associated reduction in adrenomedullin (ADM, 10^-7 M)-induced relaxation measured 20 h after CLP in (i) NE-preconstricted thoracic aortic rings (Sham: 76.4 ± 2.6%; CLP: 56.8 ± 4.2%; CLP+PTX: 73.2 ± 5.3%) and (ii) NE-preconstricted isolated small-intestine resistance vessels (Sham: 94.5 ± 2.4%; CLP: 78.4 ± 2.9%; CLP+PTX: 87.8 ± 1.9%). In Fig. 1, significance is indicated as * P<0.05 vs Sham and # P<0.05 vs CLP (ANOVA with Tukey’s test; n=6–8/group).
source_text:
*Administration of PTX.* One hour after CLP, animals were re-anesthetized with methoxyflurane inhalation and the femoral vein was cannulated using PE-50 tubing. PTX (50 mg/kg body wt in 1 mL normal saline solution; Sigma, St. Louis, MO) was infused through the venous catheter at a constant infusion rate over a period of 90 min. ... Vehicle-treated septic animals received 1 mL normal saline solution intravenously for 90 min. Sham-operated animals received neither PTX nor saline.

*Isolation of aortic rings and determination of ADM-induced relaxation.* ... Twenty hours after the onset of sepsis, ... When the basal tension became stable, a submaximal contraction of ~400 mg was induced by  $5 imes 10^{-9}$  M norepinephrine (Sigma). Synthetic rat ADM (Peninsula Labs, Belmont, CA) at a concentration of  $10^{-7}$  M was then applied ...

*Isolation of the small intestine and determination of ADM-induced relaxation.* ... Following a 15-min equilibration and pressure stabilization at a constant perfusion rate of 5 mL/min, blood vessels in the isolated gut were constricted with  $2.4 imes 10^{-7}$  M NE added to the buffer reservoir of the organ chamber. On pressure stabilization, synthetic rat ADM ( $10^{-7}$  M) was then applied ...

## RESULTS

**Effects of PTX on ADM-induced relaxation.** Application of ADM to vessels from sham-operated animals induced  $76.4 \pm 2.6\%$  relaxation in NE-preconstricted aortic rings (Fig. 1A) and  $94.5 \pm 2.4\%$  relaxation in intestinal vessels (Fig. 1B). Vascular responsiveness to ADM 20 h after CLP was significantly reduced in both the aortic rings ( $56.8 \pm 4.2\%$ ) and intestinal vessels ( $78.4 \pm 2.9\%$ ). However, vessels isolated from septic animals that received PTX treatment displayed no significant reduction in ADM responsiveness 20 h after CLP (aortic rings,  $73.2 \pm 5.3\%$ ; intestinal vessels,  $87.8 \pm 1.9\%$ ) as compared with vessels from sham-operated animals (Fig. 1).

**FIG. 1.** ... The data are presented as means  $\pm$  SEM and compared by ANOVA and Tukey's test.  $n = 6-8$  animals/group. \* $P < 0.05$  versus Sham group; # $P < 0.05$  versus CLP group.
verdict_explanation: Supported: animal model (adult male Sprague–Dawley rats; CLP), PTX regimen (50 mg/kg IV via femoral vein cannulation; started 1 h post-CLP; infused over 90 min), endpoint timing (measurements at 20 h after CLP), ADM concentration (10^-7 M), NE preconstriction concentrations (aorta: 5 × 10^-9 M NE; small intestine: 2.4 × 10^-7 M NE), and the exact relaxation means ± SEM for sham, CLP, and CLP+PTX in both tissues. Not supported as written: the candidate claim asserts specific pairwise P-values and comparisons (e.g., “P<0.05 vs CLP; vehicle lower than sham ... PTX P=NS vs sham”) that are not reported numerically in the RESULTS text; the paper provides only symbol-based significance definitions (* vs Sham; # vs CLP) in the Fig. 1 legend, and the RESULTS states only that PTX-treated vessels showed “no significant reduction ... as compared with ... sham-operated animals.” Also, the claim’s wording “vehicle lower than sham” is misleading for Fig. 1 because Sham animals “received neither PTX nor saline.”
