source_text:
*Administration of PTX.* One hour after CLP, animals were re-anesthetized with methoxyflurane inhalation and the femoral vein was cannulated using PE-50 tubing. PTX (50 mg/kg body wt in 1 mL normal saline solution; Sigma, St. Louis, MO) was infused through the venous catheter at a constant infusion rate over a period of 90 min. ...

**Determination of plasma ADM and inflammatory cytokines.** Twenty hours after CLP or sham operation, whole blood was drawn from a femoral artery catheter into a syringe. ... Plasma levels of ADM were determined using a radioimmunoassay kit ... Plasma levels of tumor necrosis factor  $\alpha$  (TNF- $\alpha$ ), interleukin-1 $\beta$  (IL-1 $\beta$ ), and interleukin-6 (IL-6) were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits ...

**Effects of PTX on plasma ADM and inflammatory cytokines.** Twenty hours after CLP, the plasma level of ADM was increased from  $164 \pm 12.7$  to  $673 \pm 142$  pg/mL ( $P < 0.05$ ) and the level was unaffected by treatment with PTX ( $661 \pm 95$  pg/mL) (Fig. 2). Plasma levels of TNF- $\alpha$ , IL-1 $\beta$ , and IL-6 were all significantly elevated 20 h after the onset of sepsis. However, treatment with PTX significantly attenuated the increase in inflammatory cytokines in septic animals (Fig. 3). Although the plasma cytokine levels in PTX-treated animals were slightly elevated when compared with those of sham-operated animals, there were no statistically significant differences between these two groups (Fig. 3).

**FIG. 2.** Alterations in plasma levels of adrenomedullin (ADM) after sham operation, cecal ligation and puncture (CLP), or cecal ligation and puncture with pentoxifylline treatment (CLP + PTX). All measurements were performed 20 h after CLP or sham operation. The data are presented as means  $\pm$  SEM and compared by ANOVA and Tukey's test.  $n = 6-8$  animals/group. \* $P < 0.05$  versus Sham group.

source_text:
### 2.5. Survival studies

Survival studies were performed with mice (28–35 g), whose stock originated from the Institute of Cancer Research of National Institute of Health, USA, were purchased from the National Animal Centre (Taipei, Taiwan, R.O.C.). Lipopolysaccharide (60 mg/kg, i.p.) was injected in the presence of vehicle or drugs and survival was monitored every 6 up to 36 h. Different groups of animals received vehicle (saline) together with lipopolysaccharide ( $n = 20$ ) or lipopolysaccharide plus pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, i.p. at 0, 6, 15 and 24 h after lipopolysaccharide,  $n = 20$ ).
...
### 2.7. Statistical analysis

All values in the figures and text are expressed as means  $\pm$  S.E.M. of  $n$  observations, where  $n$  represents the number of animals studied. Statistical evaluation was performed with an analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by a multiple comparison test (Scheffe's test), except for the inducible NO synthase expression which was analysed by unpaired Student's *t*-test. The chi-square test was used for determining the significance of differences in survival rate between control and drug-treated groups. A *P* value less than 0.05 was considered to be statistically significant.
...
Fig. 5. Effects of pentoxifylline (PTF) on the survival rate of mice treated with endotoxin. Depicted are the changes in survival during the experimental period of different groups of ICR mice which received intraperitoneal injection of *E. coli* LPS (60 mg/kg; solid triangles;  $n = 20$ ) or PTF (3 mg/kg; at time 0, 6, 15 and 24 h after LPS,  $n = 20$ ) plus LPS. Data are expressed as percentage of mice surviving at the observed time point.
...
### 3.5. Effects of pentoxifylline on the survival rate of mice treated with lipopolysaccharide

The administration of a high dose (60 mg/kg, i.p.) of lipopolysaccharide to mice was associated with a 36-h survival rate of only 10% of the animals. In contrast, lipopolysaccharide-mice treated with pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, i.p. at 0, 6, 15 and 24 h after lipopolysaccharide,  $n = 20$ ) had a higher survival rate, 35%, at 36 h (Fig. 5).
...
Treatment of conscious mice with a high dose of endotoxin (60 mg/kg, i.p.) resulted in a survival rate of only 10% at 36 h ( $n = 20$ ). However, therapeutic application of pentoxifylline (3 mg/kg, i.p. at 0, 6, 15 and 24 h after lipopolysaccharide) increased the 36-h survival to 35% ( $n = 20$ ).

source_text:
The animals were randomly allocated to 5 groups. Group 1 had CLP. Group 2 was given PTF 1 hour before CLP. Groups 3, 4, and 5 had PTF administered after CLP, at 1, 10, or 16 hours, respectively.

ANOVA showed a significant difference between the study groups for intracellular sodium, potassium, and chloride concentrations (*P* < .001, *P* < .05, and *P* < .001, respectively), but not for intracellular water. The Bonferroni test was used to compare the means of the groups receiving PTF to those of the CLP group, at each time point.

Administration of PTF 1 hour before CLP significantly lowered intracellular sodium at 18 hours (*P* < .001, Bonferroni test) (Fig 1). Giving PTF 1 hour after CLP resulted in a significant decrease in intracellular sodium at 12 and 18 hours (*P* < .001 and *P* < .0001, respectively, Bonferroni test) (Fig 1). In the group given PTF 10 hours after CLP, there was a significant decrease in intracellular sodium at 12 hours (*P* < .001, Bonferroni test) (Fig 1).

source_text:
We studied 24 patients (16 women and 8 men; mean [ ± SD] age, 38±12 years), each of whom had Cushing's syndrome due to a hyperfunctioning adrenocortical adenoma. ... During this two-year period, symptomatic thyroid dysfunction developed in 3 of the 24 patients; they are described in detail in Results. The other 21 patients had no thyroid dysfunction at any time after adrenalectomy.

In 3 of the 24 patients who had Cushing's syndrome due to a hyperfunctioning adrenocortical adenoma, thyroid dysfunction developed after unilateral adrenalectomy. Patient 1 had transient hyperthyroidism, with low uptake of 131I by the thyroid, presumably because of thyroiditis. Patient 2 had permanent hypothyroidism, and in Patient 3 hypothyroidism developed gradually after an initial period of hyperthyroidism.

Patient 1, a 31-year-old woman, had transient hyperthyroidism with low 24-hour uptake of 131I by the thyroid three months after unilateral adrenalectomy (Fig. 1).

Patient 2, a 27-year-old woman, had permanent hypothyroidism after unilateral adrenalectomy. ... After six months she noticed thyroid enlargement and weakness. ...

Patient 3, a 40-year-old woman, had transient hyperthyroidism followed by hypothyroidism after unilateral adrenalectomy (Fig. 2). ... Two and a half months after surgery, she had increased fatigability. ... Her serum T4 and T3 values increased to 192 nmol per liter and 4.8 nmol per liter, respectively, but the 24-hour thyroid uptake of 131I was only 3.2 percent. ... Seventeen months after surgery, she had increased intolerance to cold, constipation, fatigability, and pretibial myxedema and was found to have overt biochemical hypothyroidism (serum levels of T4, 50 nmol per liter; T3, 0.9 nmol per liter; and TSH, 22 mU per liter).

Of the remaining 21 patients with a hyperfunctioning adrenocortical adenoma, 2 had positive antimicrosomal-antibody titers (1:100 in both) and negative antithyroglobulin-antibody titers at first. After surgery, the antimicrosomal-antibody titers for these patients did not change, and their thyroid function remained normal. The remaining 19 patients had no symptoms or signs of thyroid disease, no abnormalities in thyroid-function tests, and no thyroid autoantibodies at any time after the operation.

Figure 1. Transient Hyperthyroidism with Low 24-Hour Thyroid 131I Uptake after Unilateral Adrenalectomy for Cushing's Syndrome Due to an Adrenocortical Adenoma (Patient 1).

Figure 2. Transient Hyperthyroidism Followed by Hypothyroidism after Unilateral Adrenalectomy for Cushing's Syndrome Due to an Adrenocortical Adenoma (Patient 3).
verdict_explanation: Correct that 3/24 developed postoperative thyroid dysfunction and that the other 21/24 had no thyroid dysfunction after adrenalectomy. Timing/phenotype details are partly mismatched: Patient 1 is described at 3 months (not ~2.5 months) with transient hyperthyroidism and low 131I uptake; Patient 2 is described with hypothyroidism after surgery, with onset/details at 6 months; Patient 3 is described at 2.5 months with transient hyperthyroidism and at 17 months with overt hypothyroidism. claim: In this review of BPH/LUTS pharmacotherapy in older men, the authors report that the LUTS-FORTA classification labeled silodosin and tamsulosin as “caution” due to no data on efficacy/safety in older people and risk of hypotension, especially with other anti-hypertensive medications; and labeled alfuzosin, doxazosin, and terazosin as “avoid” due to increased risk for orthostatic hypotension, vasodilatory effects, cardiac arrhythmias, and syncope.
source_text: The Fit fOR The Aged (FORTA) classification, introduced in 2008, is a classification system aimed at helping physicians in the screening process for harmful or inappropriate medications in older patients. Involving over 200 medications and 25 experts, the classification system labels medications from class A to D, with A being “absolutely,” B being “beneficial,” C being “caution,” and D being “do not or avoid” for men over 65 years old based on available research information. The FORTA classification system for medications in older adults studied the various alpha-blockers commercially available and labeled silodosin and tamsulosin as “caution” due to there being no data on efficacy and safety in older people and for their risks of hypotension, especially in the setting of other anti-hypertensive medications. It labeled alfuzosin, doxazosin, and terazosin as “avoid” due to their increased risk for orthostatic hypotension, vasodilatory effects, cardiac arrhythmias, and syncope [15••].
verdict_explanation: Supported: the review reports FORTA meanings (A–D) and states that silodosin and tamsulosin are labeled “caution” (corresponding to Class C), and that alfuzosin, doxazosin, and terazosin are labeled “avoid” (corresponding to Class D), with the stated rationales including hypotension (including orthostatic hypotension) and, for the avoid group, syncope and cardiac arrhythmias. Not supported as written: the candidate claim says the review states that “co-administration of alpha-blockers with antihypertensives increases risk of orthostatic blood pressure drops and syncope.” The source ties the antihypertensive co-medication context to “risks of hypotension” (not explicitly orthostatic hypotension or syncope) for the caution group; and it mentions syncope as part of the avoid group rationale without explicitly linking syncope to co-administration with antihypertensives.
readiness_reason: The repaired claim is directly supported by explicit statements in the provided source text, including medication-specific FORTA category terms (“caution,” “avoid”) and the stated rationales; it avoids the unsupported linkage of antihypertensive co-administration to orthostatic hypotension/syncope.
original_claim: A review of BPH/LUTS pharmacotherapy in older men states that co-administration of alpha-blockers with antihypertensives increases risk of orthostatic blood pressure drops and syncope, and reports FORTA classifications in which non-selective alpha-blockers (alfuzosin, doxazosin, terazosin) are Class D ('Avoid') due to severe orthostatic hypotension/cardiac arrhythmia risks, while selective agents (tamsulosin, silodosin) are Class C ('Caution').

Table 1 values and units (cells/mm²) for total inflammatory cells and eosinophils match the candidate, and Table 1 footnote supports P<0.01 for the day-1 vs day-31 anti-IgE comparisons. However, the candidate adds an unsupported precision for the immediate wheal claim: the paper states no significant (P>0.05) effect on wheal area (immediate reaction) and cites Figures 1 and 2, but Figure 2’s caption does not explicitly state that the 20-minute wheal area on day 30 is non-significant; it only defines a † marker as P = 0.01 without tying it to the 20-minute panel in text. Also, the candidate’s parenthetical 'Day 2–30' is directionally consistent but the text specifies initiation on day 2 and continuation until (2 hours before sedation on) day 30, rather than an explicit inclusive date range phrased as 'Day 2–30'. Finally, the provisional evidence label should not be PRECLINICAL under this schema because the study is an in vivo prospective experimental study in live dogs (a veterinary in vivo study, not in vitro/animal-model preclinical work aimed at humans).
readiness_reason: The Results text explicitly states non-significance (P>0.05) for wheal area for the immediate reaction.
original_claim: Pucheu-Haston et al. (2014) report that in dogs given oral pentoxifylline 20 mg/kg three times daily (60 mg/kg/day) for 29 consecutive days (Day 2–30), 24-hour biopsy inflammatory cell counts decreased from 1819 ± 275.7 to 810.4 ± 71.1 cells/mm² (P<0.01) and eosinophils decreased from 425.5 ± 140.6 to 67.07 ± 21.7 cells/mm² (P<0.01), while the immediate (20 min) wheal area on Day 30 was not significantly reduced vs baseline (P>0.05).

claim: In cured Cushing’s syndrome patients who became severely hypocortisolemic after transsphenoidal surgery, postoperative days 4–5 (vs pre-op) were associated with higher mean±SE plasma IL-6 (1.98±0.44 to 9.38±0.58 pg/mL; P<0.0001) and TNF-α (3.53±1.20 to 5.93±2.12 pg/mL; P<0.02) and higher body temperature (36.74±0.12°C to 37.35±0.15°C; P<0.02 vs pre-op). In the Results text, the authors report that 15 patients had severe hypocortisolism after TSS and that they all experienced anorexia, fatigue, somnolence, and nausea by postoperative day 4, with symptoms ameliorated after the first dose of glucocorticoid replacement; the authors also report that patients without postoperative hypocortisolism (n=3) had no significant elevation of plasma IL-6 and none experienced symptoms compatible with steroid withdrawal syndrome.
source_text:
Fifteen patients had severe hypocortisolism after TSS (morning plasma cortisol, <2 µg/dL). They all experienced anorexia, fatigue, somnolence of variable degree, and nausea by postoperative day 4. These symptoms were ameliorated

after the first dose of glucocorticoid replacement. ...

The body temperature and the plasma inflammatory cytokine values of all patients with severe postoperative hypocortisolism are shown in Table 2. They experienced average temperature elevation of 0.6 C by days 4–5 while they were hypocortisolemic (P < 0.02 vs. baseline); their body temperatures returned to preoperative levels by days 9–10, after they had been placed on hydrocortisone replacement. A 5-fold increase in plasma IL-6 levels was observed by days 4–5 (P < 0.0001 vs. baseline), whereas glucocorticoid replacement resulted in a significant decrease in plasma IL-6 levels (P < 0.0001), although they remained elevated compared to the baseline levels (P < 0.0005). A less dramatic increase in plasma TNF α levels occurred while the patients were hypocortisolemic (P < 0.02 vs. baseline), which persisted when they were on glucocorticoid replacement (P < 0.002). A small increase in the plasma IL-1 β concentration was observed only on days 9–10 (P < 0.02). ...

TABLE 2. Plasma cytokine levels and body temperature in cured patients with Cushing's syndrome

|                      | Pre-op (n = 17) | Postop D 4–5 (n = 15)  | Postop D 9–10 (n = 17) |
|----------------------|--------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| Temperature (C)      | 36.74 ± 0.12       | 37.35 ± 0.15 a | 36.82 ± 0.11              |
| TNF α (pg/mL) | 3.53 ± 1.20        | 5.93 ± 2.12 b  | 5.10 ± 1.54 c  |
| IL-1 β (pg/mL) | 0.16 ± 0.02        | 0.21 ± 0.03               | 0.29 ± 0.07 d  |
| IL-6 (pg/mL)         | 1.98 ± 0.44        | 9.38 ± 0.58 e  | 5.24 ± 0.52 f  |

... a P < 0.02 vs. pre-op and P < 0.004 vs. postop D 9–10.

b P < 0.02 vs. pre-op.

c P < 0.002 vs. pre-op.

d P < 0.02, by Fisher's exact test.

e P < 0.0001 vs. pre-op; P < 0.0001 vs. postop D 9–10.

f P < 0.0005 vs. pre-op. ...

The IL-6 levels in the patients with severe postoperative hypocortisolism are shown in Fig. 1A, and those for the patients without postoperative hypocortisolism are presented in Fig. 1B. There was no significant elevation of plasma IL-6 levels in the absence of hypocortisolism, and none of these patients experienced symptoms compatible with the steroid withdrawal syndrome, including elevation of body temperature (Table 1).
verdict_explanation: Table 2 numeric values, timepoints (Pre-op vs Postop D 4–5 vs Postop D 9–10), and p-values for temperature, IL-6, and TNF-α match the candidate claim. However, the candidate adds unsupported specifics: (1) it says the inflammatory response 'peaked on postoperative days 4–5' for all listed measures; Table 2 shows TNF-α is higher at D4–5 than pre-op, but TNF-α at D9–10 remains elevated (and Table 2 does not label D4–5 as the overall peak for TNF-α), and IL-1β is described as increasing only on days 9–10; (2) it claims 15/15 'hypocortisolemic Cushing’s patients after surgery'—the text supports 15 patients with severe hypocortisolism after TSS and that 'they all experienced' symptoms, but Table 2 is 'cured patients with Cushing's syndrome' with n=17 pre-op and n=15 at D4–5, so equating this strictly to '15/15 hypocortisolemic Cushing’s' is over-specific; (3) it claims non-hypocortisolemic controls had 'no cytokine elevation'—the Results specifically supports 'no significant elevation of plasma IL-6' and no withdrawal-like symptoms, but does not state no elevation for TNF-α or IL-1β in that subgroup; (4) it states 'resolved with hydrocortisone replacement' whereas the Results sentence states symptoms were ameliorated after the first dose of glucocorticoid replacement (and earlier Protocol mentions starting dexamethasone for those meeting hypocortisolism criterion; Table 2 narrative mentions hydrocortisone replacement by days 9–10). Provisional label CLINICAL is appropriate (human patients).

claim: Support is only partially established in Vogel 2023: the paper reports that CRP and IL-6 increase at 1 month after successful surgery for Cushing’s syndrome vs active CS with the stated medians/IQRs and P≤.001; CRP remains significantly elevated vs baseline through 12 months and IL-6 remains significantly increased at 3 and 6 months (subgroup). The paper also reports a relative 24% increase in median platelet counts at 1 month (P≤.001) remaining significantly higher vs baseline through 6 months. At 3 months, CRP is inversely correlated with 12-month normalized grip strength (Spearman −0.371, P=.008) and 12-month SF-36 Physical Component Summary (Spearman −0.356, P=.028), and group definitions include CRP >0.5 mg/dL and IL-6 ≥6.0 pg/mL at 3 months; multivariable regression is reported only for muscle function (not QoL), with the influence of 3-month CRP remaining significant after adjustment for age and BMI (details located in Table S6, not included in the supplied source text). The source does not report a specific ‘peaking around 1 month’ statement nor does the supplied text include Table S4 or Table S6 values.
source_text:
**Abstract – Results:** "One month following surgery, median (interquartile range) C-reactive protein was  $0.48 \text{ mg dL}^{-1}$  (0.14–0.90) vs  $0.10 \text{ mg dL}^{-1}$  (0.06–0.39) during active CS ( $P \leq .001$ ). Similarly, interleukin-6 1 month after surgery was  $7.2 \text{ pg mL}^{-1}$  (3.3–11.7) vs  $1.7 \text{ pg mL}^{-1}$  (1.5–2.5) during active CS ( $P \leq .001$ )." ... "This proinflammatory state lasted until 1 year following surgery." ... "Moreover, inflammatory markers during early remission showed an inverse correlation with long-term muscle function." 

**Results – Remission phase after surgery for CS is characterized by a state of low-grade inflammation:** "In the cohort of 80 patients, early remission 1 month after surgery was characterized by a 4.8-fold increase in CRP concentrations compared with the time of active CS [median CRP 0.48 mg dL<sup>-1</sup> (0.14–0.90) vs 0.10 mg dL<sup>-1</sup> (0.06–0.39),  $P \leq .001$ ]. C-reactive protein levels remained significantly elevated compared with baseline including the 12 months follow-up (Figure 1)." ... "Interleukin-6 levels showed a 4.2-fold increase 1 month after surgery compared with the time point of active CS [median IL-6 7.2 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (3.3–11.7) vs 1.7 pg mL<sup>-1</sup> (1.5–2.5),  $P \leq .001$ ]" ... "Interleukin-6 levels remained significantly increased at 3- and 6-month follow-up visits compared with baseline and matched controls (Figure 2A)."

claim: In a monocentric, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2×2 factorial randomized trial in women with superficial radiation-induced fibrosis (RIF), participants were randomly assigned for 6 months to: (A) pentoxifylline (PTX) 800 mg/day (two 400-mg tablets) plus vitamin E (Vit E) 1,000 U/day (two 500-U capsules), (B) PTX plus placebo capsules, (C) placebo tablets plus Vit E, or (D) placebo tablets and capsules. At 6 months, mean relative RIF surface regression (index 6 months, %) was −60.2 (SD 10.7) in group A versus −42.6 (SD 17.4) in group D, with P = .038 for A vs D (Wilcoxon rank sum test). A two-way ANOVA across the four groups found no significant marginal effects and reported a trend toward an interaction between PTX and Vit E (P = .09).
source_text:
To assess the efficacy and synergism of PTX and Vit E as an antifibrotic treatment in patients with measurable areas of symptomatic chronic radiotherapy damage, we performed the present monocentric, double-blind, randomized clinical trial of combined PTX/Vit E versus placebo. A  $2 \times 2$  factorial design was used to allow testing for drug interactions and the marginal effects of each treatment.

In an individual double-blind design, the 24 women included were randomly assigned, for 6 months, to a combination of 800 mg/d of PTX in two 400-mg tablets and 1,000 U/d of Vit E in two 500-U capsules (group A), PTX and placebo capsules (group B), placebo tablets and Vit E (group C), and placebo tablets and capsules (group D).

For the main treatment comparison (A *v* D) involving the main and secondary end points, we used the Wilcoxon rank sum test. ... Two-way analyses of variance (ANOVA) were performed to test the respective marginal effects of PTX and Vit E and their interactions, resulting in a procedure that involved comparison of the four groups.

At 6 months, we observed a significant mean RIF surface regression of 60% with combined PTX/Vit E in group A, versus 43% for double placebo in group D ( $P = .038$ ). ... Two-way ANOVA for the four groups disclosed no significant effects, though there was a trend toward significance for the effect of PTX and Vit E interaction ( $P = .09$ ).

Table 3. ... Index 6 months, % ... Group A ... Mean -60.2 ... SD 10.7 ... Group D ... Mean -42.6 ... SD 17.4
verdict_explanation: All key elements are supported: monocentric double-blind 2×2 factorial randomization; 6-month duration; doses (PTX 800 mg/day; Vit E 1,000 U/day) and four groups; Table 3 provides the mean and SD for relative surface regression at 6 months (index 6 months, %) as −60.2 (SD 10.7) for PTX/Vit E vs −42.6 (SD 17.4) for double placebo; Primary Analyses reports P = .038 and a two-way ANOVA with no significant effects and an interaction trend P = .09. readiness_reason: Claim components (design, dosing/duration, group arms, outcome definition as index %, group means/SD, and reported P-values including ANOVA interaction trend) are directly supported by verbatim text and Table 3 in the supplied source, with only a minor clarification about the test attribution for P=.038.

claim: Akin, Valent, and Metcalfe (2010) propose MCAS diagnostic criteria requiring: (1) episodic symptoms consistent with mast cell mediator release affecting two or more organ systems; (2) a decrease in frequency or severity, or resolution, of symptoms with anti-mediator therapy (H1 and H2 histamine receptor antagonists, anti-leukotriene medications [cysLT receptor blockers or 5-LO inhibitor], or mast cell stabilizers [cromolyn sodium]); (3) elevation of a validated urinary or serum marker above the patient’s baseline during a symptomatic period on at least two occasions, or (if baseline tryptase is persistently >15 ng) elevation of tryptase above baseline on one occasion; and (4) primary (clonal) and secondary disorders of mast cell activation ruled out.
source_text:
“**We therefore propose** that the diagnosis of MCAS is appropriate when primary and secondary diseases associated with mast cell activation (Table I) are eliminated and if the three additional criteria in Table II are met.

In the proposed diagnostic criteria, patients with a presumptive diagnosis of “MCAS” must have two or more of the organ manifestations of mast cell activation such as flushing, urticaria, diarrhea, wheezing. The diagnosis requires that a patient has evidence of an elevation in mediators such as serum tryptase, 24-hour N-methylhistamine, or 11 β PGF2 during at least two episodes with a negative workup for systemic mastocytosis or clonal mast cell disease in bone marrow biopsies; or one episode in patients whose serum tryptase is consistently > 15 ng/ml (8).” ...

“**Table II**

**Proposed criteria for the diagnosis of mast cell activation syndrome\***

“**1**  Episodic symptoms consistent with mast cell mediator release affecting two or more organ systems evidenced as follows: ...

“**2**  A decrease in the frequency or severity; or resolution of symptoms with anti-mediator therapy: **H1 and H2 histamine receptor antagonists, anti-leukotriene medications (cysLT receptor blockers or 5-LO inhibitor), or mast cell stabilizers (cromolyn sodium)**

“**3**  Evidence of an elevation in a validated urinary or serum marker of mast cell activation: **Documentation of elevation of the marker above the patient's baseline during a symptomatic period on at least two occasions; or if baseline tryptase levels are persistently >15ng, documentation of elevation of the tryptase above baseline on one occasion.** Total serum tryptase is recommended as the markers of choice; less specific (also from basophils) 24 hour urine histamine metabolites, or **11-beta-prostaglandin F2** .

“**4**  **Primary (clonal) and secondary disorders of mast cell activation ruled out (Table I).**”

claim: Gülen (2024) states that to confirm a diagnosis of MCAS, all three diagnostic criteria must be fulfilled: (A) typical, severe, episodic mast cell activation symptoms in ≥2 organ systems (events typically meet the clinical criteria of anaphylaxis); (B) laboratory evidence of an event-related mast-cell activation marker increase, with serum tryptase criterion given as event-related tryptase > (sBT * 1.2 + 2) ng/mL; and (C) a favorable response to mast cell mediator–targeting therapy, including H1- and H2-antihistamines, leukotriene blockers, mast cell stabilizers, and aspirin or NSAIDs.
source_text:
There are three sets of criteria required for an MCAS diagnosis as illustrated in Fig. 1: (1) the presence of typical, severe, episodic MC activation symptoms in  $\geq 2$  organ systems; (2) the detection of a substantial transient increase in a validated marker of MC activation during the symptomatic event; (3) the control of symptoms with MC mediator–targeting drugs.

The clinical criterion of MCAS requires the simultaneous involvement of  $\geq 2$  organ systems [17••, 18••]. Thus, MCAS events typically meet the clinical criteria of anaphylaxis.

To diagnose MCAS, the event-related tryptase should be greater than  $\text{sBT} * 1.2 + 2$  ng/mL to confirm the clinical suspicion of MC activation, i.e., typical clinical symptoms of anaphylaxis are also present [17••, 18••, 19•].

Thirdly, the MCAS diagnosis requires a favorable response to agents that act as MC stabilizers or inhibitors of MC mediators, such as histamine receptor antagonists (H1- and H2-antihistamines), leukotriene blockers, MC stabilizers, and aspirin or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs) [15•, 58, 59•].

**Fig. 1** Diagnostic criteria for mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS). All three criteria must be fulfilled to confirm a diagnosis of MCAS: **A** clinical criterion, **B** laboratory criterion; **C** response criterion.

claim: In adult male Sprague–Dawley rats subjected to superior mesenteric artery (and collateral) occlusion for 20 min followed by 30 min reperfusion, pentoxifylline (50 mg/kg IV, given 10 min before ischemia and 1 min before reperfusion) preserved renal PGE2 release in an ex vivo perfused kidney preparation at levels similar to sham, while untreated ischemia/reperfusion decreased renal PGE2 release at both 15 and 30 min of kidney perfusion; allopurinol pretreatment (10 mg/kg enteral daily for 5 days) did not protect renal PGE2 release.
source_text:
**ABSTRACT.** This study examines the hypothesis that pentoxifylline protects renal PGE2 synthesis during mesenteric ischemia/reperfusion injury. Anesthetized Sprague–Dawley rats (300 g) were subjected to sham or superior mesenteric artery occlusion for 20 min followed by 30 min of reperfusion. The ischemia/reperfusion groups received either enteral allopurinol (10 mg/kg) daily for 5 d prior to ischemia, pentoxifylline (50 mg/kg) 10 min prior to ischemia or carrier. ... Mesenteric ischemia/reperfusion decreased renal PGE2 release by 50% (compared to sham) ... Pentoxifylline pretreatment (not allopurinol) preserved renal PGE2 release at the sham level.

Experimental animals received either enteral allopurinol (n = 8) (29, 30) (10 mg/kg), a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, daily for 5 days prior to mesenteric ischemia or pentoxifylline (n = 10) (50 mg/kg), a phosphodiesterase inhibitor, intravenously, 10 min prior to mesenteric ischemia and 1 min prior to reperfusion. A third group of untreated animals which underwent mesenteric ischemia/reperfusion and were injected with vehicle served as ischemic controls. An additional group (n = 9) served as untreated, nonischemic (sham) controls. ... After 20 min of complete ischemia, the vascular clip was removed from the superior mesenteric artery and the splanchnic bed was reperfused for 30 min.

Basal renal venous effluent was collected after 15 and 30 min of perfusion.

Subjecting the untreated rats to mesenteric ischemia for 20 min followed by reperfusion for 30 min decreased the release of endogenous PGE2 by 65% from the in vitro perfused kidney when compared to the sham group when assayed at both 15 and 30 min of perfusion (p < 0.05) (Fig. 3). In contrast, rats pretreated with pentoxifylline and subjected to mesenteric ischemia followed by reperfusion synthesized and released quantities of renal PGE2 similar to those from sham animals (Fig. 3). Pretreatment of the rats with allopurinol did not protect renal release of PGE2 following severe mesenteric ischemia followed by reperfusion (Fig. 3).

| Minutes of perfusion | Sham  | I/R   | I/R + Allo | I/R + PTX |
|----------------------|-------|-------|------------|-----------|
| 15                   | ~900  | ~300* | ~450       | ~1500     |
| 30                   | ~2250 | ~700* | ~350*      | ~1500     |

**Fig. 3** ... Data is calculated as ng PGE2 released/min of venous effluent collection. Data is reported as mean ± SEM, n = 10, * indicates significance vs PTX and sham groups at p < 0.05 by ANOVA).
verdict_explanation: Correct on the model (SMA occlusion 20 min + reperfusion 30 min), PTX dose and timing (50 mg/kg IV 10 min before ischemia and 1 min before reperfusion), allopurinol regimen (10 mg/kg enteral daily for 5 days), and the direction of effects (I/R lowers renal PGE2; PTX preserves to sham-like; allopurinol does not protect). However, the candidate misstates/overstates several specifics: (1) outcome units: the paper reports Fig. 3 as "ng PGE2 released/min", not pg/min; (2) the sham values in Fig. 3 are not ~1500 at both 15 and 30 min (they are ~900 at 15 min and ~2250 at 30 min in the provided figure rendering); thus PTX is not "sham-equivalent" at those exact numerical levels as written; (3) p-value attribution: Fig. 3 caption specifies * indicates significance vs PTX and sham groups at p < 0.05, not specifically "p<0.05 vs sham" for each comparison, and at 15 min the allopurinol bar is not marked significant in the figure rendering while at 30 min it is marked (*).
readiness_reason: mechanical check: the validator's source_text was not found in the named source file (none); A corrected, source-faithful claim about dosing/timing, model, measurement context (ex vivo perfused kidney; effluent at 15 and 30 min), and qualitative/relative results including the figure-indicated significance pattern is fully supportable from the supplied text; avoid the unsupported unit (pg/min) and the incorrect claim of sham-equivalent numeric values at both timepoints.
original_claim: In adult male Sprague-Dawley rats subjected to splanchnic ischemia/reperfusion (20 min SMA occlusion + 30 min reperfusion), pentoxifylline 50 mg/kg IV (10 min before ischemia and 1 min before reperfusion) fully preserved distant renal PGE2 release at sham-equivalent levels (~1,500 pg/min at 15 min and ~1,500 pg/min at 30 min), whereas untreated I/R reduced renal PGE2 to ~300 pg/min (15 min) and ~700 pg/min (30 min) (p<0.05 vs sham) and allopurinol pretreatment failed to prevent the loss (p<0.05 vs sham).

claim: In male Sprague–Dawley rats, endotoxin (Salmonella typhimurium, 20 mg/kg ip) impaired relaxation of isolated pulmonary artery rings studied 6 hr later; concurrent pentoxifylline (50 mg/kg ip) attenuated the impairment in endothelium-dependent relaxation to ACh (10^-6 M: 86 ± 21 mg remaining tension with PTX+endotoxin vs 216 ± 16 mg with endotoxin alone; P<0.05 vs endotoxin at the same concentration) and attenuated impairment in endothelium-independent relaxation to SNP (10^-6 M: 7 ± 4 mg with PTX+endotoxin vs 54 ± 10 mg with endotoxin alone; P<0.05 vs endotoxin at the same concentration).
source_text:
*Experimental protocol.* Awake, fed rats were administered endotoxin (Salmonella typhimurium, 20 mg/kg ip) that was freshly prepared in 0.9% saline (1 cc). Control rats received an equal volume of saline. A third group received concurrent injections of pentoxifylline (50 mg/kg ip) and endotoxin. Pulmonary vasomotor control mechanisms were studied in isolated pulmonary arterial rings 6 hr after treatment. ...

*Pulmonary vasorelaxation by endothelium-dependent and -independent mechanisms.* ... The optimal resting mechanical tension (passive load) for pulmonary artery rings of this size was determined to be 750 mg in a prior study [5]. Rings were suspended at 750 mg and allowed to reach a steady state for 1 hr, during which time the EBSS was changed every 15 min. A given ring was precontracted with phenylephrine (PE) to achieve a PE-induced ring tension between 200 and 400 mg. Cumulative concentration–response curves were then generated over the concentration range of 10-9 to 10-6 M (ACh, A23187, and SNP). ... Five rats/10 rings were studied in all groups.

Pulmonary artery rings from saline-injected rats were precontracted to 277 ± 15 mg of PE-induced tension and relaxed to 11 ± 4 mg tension with ACh 10-6 M. Rings from endotoxin-treated rats were precontracted to 274 ± 15 mg tension, and 216 ± 16 mg of PE-induced tension remained in response to ACh 10-6 M (P < 0.05 versus control). Rings from PTX plus endotoxin-treated rats were precontracted with PE to 290 ± 18 mg tension with 86 ± 21 mg of tension remaining in response to ACh 10-6 M. ... PTX plus endotoxin-treated rats had significantly less impairment ... than endotoxin (alone)-treated rats (P < 0.05).

As shown in Fig. 3, controls were precontracted to 298 ± 14 mg of PE-induced tension and relaxed to 0 mg tension with SNP 10-6 M. In endotoxin-treated rats precontracted to 299 ± 24 mg tension, 54 ± 10 mg of PE-induced tension remained in response to SNP 10-6 M (P < 0.05 versus control). Rings from PTX plus endotoxin-treated rats were precontracted with PE to 270 ± 16 mg tension with 7 ± 4 mg of tension remaining in response to SNP 10-6 M. Thus, PTX plus endotoxin-treated rats had a response to SNP that was similar to that of controls and less impaired than endotoxin (alone)-treated rats (P < 0.05).

**FIG. 1.** ... Values are means ± SEM (n = 10 rings/5 rats for each group). * P < 0.05 vs control and + P < 0.05 vs endotoxin (alone) at same concentration of agonist.

**FIG. 3.** ... Values are means ± SEM (n = 10 rings/5 rats for each group). * P < 0.05 vs control and +P < 0.05 vs endotoxin (alone) at same concentration of agonist.
verdict_explanation: Supported: species/sex/strain; endotoxin (S. typhimurium) 20 mg/kg ip; concurrent PTX 50 mg/kg ip; rings studied 6 hr later; ring passive load (750 mg); PE precontraction (200–400 mg); n=5 rats/10 rings per group; the ACh and SNP remaining-tension values at 10^-6 M; and that PTX+endotoxin differed from endotoxin alone at P<0.05 (per figure annotations and results narrative). Not fully supported as stated: the candidate’s "restored ... to SNP 10^-6 M" and "NS vs control". source_text:
**ABSTRACT**
"Male Wistar rats (250 g) were submitted to hemorrhagic shock and reperfusion followed by sepsis induced by cecal ligation and puncture. For the initial treatment of shock, rats were randomly divided into: sham, no injury, no treatment; hypertonic saline solution (HS) (7.5%, 4 mL/kg); lactated Ringer's solution (LR, 3 × shed blood volume); HS + PTX (4 mL/kg + 25 mg/kg PTX); and LR + PTX (3 × shed blood volume + 25 mg/kg PTX). After 48 h of being exposed to the double injury, leukocyte–endothelial interactions were assessed by intravital microscopy of the mesentery. Endothelial expression of P-selectin and intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) was evaluated by immunohistochemistry, as well as lung neutrophil infiltration by histology." ... "In contrast, PTX attenuated leukocyte–endothelial interactions, P-selectin and ICAM-1 expression at the mesentery when associated with either LR ( $P < 0.001$ ) or HS ( $P < 0.05$ ). Neutrophil migration into the lungs was similarly reduced by PTX ( $P < 0.05$ )."

**2.2. Hemorrhagic shock/reperfusion and CLP**
"Briefly, male rats were submitted to HSR and 24-h later to CLP, totaling to 48-h of experimental protocol (Fig. 1)." ...
"The animals were randomized into five groups: (1) sham group (only anesthesia, intubation, and catheterization), (2) HS group: HSR with HS 7.5% (4 mL/kg), (3) LR group: HSR with LR (3 × shed blood volume), (4) HSPTX group: HSR with HS and PTX (25 mg/kg), and (5) LRPTX group: HSR with LR and PTX (25 mg/kg)." ...
"After 1 h of maintenance of hemorrhagic shock, fluid resuscitation was performed, followed by reinfusion of 25% the extracted blood" ...

**Fig. 1 – Schematic presentation of the experimental protocol.**
"First, rats were submitted to controlled hemorrhagic shock model for 1 h (mean arterial pressure  $40 \pm 5$  mm Hg), and randomized into four treatment groups: (LR,  $3 \times$  shed blood volume), hypertonic saline solution (HS 7.5%, 4 mL/Kg), (LRPTX,  $3 \times$  shed blood volume + 25 mg/kg PTX), and (HSPTX, 4 mL/Kg + 25 mg/kg PTX)." ... "Twenty four hours after hemorrhagic shock, animals underwent CLP."

**3.2. Mesenteric leukocyte–endothelium interactions and expression of P-selectin and ICAM-1**
"In the sham group, the rollers were 100 ± 13 cells per 10 min, adherent leukocytes were 3 ± 1 cells per 100 µm venule length, and migrated leukocytes were 2 ± 1 cells per 5000 µm\u003csup\u003e2\u003c/sup\u003e of area." ...
"The combination of PTX with LR decreased the number of rollers (44%), adherent and migrated leukocytes (42% for both) as compared with the LR group." ...
"Similar results were observed between the hypertonic saline and pentoxifylline group and the lactated Ringer’s solution and pentoxifylline group in the number of rollers (102 and 115 cells per 10 min, respectively), adherent leukocytes (6 and 7 cells per 100 µm venule length, respectively), and migrated leukocytes (6 and 7 cells and 5000 µm\u003csup\u003e2\u003c/sup\u003e, respectively) (Fig. 3)." ...
"In contrast, the expression of both adhesion molecules decreased in PTX combined treatment groups, HSPTX, and LRPTX. Levels did not differ from the values attained in the sham group, as illustrated in Figure 4."

**Fig. 3 – Number of rolling, adherent, and migrated leukocytes at mesenteric microcirculation after the double injury.**
"Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation for 6–9 animals in each group. \* $P < 0.01$  versus sham; † $P = 0.001$  versus other groups; ‡ $P < 0.05$  versus HS."

**Fig. 4 – Expression of P-selectin and ICAM-1 on mesenteric microvessels.**
"Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation for 20 fields per sample, 2 samples per rat; 3 rats per group. \**P* < 0.001 versus sham; †*P* = 0.001 versus other groups, ‡*P* < 0.05 versus HS."

**3.3. Lung neutrophil infiltration and edema**
"Lung neutrophil infiltration and lung edema index were significantly greater in the animals which underwent hemorrhagic shock and resuscitation followed by CLP as compared with the sham group. The combined treatment of PTX, either with HS or LR, reduced neutrophil infiltration into the lung, as summarized in Table 3."

**Table 3 – Neutrophil infiltration and edema index in the lung parenchyma after the double injury.**
"Sham 0.02 ± 0.03; 3 ± 4" ...
"HS 0.10 ± 0.05*; 11 ± 4*" ...
"LR 0.11 ± 0.06*; 10 ± 5*" ...
"LRPTX 0.11 ± 0.06*; 6 ± 6†" ...
"HSPTX 0.10 ± 0.07*; 6 ± 6†" ...
"\**P* = 0.05 versus sham." ... "†*P* < 0.05 versus other groups."

However, multiple numerical values and p-values in the candidate claim are not found in the source: the text reports sham values and some PTX-group approximate counts (e.g., rollers 102 and 115 cells/10 min; adherent 6 and 7; migrated 6 and 7) plus percentage reductions, but does not provide the candidate’s exact means ± SD comparisons such as "120 ± 16 vs 210 ± 18" or "7 ± 2 vs 17 ± 3". claim: In a normotensive mouse model of endotoxemic acute renal failure using LPS, pentoxifylline (150 mg/kg, intraperitoneal) administered 30 min before LPS improved renal function at 16 h post-LPS in wild-type mice (GFR 105.2 ± 13.3 vs 50.2 ± 6.6 µl/min) and was associated with lower serum TNF-α (0.97 ± 0.55 vs 7.02 ± 2.4 pg/ml) and serum IL-1β (31.3 ± 3.6 vs 53.3 ± 5.9 pg/ml). In eNOS knockout mice given 1.0 mg/kg LPS (ip), pentoxifylline (150 mg/kg ip, 30 min before LPS) improved GFR (119.8 ± 18.0 vs 44.5 ± 16.2 µl/min), increased renal blood flow (0.86 ± 0.08 vs 0.59 ± 0.05 ml/min), and decreased renal vascular resistance (91.0 ± 10.0 vs 178.5 ± 17.0 mmHg·ml−1·min−1).
source_text:
Wild-type mice were injected intraperitoneally (ip) with a 2.5-mg/kg dose of LPS ... eNOS knockout mice were injected ip with a 1.0-mg/kg dose of LPS ... Pentoxifylline was given ip at a dose of 150 mg/kg 30 min before LPS. ... Functional studies were done at 16 h after LPS injection.

In wild-type mice, pentoxifylline protected against the fall in glomerular filtration rate (GFR; 105.2 ± 6.6 vs. 50.2 ± 6.6 µl/min, P < 0.01) at 16 h of LPS administration (2.5 mg/kg ip). This renal protective effect of pentoxifylline was associated with an inhibition of the rise in serum TNF-α (1.00 ± 0.55 vs. 7.02 ± 2.40 pg/ml, P < 0.05) and serum IL-1β (31.3 ± 3.6 vs. 53.3 ± 5.9 pg/ml, P < 0.01) induced by LPS.

The administration of 150 mg/kg pentoxifylline 30 min before LPS significantly decreased serum TNF-α level (0.97 ± 0.55 pg/ml, n = 6 vs. 7.02 ± 2.4 pg/ml, n = 6, P < 0.05; Fig. 1A) as well as IL-1β level (31.3 ± 3.6 pg/ml, n = 8 vs. 53.3 ± 5.9 pg/ml, n = 11, P < 0.01; Fig. 1B).

Effect of pentoxifylline on renal function in wild-type mice during endotoxemia. Sixteen hours after intraperitoneal injection of 2.5 mg/kg LPS caused a significant decrease in GFR in mice as shown in our previous study. Administration of pentoxifylline 150 mg/kg 30 min before LPS injection significantly improved GFR (105.2 ± 13.3 µl/min, n = 7 vs. 50.2 ± 6.6 µl/min, n = 6, P < 0.01; Fig. 4).

Effect of pentoxifylline on renal function in eNOS knockout mice. Sixteen hours after intraperitoneal injection of 1.0 mg/kg LPS caused a significant decrease in GFR in eNOS knockout mice as shown in our previous study. Administration of pentoxifylline 150 mg/kg 30 min before LPS injection significantly improved GFR (119.8 ± 18.0 µl/min, n = 6 vs. 44.5 ± 16.2 µl/min, n = 6, P < 0.05; Fig. 5A). ... RBF increased significantly (0.86 ± 0.08, n = 7 vs. 0.59 ± 0.05 ml/min, n = 7, P < 0.05; Fig. 5C) which led to a marked decrease in renal vascular resistance (RVR; 91.0 ± 10.0 vs. 178.5 ± 17.0 mmHg · ml−1 · min−1, P < 0.05 ).

claim: In this mini-review, the authors state that pentoxifylline (PTX) is orally active with low bioavailability (20–30%) due to extensive first-pass metabolism; has a short half-life of about 1.6 h; and that PTX toxicity was reported at a dose of 80 mg/kg, leading to hypotension, flushing, and convulsion. The review also states PTX indications (peripheral vascular diseases, intermittent claudication, chronic leg ulcers). The review does not state a standard clinical oral dosing range of 400–1,200 mg/day or provide examples such as 400 mg BID or TID in the Pharmacology section/Abstract.
source_text: PTX was in the clinical use since 1972 and approved by Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 1984 (Frampton and Brogden 1995). PTX is indicated in the management of peripheral vascular diseases, arterial disease-induced intermittent claudication, and chronic leg ulcers (Chandan et al. 2018). ... Common side effects of PTX are palpitation, flushing, headache, and arrhythmias (Chandan et al. 2018). PTX is orally active with low bioavailability (20–30%) due to extensive first-pass metabolism (Chandan et al. 2018). PTX has high plasma protein binding and 45% of it binds the erythrocyte membrane, it is metabolized by liver and excreted by renal route (Rasyid et al. 2018). PTX has short half-life about 1.6 h (Rasyid et al. 2018). PTX toxicity was reported at a dose of 80 mg/kg, leading to hypotension, flushing, and convulsion (Dianey et al. 2021).
verdict_explanation: Supported in the Pharmacology section: oral bioavailability (20–30%) attributed to first-pass metabolism; half-life about 1.6 h; and a reported toxicity dose of 80 mg/kg with manifestations (hypotension, flushing, convulsion). Also supported: indications are explicitly listed. Not supported in the supplied source text at the specified locations (and not located elsewhere in the provided text): a 'standard clinical oral dosing of 400–1,200 mg/day (e.g., 400 mg BID or TID)'. The toxicity statement does not specify species, route, or whether this is acute vs chronic; the candidate added those details ('acute dose' and 'severe manifestations') beyond the review's wording. The half-life statement does not specify whether it refers to parent PTX vs metabolites.
readiness_reason: The candidate claim is compound and includes an unsupported dosing-range subclaim, and it adds unsupported qualifiers about the toxicity context (acute/severe; human vs animal; route) and about whether half-life pertains to parent drug vs metabolites. A witness-ready FRD should be split to retain only the supported pharmacokinetic/toxicity statements (with no added context) and separately note that dosing-range information is not found in this source.
original_claim: A narrative review reports standard clinical oral pentoxifylline dosing of 400–1,200 mg/day (e.g., 400 mg BID or TID) and states that pentoxifylline toxicity is reported at an acute dose of 80 mg/kg with severe manifestations including hypotension, flushing, and convulsions; it also reports low oral bioavailability (20%–30%) due to first-pass metabolism and an elimination half-life of about 1.6 hours.

source_text:
Patients received pentoxifylline (1 mg/kg of body weight per hour; maximum, 1800 mg/d) during 28 days or until they were discharged from the intensive care unit or died.

Pentoxifylline concentrations were measured by gas-liquid chromatography described by Bryce and Burrows27 with a detection limit of 3 ng/mL.

The median serum concentration of pentoxifylline was 3628 ng/mL on the first day after starting infusion and 1620 ng/mL on day 2; it reached a steady state from day 3 until the end of the 28-day study. A similar pattern was demonstrated for the first metabolite of pentoxifylline (BL 194) with a 1.3- to 2.5-fold higher serum concentration than the parent drug (Figure 5).

Figure 5. Serial median concentration of pentoxifylline (solid squares) and its first metabolite, BL 194 (open squares).

source_text:
**Design:** Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.

**Setting:** Surgical intensive care units at 2 university hospitals.

**Patients:** Fifty-one surgical patients with severe sepsis were randomized to receive pentoxifylline continuously (27 patients) or saline infusion as placebo (24 patients).

**Interventions:** Patients received pentoxifylline (1 mg/kg of body weight per hour; maximum, 1800 mg/d) during 28 days or until they were discharged from the intensive care unit or died.

... No adverse effects of pentoxifylline treatment were observed. The 28-day mortality rate was 30% (8/27) in pentoxifylline-treated patients and 33% (8/24) in the placebo group. Hospital mortality was 41% (11/27) in the pentoxifylline group and 54% (13/24) in the placebo group. The multiple organ dysfunction score decreased in patients receiving pentoxifylline 4 days after diagnosis of sepsis compared with placebo-treated patients; a significant difference was reached on day 14 ( $P < .05$ ; Student  $t$  test, Bonferoni correction). The  $\text{PaO}_2/\text{FIO}_2$  (fraction of inspired oxygen) ratio was significantly improved in pentoxifylline-treated patients on days 14 and 17 ( $P < .05$ ), and the pressure-adjusted heart rate was significantly improved on day 6 ( $P < .05$ ) compared with the placebo group.

...

Fifty-one surgical patients were randomly assigned within 12 hours after diagnosis of sepsis to receive a continuous intravenous infusion of pentoxifylline (Rentyllin, Rentschler, Germany) 1 mg/kg of body weight per hour, to a maximum of 1800 mg/d or normal saline solution as placebo during 28 days or until patients were discharged from the ICU or died.

...

The statistical analysis for normally distributed data was performed with unpaired Student *t* test with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons to test differences between the groups. ... The 28-day and in-hospital survival rates were estimated in each of the treatment groups using the Kaplan-Meier method, and these estimates were compared with the log-rank test.

...

The 28-day mortality rate was 30% (8/27) in patients receiving pentoxifylline and 33% (8/24) in the placebo group. In-hospital mortality was 41% (11/27) in the pentoxifylline group and 54% (13/24) in the placebo group (**Figure 1**). There were no significant differences in the survival curves of the groups (log-rank analysis,  $P=.85$  for 28-day survival and  $P=.43$  for hospital survival). Adverse effects were not reported in any patient.

...

This difference reached significance on day 14 after the diagnosis of sepsis ( $P<.05$ ). The  $\text{PaO}_2/\text{FiO}_2$  ratio as a parameter for pulmonary dysfunction increased from day 7 in patients receiving pentoxifylline compared with patients receiving placebo (**Figure 3**). The difference was statistically significant on days 14 and 17 after the diagnosis of severe sepsis ( $P<.05$ ).

...

**Figure 1.** *Kaplan-Meier 28-day survival (top) and Kaplan-Meier hospital survival (bottom) analysis for all patients assigned to receive pentoxifylline (solid squares) or placebo (open squares). Survival did not differ significantly between patient groups (*P *= .85 for 28-day survival and* P *= .43 for hospital survival).*

...

**Figure 2.** *Serial multiple organ dysfunction (MOD) score according to Marshall<sup>12</sup> from surgical patients with severe sepsis. Asterisk indicates* P*<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline (solid bars) vs patients receiving placebo (shaded bars); Student* t *test with Bonferroni correction. Values are mean±SEM.*

...

**Figure 3.** *Changes in  $\mathrm{PaO_2/FIO_2}$  (fraction of inspired oxygen) ratio from day 1 to day 28 after diagnosis of sepsis. Asterisks indicate* P*<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline (solid squares) vs patients receiving placebo (open squares); Student* t *test with Bonferroni correction. Values are mean±SEM.*

...

The pressure-adjusted heart rate characterizing cardiac function was significantly different on day 6 after diagnosis (*P*<.05) and remained decreased compared with the placebo group (**Figure 4**).

claim: Support is PARTLY established. Roberts et al. (1993) report that in purified human neutrophils, pre-incubation with pentoxifylline (PTX) inhibited FMLP-stimulated superoxide generation (at 10 µM: maximal linear rate 85%* and total 75%* of control; at 100 µM: rate 65%* and total 55%* of control; *p<0.05 vs control), and that 100 µM PTX shortened FMLP burst duration from 177±26 s to 124±14 s (p=0.015, n=5). They also report that PTX did not inhibit TPA-stimulated respiratory burst at 100 µM (and Table/Figure show 1 mM gives 95% of control without an asterisk). In anesthetized cynomolgus monkeys, IV PTX produced plasma levels of 398 and 930 µmol/L at neutrophil nadir, and despite this, GM-CSF still induced a comparable rise in neutrophil CD11b expression; however, the statement that PTX “failed to block GM-CSF-induced leukopenia/margination” is not fully supported because one animal at 400 mg/kg/2 h showed an attenuated fall (to 26% of initial levels) suggesting some amelioration, while the 200 mg/kg/2 h animal showed no effect.
source_text:
“Pre-incubation of purified neutrophils for 15 min with 1 µmol/l PTX did not inhibit either the rate or the total amount of superoxide produced in response to FMLP, whereas concentrations of 5 µmol/l and greater inhibited both these parameters (Fig. 1a).”

“In addition to decreasing the rate of superoxide generation, PTX at concentrations greater than 50 µmol/l significantly shortened the duration of the respiratory burst so that the total amount of superoxide generated was inhibited to a greater extent than the linear rate (Fig. 1a). 50 µmol/l PTX decreased the mean duration of the FMLP-stimulated burst from 156 ± 45 s (mean ± 1 SD) to 125 ± 44 s (p > 0.05, n = 3), 100 µmol/l PTX from 177 ± 26 s to 124 ± 14 s (p = 0.015, n = 5), and 500 µmol/l PTX from 202 ± 14 s to 114 ± 12 s (p = 0.003, n = 7).”

“Fig. 1. a) The effect of PTX on superoxide production by purified neutrophils stimulated by FMLP (1 µmol/l) or TPA (170 nmol/l). Cells were incubated with PTX for 15 min before stimulation. ... The asterisk indicates a significant difference from control at the p < 0.05 level, estimated by Student's t-test.”

| Pentoxifylline Concentration (µM) | Rate FMLP (%) | Total FMLP (%) | Rate TPA (%) |
|-----------------------------------|---------------|----------------|--------------|
| 10                                | 85*           | 75*            | 100          |
| 100                               | 65*           | 55*            | 100          |
| 1000                              | 45*           | 35*            | 95           |

“In contrast to stimulation via FMLP, PTX did not inhibit the TPA-stimulated respiratory burst until much higher concentrations of 5 and 10 mmol/l were used (Fig. 1a), indicating that the inhibition of the FMLP response by lower concentrations of pentoxifylline was not due to non-specific toxicity. There was no inhibition of the TPA response by 100 µmol/l PTX, even when the concentration of agonist was reduced to 8.5 nmol/l.”

“Experiments were performed on anesthetized animals which were sacrificed at the end of the experiments. PTX was administered to 3 cynomolgus monkeys as an intravenous infusion in sterile 0.9% saline over 40 min. One animal received 200 mg/kg/2 h and 2 others received 400 mg/kg/2 h. GM-CSF (2 µg/kg) was administered by slow intravenous bolus in sterile saline 15 min after commencing the PTX infusion.”

“Control animals receiving an infusion of saline demonstrated a rapid fall in the peripheral neutrophil count after the administration of GM-CSF to 2.1 ± 0.6% of initial levels (mean ± 1 SE) (Fig. 4a). In the animal receiving 200 mg/kg/2 h there was no effect on the GM-CSF-induced neutropenia, whereas in the animal receiving 400 mg/kg/2 h the count only fell to 26% of initial levels, suggesting some amelioration of GM-CSF-induced margination.”

“The PTX levels at the time of the neutrophil nadir in the 2 animals were 398 µmol/l and 930 µmol/l, respectively. In spite of this, both animals that received PTX demonstrated a rise in the neutrophil surface expression of CD11b following GM-CSF, which was comparable to that of control animals (Fig. 4b).”
verdict_explanation: The purified human neutrophil FMLP superoxide % of control values at 10 µM (rate 85%, total 75%) and 100 µM (rate 65%, total 55%) with p<0.05 (asterisk) are supported, as is the 100 µM burst duration change (177±26 s to 124±14 s, p=0.015, n=5). The non-inhibition of TPA/TPA(PMA)-stimulated burst at 100 µM is explicitly supported; the “95% of control, NS” at 1 mM is consistent with the table (95 without asterisk) but the source does not print “NS” (it only explains that * indicates p<0.05). The primate system (anesthetized cynomolgus monkeys; n=3; dosing 200 mg/kg/2 h and 400 mg/kg/2 h; GM-CSF 2 µg/kg) and plasma PTX levels 398 and 930 µmol/L are supported, and the lack of blockade of GM-CSF-induced CD11b upregulation is supported. However, the claim that PTX “failed to block GM-CSF-induced leukopenia/margination” is overstated because one high-dose animal showed attenuation of the neutrophil fall (to 26% of initial) and authors note this suggests some amelioration; thus complete failure to block margination/leukopenia is not fully supported as worded.
readiness_reason: Compound claim includes at least one overstated element (unequivocal failure to block GM-CSF-induced leukopenia/margination) and an unsupported qualifier (“NS”) that is not explicitly stated in the source; needs splitting and tightening to match exact source wording.

claim: Unestablished as written as a single combined claim; the INTRODUCTION of Rademakers et al. (2016) reports long-term follow-up comparisons and within-TURP-group pre-op vs long-term follow-up null findings in men with detrusor underactivity, and reports specific between-group BOOI, PVR, and voiding efficiency results (with some values needing corrected direction).
source_text:
After a minimum follow-up of 10 years (mean follow-up of  $14.5 \pm 3.2$  years in men with TURP and  $13.6 \pm 3.3$  years in untreated men), patients with TURP did not show any significant LUTS improvement compared with the preoperative situation and, additionally, no significant change of maximum urinary flow rate ( $Q_{\max}$ ), PVR, voiding efficiency or any other voiding parameter, bladder contractility index ( $BCI = P_{\det, q_{\max}} + 5Q_{\max}$ ) included. Compared with untreated patients with detrusor underactivity, men with TURP had no significant advantages in the long term with regard to the type

or amount of LUTS,  $Q_{\max}$ , or PVR. Although patients with TURP had a significantly lower BOO-grade at follow-up [bladder outlet obstruction index (BOOI)  $9 \pm 11.9$  vs.  $14 \pm 15.3$  cm H<sub>2</sub>O,  $P = 0.008$ ], PVR was even significantly higher ( $80 \pm 172$  vs.  $217 \pm 336$  ml,  $P = 0.049$ ), voiding efficiency significantly lower ( $82 \pm 28$  vs.  $58 \pm 29\%$ ), and more patients suffered from chronic urinary retention.
verdict_explanation: Design/population and duration: supported in the INTRODUCTION (minimum 10 years; mean 14.5±3.2 years TURP; 13.6±3.3 years untreated). Between-group BOOI: supported with exact values and P=0.008. Voiding efficiency: supported as significantly lower with the stated means, but the candidate’s direction matches (58±29% vs 82±28%) only if interpreted as TURP vs untreated; the source lists “82±28 vs. 58±29%” without explicitly restating which group comes first in that clause. PVR: the candidate states TURP higher (217±336) vs untreated (80±172); however the source text prints “PVR was even significantly higher (80±172 vs. 217±336 ml, P=0.049)”, which conflicts with the candidate’s ordering; thus the candidate is not fully supported as written for PVR direction/assignment. Null findings vs baseline (no significant LUTS improvement; no significant change in Qmax, PVR, voiding efficiency, or any other voiding parameter including BCI): supported. The source does not provide a P-value for the voiding efficiency difference nor the candidate’s “P<0.05” for voiding efficiency; therefore that part is not supported in this source text.
readiness_reason: As written, the claim contains an unsupported P-value threshold for voiding efficiency (P<0.05 not given) and a mismatch/ambiguity in which group corresponds to the reported PVR means; these must be repaired/split into only what the source text unambiguously supports.

claim: In adult male Sprague–Dawley rats subjected to 20 min superior mesenteric artery (SMA) occlusion followed by 30 min reperfusion, pentoxifylline (50 mg/kg IV) was administered 10 min prior to mesenteric ischemia and 1 min prior to reperfusion. After reperfusion, kidneys were removed and perfused in vitro; renal venous effluent collected after 15 and 30 min of perfusion was assayed for PGE2. In Fig. 3 (units: ng PGE2 released/min), untreated I/R is shown at ~0.3 (15 min) and ~0.7 (30 min), while I/R + PTX is shown at ~1.5 at both 15 and 30 min; the Fig. 3 legend indicates an asterisk denotes significance vs PTX and sham groups at p < 0.05 by ANOVA (i.e., the asterisked groups differ from PTX and sham).

Experimental animals received either enteral allopurinol ( $n = 8$ ) (29, 30) (10 mg/kg), a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, daily for 5 days prior to mesenteric ischemia or pentoxifylline ( $n = 10$ ) (50 mg/kg), a phosphodiesterase inhibitor, intravenously, 10 min prior to mesenteric ischemia and 1 min prior to reperfusion. ... After 20 min of complete ischemia, the vascular clip was removed from the superior mesenteric artery and the splanchnic bed was reperfused for 30 min.

Basal renal venous effluent was collected after 15 and 30 min of perfusion. ... Eicosanoid data is reported as ng eicosanoid released/min of venous effluent collection.

"Subjecting the untreated rats to mesenteric ischemia for 20 min followed by reperfusion for 30 min decreased the release of endogenous PGE2 by 65% from the in vitro perfused kidney when compared to the sham group when assayed at both 15 and 30 min of perfusion ( $p < 0.05$ ) (Fig. 3). In contrast, rats pretreated with pentoxifylline and subjected to mesenteric ischemia followed by reperfusion synthesized and released quantities of renal PGE2 similar to those from sham animals (Fig. 3)."

"Fig. 3  The effect of pentoxifylline on rat renal PGE2 release. ... Kidneys were perfused in vitro and the venous effluent collected after 15 and 30 min of perfusion and assayed for PGE2. verdict_explanation: Dosing/timing and the ischemia/reperfusion model are supported (50 mg/kg IV PTX, 10 min pre-ischemia and 1 min pre-reperfusion; 20 min SMA occlusion + 30 min reperfusion). Statistical direction is also misstated: the Fig. 3 legend defines the asterisk as significance vs PTX and sham groups (p<0.05 by ANOVA), not 'both P<0.05 vs sham' and not explicitly 'PTX different vs untreated I/R' (though the legend implies a difference for asterisked I/R vs PTX).
readiness_reason: As written, the candidate relies on incorrect units (pg/min vs ng/min) and treats approximate figure read-offs as reported means; it also mis-specifies which comparisons the p-values apply to. source_text:
To assess the efficacy and synergism of PTX and Vit E as an antifibrotic treatment in patients with measurable areas of symptomatic chronic radiotherapy damage, we performed the present monocentric, double-blind, randomized clinical trial of combined PTX/Vit E versus placebo. A  $2 \times 2$  factorial design was used to allow testing for drug interactions and the marginal effects of each treatment.

The randomization code was generated by computer ... In an individual double-blind design, the 24 women included were randomly assigned, for 6 months, to a combination of 800 mg/d of PTX in two 400-mg tablets and 1,000 U/d of Vit E in two 500-U capsules (group A), PTX and placebo capsules (group B), placebo tablets and Vit E (group C), and placebo tablets and capsules (group D).

Complete data were available for 22 (92%) of 24 of the eligible participants and 27 RIF areas.

For the main treatment comparison (A *v* D) involving the main and secondary end points, we used the Wilcoxon rank sum test.

At 6 months, we observed a significant mean RIF surface regression of 60% with combined PTX/Vit E in group A, versus 43% for double placebo in group D ( $P = .038$ ). Detailed results are given in Table 3 and Figure 2, and are illustrated in Figure 3. Two-way ANOVA for the four groups disclosed no significant effects, though there was a trend toward significance for the effect of PTX and Vit E interaction ( $P = .09$ ).

source_text:
After treatment discontinuation, mean RIF surface area at 1 year had increased by +40% in the SPE group (rebound) and +8.5% in the LPE group.
...

This fibrotic increase was significantly lower and asymptomatic in the LPE group with (8.5%/yr; 95% CI, 1% to 16%/yr) compared with the SPE group with (40%/yr; 95% CI, 24% to 56%/yr;  $P = .0012$ ). “This randomized, double-blind clinical trial recruited 60 patients with BPH from a single center in 2022. “This randomized clinical trial recruited 60 male patients with BPH from a single center between February 2022 and May 2022.”

“Afterward, 60 out of 75 patients were qualified and randomized with a random sequence generator into two groups: Pentoxifylline (Farabi company, Iran) and tamsulosin (Astellas international company). An equal number of patients received either fixed doses of Pentoxifylline 400 mg/Q8h plus tamsulosin 0.4 mg/day (Intervention Group)17 or tamsulosin 0.4 mg/day with placebo (Control Group) for 12 weeks.”

“Regarding blinding techniques, the placebo and Pentoxifylline were prepared in identical capsules by a third person (pharmacist) in numbered boxes. Hence, all the individuals received two capsules, one tamsulosin and the other contained either PTX or placebo. This study was blinded to both patients and the investigator.”

“Age, year ± SD (min-max) ... Intervention Group ... 61.27 ± 5.11 (50–70) ... Control Group ... 61.87 ± 5.20 (52–70)”

“Out of 75 patients who were recruited into the study, 60 subjects were randomly allocated to the study groups. The intervention group was composed of 30 men treated with PTX + tamsulosin, while the control group was composed of 30 men treated with placebo + tamsulosin for 12 weeks.”

“From the included patients, mild adverse events were observed in 11 patients of the intervention group and 13 patients of the control group, as shown in Table 5.”

“During the study, none of the patients reported any evidence of a severe adverse effect, neither threatening hypotension nor syncope. Vital signs remained almost stable in the participants. Also, none of the subjects experienced any urinary retention episodes. Overall, all the patients continued receiving their allocated medicines, and therapy did not stop for TEAEs (treatment-emergent adverse events).”

claim: Staubach et al. report a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in 51 surgical ICU patients with severe sepsis randomized within 12 hours after diagnosis to continuous IV pentoxifylline 1 mg/kg/hour (maximum 1800 mg/day) (n=27) or saline placebo (n=24), administered for up to 28 days or until ICU discharge or death. Pentoxifylline serum concentrations were measured by gas-liquid chromatography; the median serum pentoxifylline concentration was 3628 ng/mL on day 1 and 1620 ng/mL on day 2, reaching a steady state from day 3 until the end of the 28-day study. The first metabolite (BL 194) showed a similar pattern and had 1.3- to 2.5-fold higher serum concentrations than parent drug. The multiple organ dysfunction score decreased from day 4 in the pentoxifylline group vs placebo and reached a significant difference on day 14 (P<.05; Student t test with Bonferroni correction). PaO2/FIO2 was significantly improved on days 14 and 17 (P<.05; Student t test with Bonferroni correction). Pressure-adjusted heart rate (PAHR) was significantly improved on day 6 (P<.05) and remained decreased compared with placebo. Survival did not differ significantly between groups (log-rank P=.85 for 28-day survival; P=.43 for hospital survival); 28-day mortality was 30% (8/27) vs 33% (8/24) and hospital mortality was 41% (11/27) vs 54% (13/24).
source_text:
**Design:** Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.

**Patients:** Fifty-one surgical patients with severe sepsis were randomized to receive pentoxifylline continuously (27 patients) or saline infusion as placebo (24 patients).

**Interventions:** Patients received pentoxifylline (1 mg/kg of body weight per hour; maximum, 1800 mg/d) during 28 days or until they were discharged from the intensive care unit or died.

... 

Fifty-one surgical patients were randomly assigned within 12 hours after diagnosis of sepsis to receive a continuous intravenous infusion of pentoxifylline (Rentyllin, Rentschler, Germany) 1 mg/kg of body weight per hour, to a maximum of 1800 mg/d or normal saline solution as placebo during 28 days or until patients were discharged from the ICU or died.

... 

Pentoxifylline concentrations were measured by gas-liquid chromatography described by Bryce and Burrows<sup>27</sup> with a detection limit of 3 ng/mL.

... 

The statistical analysis for normally distributed data was performed with unpaired Student *t* test with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons to test differences between the groups. ... The 28-day and in-hospital survival rates were estimated in each of the treatment groups using the Kaplan-Meier method, and these estimates were compared with the log-rank test. Differences were considered significant at  $P < .05$ .

... 

There were no significant differences in the survival curves of the groups (log-rank analysis,  $P=.85$  for 28-day survival and  $P=.43$  for hospital survival).

... 

At baseline, the multiple organ dysfunction score was not different between the groups. From day 4 after the diagnosis of sepsis, the score decreased in patients receiving pentoxifylline compared with placebo-infused patients (**Figure 2**). This difference reached significance on day 14 after the diagnosis of sepsis ( $P<.05$ ). The  $\text{PaO}_2/\text{FiO}_2$  ratio as a parameter for pulmonary dysfunction increased from day 7 in patients receiving pentoxifylline compared with patients receiving placebo (**Figure 3**). The difference was statistically significant on days 14 and 17 after the diagnosis of severe sepsis ( $P<.05$ ).

**Figure 2.** *Serial multiple organ dysfunction (MOD) score according to Marshall<sup>12</sup> from surgical patients with severe sepsis. Asterisk indicates* P*<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline (solid bars) vs patients receiving placebo (shaded bars); Student* t *test with Bonferroni correction. Values are mean±SEM.*

**Figure 3.** *Changes in  $\mathrm{PaO_2/FIO_2}$  (fraction of inspired oxygen) ratio from day 1 to day 28 after diagnosis of sepsis. Asterisks indicate* P*<.05 for patients receiving pentoxifylline (solid squares) vs patients receiving placebo (open squares); Student* t *test with Bonferroni correction. Values are mean±SEM.*

... 

The pressure-adjusted heart rate characterizing cardiac function was significantly different on day 6 after diagnosis (*P*<.05) and remained decreased compared with the placebo group (**Figure 4**).

... 

The median serum concentration of pentoxifylline was 3628 ng/mL on the first day after starting infusion and 1620 ng/mL on day 2; it reached a steady state from day 3 until the end of the 28-day study. A similar pattern was demonstrated for the first metabolite of pentoxifylline (BL 194) with a 1.3- to 2.5-fold higher serum concentration than the parent drug (**Figure 5**).

... 

The 28-day mortality rate was 30% (8/27) in patients receiving pentoxifylline and 33% (8/24) in the placebo group. In-hospital mortality was 41% (11/27) in the pentoxifylline group and 54% (13/24) in the placebo group (**Figure 1**).

... 

**Figure 1.** *Kaplan-Meier 28-day survival (top) and Kaplan-Meier hospital survival (bottom) analysis for all patients assigned to receive pentoxifylline (solid squares) or placebo (open squares). Survival did not differ significantly between patient groups (*P *= .85 for 28-day survival and* P *= .43 for hospital survival).*

In contrast, when PTX was administered 1 minute into ischemia or 60 minutes after clamp release, renal function parameters in Table 1 are not marked as significantly different versus the respective controls (only the pretreatment group values are starred as P < .001 vs controls).
source_text:
PTX 100 mg/kg body weight (dosage with reported immunomodulating effects [18,19]) or 0.9% NaCl 1 mL were given subcutaneously either 60 minutes before renal ischemia (groups 1 and 2, respectively), 1 minute into ischemia (groups 3 and 4), or 60 minutes after clamp release (groups 5 and 6). ... Creatinine clearance ( $Cl_{Cr}$ ; mL/min/kg body weight), fractional excretions of sodium ( $FE_{Na}$  [%]) and potassium ( $FE_K$  [%]), and urine protein/ $Cl_{Cr}$  ratio ( $U_{prot}/Cl_{Cr}$  [mg/1 mL  $Cl_{Cr}$ ]) at 48 hours after IRI were compared between PTX-treated animals and respective controls (Mann-Whitney *U* test).

Kidney function was improved in rats given PTX before IRI compared with controls:  $Cl_{Cr}$   $2.10 \pm 0.44$  versus  $1.03 \pm 0.18$ ;  $FE_{Na}$   $0.16 \pm 0.12$  versus  $0.84 \pm 0.55$ ;  $FE_K$   $40.3 \pm 13.0$  versus  $75.5 \pm 17.9$ , respectively (all  $P < .001$ ).

| $FE_{Na}$ (%)                          | 0.16 ± 0.12*               | 0.84 ± 0.55                   | 2.98 ± 2.71              | 3.16 ± 3.05                  | 4.25 ± 3.55                  | 3.80 ± 3.94                  |

verdict_explanation: The model, dose (100 mg/kg SC), timing groups (60 min before ischemia; 1 min into ischemia; 60 min after clamp release), and the 48-hour Table 1 means±SD for creatinine clearance and fractional excretion of sodium match the source; significance for the pretreatment group is supported as P < .001 (Mann-Whitney U). However, the candidate claim adds details not stated in the source text provided: (1) it states creatinine clearance units as mL/min (candidate) and omits the Methods statement that ClCr was expressed per kg body weight (mL/min/kg body weight); Table 1 itself shows mL/min. (2) it claims that the during-ischemia and post-reperfusion groups had 'no statistically significant differences ... (P=NS)' and includes 'electrolyte fractional excretions' broadly; the table/footnote do not report any 'P=NS' values and do not explicitly state non-significance per parameter—only that significance is indicated by a star for P < .001 vs controls and only the pretreatment group is starred. Thus the 'P=NS' phrasing is unsupported and over-specific compared with the source.
readiness_reason: After removing the unsupported 'P=NS' wording and aligning units/timing with the Methods/Table 1 reporting, the remaining claim is directly supported by explicit text and table values including the statistical test and P-threshold definition.
original_claim: In a rat solitary-kidney ischemia-reperfusion model, a single 100 mg/kg subcutaneous dose of pentoxifylline given 60 minutes before ischemia improved creatinine clearance versus control at 48 hours (2.10±0.44 vs 1.03±0.18 mL/min; P<.001) and reduced fractional excretion of sodium (0.16±0.12% vs 0.84±0.55%; P<.001), while dosing 1 minute into ischemia or 60 minutes after reperfusion showed no statistically significant differences versus controls for creatinine clearance and electrolyte fractional excretions (P=NS).

claim: Support is unestablished in this paper for the specific mechanism claim that, in “non-occluded or resuscitated tissue beds,” chronic pentoxifylline maintains microvascular blood flow/restores detrusor wall oxygenation and enhances smooth muscle contractility during micturition (e.g., via cyclic AMP accumulation), thereby supporting long-term oral combination therapy. In the Discussion, the authors instead propose that the combination’s superior clinical effects “may be related” to improved detrusor muscle contractility with pentoxifylline use, citing a rat-model study (ref 14).
source_text:
“Therefore, tamsulosin + Pentoxifylline (a combination therapy) seems more profitable than tamsulosin alone. This positive effect may be related to the fact that detrusor muscle contractility of an obstructed bladder improves with Pentoxifylline use.14 Hence, it makes sense to attribute

the higher improvement of LUTS symptoms to improved bladder contractile strength when using PTX.”
verdict_explanation: The candidate claim attributes multiple specific statements (non-occluded/resuscitated tissue beds; maintaining microvascular blood flow/restoring detrusor wall oxygenation; enhancing smooth muscle contractility “during micturition”; “via cyclic AMP accumulation”; and support for “long-term oral combination therapy”) to the Discussion. In the supplied source, the Discussion only contains a tentative/hypothesis-level linkage: the positive effect “may be related” to improved detrusor contractility with PTX (citing ref 14). It does not mention non-occluded/resuscitated tissue beds, restoration of detrusor wall oxygenation, cyclic AMP accumulation, or chronic/long-term therapy rationale in the manner claimed.
readiness_reason: As written, the claim contains multiple unsupported mechanistic details not present in the source. Only a narrower, qualified mechanism statement about possible improved detrusor contractility (as an explanation for better LUTS outcomes) is supported.
original_claim: The response attributes to the clinical BPH/LUTS paper the mechanism claim that, in non-occluded or resuscitated tissue beds, chronic pentoxifylline maintains microvascular blood flow/restores detrusor wall oxygenation and enhances smooth muscle contractility during micturition (e.g., via cyclic AMP accumulation), supporting long-term oral combination therapy.

citation.locator: Introduction (paragraph beginning “The interpretation of the effects of PTX on phagocyte function are confused...”)

claim: Roberts et al. (1993) state that with oral preparations of pentoxifylline, peak plasma levels are less than 5 μmol/l, and that pentoxifylline is converted to active metabolites but the combined level of all active forms of the drug are unlikely to exceed 10 μmol/l.
source_text: “The interpretation of the effects of PTX on phagocyte function are confused in many cases by the use of PTX in in vitro experiments at much higher concentrations than are obtained clinically. With oral preparations of PTX peak plasma levels are less than 5 μmol/l (6, 21). PTX is converted to active metabolites but the combined level of all active forms of the drug are unlikely to exceed 10 μmol/l.”
verdict_explanation: Supported in substance for: (1) oral preparations having peak plasma levels <5 μmol/l, and (2) combined active forms unlikely to exceed 10 μmol/l. Not supported as written for several added specifics: “standard oral sustained-release” (the source says only “oral preparations”), specifying “parent-drug” (the source does not explicitly distinguish parent vs metabolites in the <5 μmol/l sentence), naming metabolites “(M1, M4, M5)” (not mentioned here), restricting to “during oral therapy” (not stated), and the unit conversion “(~1.4 µg/mL)” (not stated in the source). Evidence label corrected: these are pharmacokinetic statements cited from prior clinical literature, but no trial data are presented here; still, they pertain to clinically obtained plasma levels.
readiness_reason: The candidate claim contains multiple unsupported qualifiers/specifications (sustained-release; parent-drug wording; metabolite names M1/M4/M5; numeric unit conversion; “during oral therapy”). A repaired claim (without those additions) would be suitable.
original_claim: Roberts et al. (1993) state that after standard oral sustained-release pentoxifylline, peak parent-drug plasma levels are <5 µmol/L (~1.4 µg/mL), and that the combined total concentration of parent pentoxifylline plus active metabolites (M1, M4, M5) in plasma is unlikely to exceed 10 µmol/L during oral therapy.
